0.title: How to Behave in the Household of God
0.overview:
The message. First Timothy is a letter from a seasoned apostle to a younger colleague with a hard assignment, as practical and urgent as anything Paul wrote. Its purpose stands at its centre: “I am writing these things to you so that, if I delay, you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth” (3:14–15). Because the church is God’s family and holds up his truth, false teaching must be silenced, worship and leadership ordered, every member cared for, and the pastor must watch his own life and doctrine. Beneath it all lies the gospel of 1:15: “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost.”

Background: the writer. The letter names Paul as its author (1:1). He had urged Timothy to stay at Ephesus while he went on to Macedonia (1:3), and he hoped to return soon (3:14). That journey most likely came after his release from the Roman house arrest with which Acts closes (Acts 28:30–31), and he probably wrote from Macedonia, about AD 62–65, a few years before his final imprisonment and death under Nero.

Timothy. Timothy came from Lystra, “the son of a Jewish woman who was a believer, but his father was a Greek” (Acts 16:1), taught the Scriptures by his mother and grandmother (2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15). He joined Paul on his second journey and became his most trusted helper, Paul’s “true child in the faith” (1:2). He was still young, probably in his thirties (4:12), and often unwell (5:23), but set apart when the elders laid their hands on him (4:14). He was not a bishop of Ephesus in the later sense, but Paul’s delegate, sent with apostolic authority for a time, “Until I come” (4:13), to correct false teaching and see that qualified elders led the church (3:1–7; 5:17–22).

Ephesus and its church. Ephesus, a great port and the leading city of the province of Asia, was proud of its temple of Artemis and famous for magic (Acts 19:19, 23–41). Paul had spent about three years there planting one of the most strategic churches in the Roman East (Acts 19:8–10; 20:31). He had warned its elders that “from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things, to draw away the disciples after them” (Acts 20:30). Now it had happened. The false teachers were insiders who had “made shipwreck of their faith”, and two of them, Hymenaeus and Alexander, Paul had already put out of the church (1:19–20).

What prompted the letter. We see the error only through Paul’s reply. It taught a “different doctrine”, devoted to “myths and endless genealogies” (1:3–4), by men who wanted to be “teachers of the law” without understanding it (1:7). It forbade marriage and certain foods (4:3), bred quarrels about words, treated godliness as “a means of gain” (6:4–5), and prized what Paul calls “falsely called ‘knowledge’” (6:20). Some younger widows, going from house to house, were drawn in (5:13–15). Its exact shape is debated; this commentary takes it to be Jewish speculation about the law joined to a harsh self-denial, perhaps an early form of ideas later developed in Gnosticism, and to a love of money and argument.

Did Paul really write it? Many modern scholars think a later follower wrote the Pastoral Letters (1 and 2 Timothy and Titus) in Paul’s name, pointing to their different vocabulary and style, a church order that looks later, and travels that do not fit Acts. But each letter names Paul as author, the early church received them as his, and their church order is simple: plural elders and deacons, as Paul appointed from his first journey (Acts 14:23; Philippians 1:1). Differences of style suit an older apostle writing to trusted co-workers on new subjects, perhaps with a secretary’s help. The travels fit if Paul was released, as the early church believed, and travelled again, to Macedonia (1:3), Crete (Titus 1:5) and elsewhere, before a final arrest. A false claim to be Paul’s would make it a forgery, which the early church rejected. The more likely conclusion is that Paul wrote it.

How the letter makes its case. Chapter 1 gives Timothy his charge: stop the false teachers, whose use of the law misses its aim, “love that issues from a pure heart and a good conscience and a sincere faith” (1:5). Against them stand “the gospel of the glory of the blessed God” (1:11) and Paul’s own story of mercy (1:12–17). Chapters 2–3 set the household in order. The church prays for all people, kings included, because God “desires all people to be saved” (2:1–7). Men are to pray without anger, women to adorn themselves with good works and learn quietly; the teaching and oversight of the gathered church belong to qualified men, a much-debated instruction that Paul grounds not in local custom but in creation (2:8–15). Overseers and deacons must be of tested character (3:1–13), and the section ends with the letter’s purpose and a hymn to Christ (3:14–16). Chapter 4 answers those who forbid what God made good, since “everything created by God is good” (4:4), and calls Timothy to train himself for godliness: “Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching” (4:16). From 5:1 to 6:2 Paul shows how to treat each member of the family, young and old, widows, elders and slaves. Chapter 6 exposes the teachers’ love of money, for “godliness with contentment is great gain” (6:6), charges Timothy to fight the good fight, tells the rich to be generous (6:17–19) and closes: “O Timothy, guard the deposit entrusted to you” (6:20). The letter’s three “trustworthy sayings” (1:15; 3:1; 4:9) sound like summaries already familiar in the church.

Where it leads: to Christ. The order of the household is never the centre; Christ is. He came to save sinners, and his mercy to Paul displays his patience to all who will believe (1:15–16). He is the only way to God: “there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all” (2:5–6). The truth the church upholds is a person: “Great indeed, we confess, is the mystery of godliness: He was manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory” (3:16). So godliness, a word used here more than in any other New Testament book, is not a set of rules but a life that grows from knowing him. Christ “in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession” (6:13), and Timothy must hold fast to his, looking for Christ’s appearing, which God will display, “the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords” (6:15). The household must be governed well because the God who lives in it is that King.

For us. First Timothy tells the church what it is: not a voluntary association or a religious club, but the family of the living God, set to hold up the truth in a confused world. It tells churches to choose leaders for character, not only gifts, and to care for the needy without excusing families. It tells pastors that their own life and doctrine come first. It frees believers to receive God’s gifts with thanksgiving, and warns that the desire to be rich is a snare. And through the story of a forgiven persecutor it reminds every believer that if Christ saved the foremost of sinners, he can save anyone.

1.title: The Glorious Gospel and the Worst of Sinners
1.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 opens the letter and draws its battle lines. Paul has left Timothy in Ephesus to deal with false teachers, and this chapter gives him his charge, before chapters 2–6 set the household of God in order.

The message. The gospel produces love; false teaching produces only talk. Teachers who use God’s good law for speculation have missed its aim, for the law exists to convict sinners and the gospel exists to save them. Paul himself is the proof: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and if his patience reached the foremost of them, it can reach anyone. So guard that gospel, and fight for it with faith and a clean conscience.

Why it was said. The wolves Paul had warned the Ephesian elders about had arrived, some from inside the church, with myths, genealogies and a confident misuse of the law (see the introduction). Timothy, young and often unwell, was left to stop them, and he needed both authority and courage.

How the chapter makes its case. After a greeting that gives mercy before orders (vv. 1–2), Paul names the problem: speculations that breed argument instead of serving God’s plan (vv. 3–4). The aim of his charge is love from a pure heart, a good conscience and a sincere faith (v. 5), and the teachers swerved from it into empty, confident talk (vv. 6–7). The law is good when used lawfully, to expose the sins its list follows commandment by commandment, and the measure of all teaching is the gospel of the glory of the blessed God (vv. 8–11). Then Paul tells his own story, a persecutor flooded with grace (vv. 12–14), sums it up in a trustworthy saying (v. 15), and breaks into praise (vv. 16–17). Finally he hands the charge to Timothy, with the warning of two men whose faith was shipwrecked (vv. 18–20).

Where it leads. A chapter about false teachers turns out to be a chapter about mercy. At its centre stands Christ, who came into the world for sinners, met his fiercest enemy at full speed on the Damascus road and made him a preacher, and has set that patience on display for every believer since. The only safe guardian of the gospel is a man who knows he needed it more than anyone, and the chapter’s high point is not a rebuke but a doxology to the King of the ages.

For us. Test every teaching by what it grows. Let God’s law show you your sin and send you to Christ. Never think yourself, or anyone else, too far gone for his patience. And keep your conscience clean, because that is where shipwrecks begin.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul writes as Christ’s apostle, under orders, to his true son in the faith, and gives mercy before instructions. His title (v. 1) tells Timothy and the church that what follows carries Christ’s authority, not an old friend’s opinion, and points them to Christ as their hope; his greeting (v. 2) sets grace, mercy and peace from the Father and the Son beneath a hard assignment, before a single problem is named.
verseByVerse.theology:
God Our Saviour, and Mercy Added

These letters call the Father ‘Saviour’, and only the letters to Timothy add ‘mercy’ to grace and peace (see the note on vv. 1–2).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Timothy was young and no fighter by nature (4:12; 2 Timothy 1:7). He needed an apostle’s authority visibly behind him.

Now: On ‘Christ Jesus our hope’ for anyone in a hard post, see the note on vv. 1–2.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope, To Timothy, my true child in the faith: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul writes to his true son in the faith with Christ’s authority, and gives him mercy before he gives him orders.

An apostle of Christ Jesus. An apostle (apostolos) is one sent with authority, carrying the word of the one who sent him. The letter is a father writing to a son, but it is also official: the men Timothy had to correct needed to know that these instructions carried Christ’s authority, not merely an old friend’s opinion.

By command of God. Command (epitagē) is the word used of royal orders. Paul did not volunteer and was not elected; he was commanded. That matters to a young man, probably not a fighter by temperament, left with a job he did not choose. Neither of them is in charge of this church. They are both under orders.

God our Saviour. Here the title is given to the Father, as often in these letters (2:3; 4:10; Titus 1:3): he is Saviour because salvation was his design before the world began, the Son because he accomplished it. It echoes the Old Testament, where the LORD is Israel’s Saviour and there is no other (Isaiah 43:3, 11). And it had an edge in Ephesus, where emperors and Artemis herself were hailed as saviours: Paul gives the title to the living God alone, in a letter read aloud a short walk from her altar.

Christ Jesus our hope. Not our example or our teacher, though he is both: our hope (Colossians 1:27). What we wait for is not first a place or a feeling but him: to see him and to be with him for ever (1 John 3:2). Before he names a single problem, Paul names the direction to look, for anyone left in a hard post they would leave tomorrow if they could. The one who commands is the same one who is coming back.

He is also the reason we can hope. In the Bible hope is not wishful thinking (“I hope it doesn’t rain”) but confident expectation resting on something already done: God has caused us “to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” (1 Peter 1:3). Christ has died, so no condemnation waits (Romans 8:1); he has risen, so death has been beaten in one human body, and ours will follow; he “always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25); and he has promised to come for us (John 14:3). A hope that rests on our progress or circumstances rises and falls with them; this one rests on him, “a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul” (Hebrews 6:19). When your hope sags, do not first check how you are doing. Look again at what he has done, and is still doing.

My true child in the faith. True (gnēsios) means genuine, legitimately born, the real thing as against a counterfeit. Timothy was Paul’s spiritual son, probably converted on Paul’s first visit to Lystra (Acts 14:6–20), and genuinely like his father in faith and service (Philippians 2:20–22). Ephesus was full of men who wanted to be teachers (v. 7); Timothy is the genuine article, and Paul says so publicly, a father’s hand on a nervous son’s shoulder in front of the whole room.

Grace, mercy, and peace. Paul’s letters to churches say grace and peace; mercy (eleos) is added only in the letters to Timothy (see the textual note below). Grace is God’s favour to the undeserving; mercy is his pity on the miserable; peace is the wholeness that follows. Mercy is the right word for a tired minister, whose standing with God is not measured by how well he is coping. God gives it to people who are not coping, and he gives it first, before the instructions.

From God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord. One preposition, “from”, governs both. The Father and Christ are the single source of grace, mercy and peace, which only God gives, so without stopping to argue it Paul places Christ on the side of God, not of creatures. The man who will call himself the foremost of sinners prays to a Saviour who is himself God.

The setting. 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy and Titus are called the Pastoral Letters, because they are written to Paul’s co-workers about leading churches. Paul had left Timothy in Ephesus and Titus in Crete (see the introduction). Timothy was still relatively young (4:12), perhaps timid (2 Timothy 1:7), and often unwell (5:23). The wolves Paul had foretold to the Ephesian elders at Miletus had come (Acts 20:29–30), and some of them were elders of the church.

Did Paul really write this letter? The introduction weighs the question. In brief: the letters claim Paul as author repeatedly and personally (1:12–16; 2 Timothy 4:9–21); the early church received them as his (they are echoed by Polycarp and named as Paul’s by Irenaeus); differences of vocabulary suit new subjects, a later stage of life and perhaps a secretary (possibly Luke, who alone was with him, 2 Timothy 4:11); and a letter with forged personal details, such as the request for a cloak and some parchments, would have been rejected as a deception. We receive them as Paul’s, and as Scripture.

Is this letter for me if I am not a pastor? Yes. It was read to the whole congregation, and most of it concerns them: how they pray, whom they choose as elders and deacons, how they treat widows, older men and younger women, what they do with money. A church member needs to know what sound teaching sounds like, what a faithful elder looks like, and how God wants his household run, because he lives in it. Reading a letter to a minister is also the best way to learn how to pray for one.

How do I find, or become, a spiritual father or mother? Timothy had a mother and grandmother who taught him the Scriptures (2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15), and then Paul. You do not need an apostle. Ask an older believer whose life you respect for an hour: to read the Bible together, to hear how they have walked with Christ, to pray. Most will be surprised and glad. If you are older, do not wait to be asked. Pick one younger believer, of the same sex where the friendship will be close, and begin with a meal, a question about their soul, an open Bible. Paul did not run a programme. He took a young man with him.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add mercy to the greeting of Titus (Titus 1:4) as well; the better reading has it only in the letters to Timothy.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy came from Lystra, the son of a Jewish mother and a Greek father, and joined Paul on his second journey. The letter seems to come from after the events of Acts, probably after Paul’s release from his first Roman imprisonment, in the early to mid 60s AD.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Teaching is judged by what it grows, and the gospel grows love. Paul tells Timothy to stop teachers whose myths and genealogies breed speculation instead of serving God’s plan (vv. 3–4). The aim of his charge is love from a pure heart, a good conscience and a sincere faith (v. 5); these men missed it and wandered into confident, empty talk about the law (vv. 6–7). The law itself is good when used for its purpose, to expose sin, as its list shows commandment by commandment (vv. 8–10), and the measure of all teaching is the gospel of the glory of the blessed God, entrusted to Paul (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology:
What Teaching Is For

The goal (telos) of the whole charge is love (see the note on v. 5), and the law is good when used lawfully (see the note on v. 8).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul judged the Ephesian teaching by what it produced (see the note on vv. 3–4).

Now: The list of sins in vv. 9–10 must be read where Paul put it (see the note on vv. 9–10).

verseByVerse.quote: As I urged you when I was going to Macedonia, remain at Ephesus so that you may charge certain persons not to teach any different doctrine, nor to devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies, which promote speculations rather than the stewardship from God that is by faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy must stay at his hard post and order certain teachers to stop, because their speculations breed argument instead of serving God’s plan, which is received by faith.

No thanksgiving. In most of his letters Paul begins by giving thanks for his readers; here he goes straight to the problem. Of his other letters, only Galatians and Titus so clearly lack one, and in Galatians the gospel itself was being abandoned. Paul loves this church (Acts 20:36–38), but a father who sees a fire in the house does not begin with pleasantries.

Remain at Ephesus. Urged (parakaleō) means pleaded; remain (prosmeinai) means stay on. Paul had asked him face to face, and now he puts the charge in writing, where Timothy can reread it on hard days. This journey to Macedonia is not recorded in Acts, which supports the view that Paul was released after his first imprisonment (see the introduction).

Charge certain persons. To charge (parangellō) is to give an order with authority, a key word in this letter (1:5, 18; 4:11; 6:13). Timothy is not to start a discussion with these men but to tell them to stop. Paul does not name them yet, perhaps hoping they will repent; he names two at the end of the chapter. Some were probably elders of the church itself (Acts 20:30).

Any different doctrine. One compound verb (heterodidaskaleō), found in the New Testament only in this letter: to teach other-ly, to teach a different thing. Not necessarily outright falsehood, but teaching of a different kind from what was handed down (6:3). There is a fixed body of truth, “the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints” (Jude 3), and a teacher’s job is to deliver it, not to improve it.

Myths and endless genealogies. Myths (mythoi) are invented stories; genealogies are lists of ancestry (see “Uncertain wording” below). Paul does not bother to describe the teaching; he judges it by its fruit. “Endless” (aperantos) is the giveaway: never reaching a conclusion. Such subjects make the pursuer feel sophisticated and never require him to do anything. A man can spend twenty years on the names in a genealogy and never once be told to forgive his brother.

Speculations rather than the stewardship. Two words set against each other. Speculations (ekzētēseis) are controversial questions, enquiry that never lands; their fruit was argument and division (6:4–5). Stewardship (oikonomia) is the management of a household, and more widely God’s own plan for running his household and saving his people, received by faith.

A plan with a Head. Paul used the same word when he wrote to this church of “a plan for the fullness of time”, to unite all things in Christ (Ephesians 1:10). God’s plan has a centre, and the centre is Christ. That is why the genealogies were never meant to be endless: in Scripture they run somewhere, and Matthew’s list stops at Jesus, who is called Christ (Matthew 1:16). The false teachers kept the family trees and lost sight of the Son they were written to reach.

What are the myths and genealogies today? Anything that turns the Bible into raw material for a system it does not teach, and keeps people busy without making them holy: date-setting for the Lord’s return, charts that decode the news, hidden numerical codes, conspiracy theories baptised with proof-texts, online controversies whose main fruit is a following, claims about angels, demons or the hidden meaning of names that Scripture never makes. The test is Paul’s: where does it lead? If it leaves you more anxious, superior and argumentative, and no more prayerful, loving or obedient, it is speculation, however clever it sounds.

How do I tell healthy study from speculation? Healthy study stays with what Scripture actually says, reads each passage in its setting, and is content to stop where the Bible stops (Deuteronomy 29:29). It asks the questions the text is answering, makes you know Christ better and love people more, and can be deep and demanding: Paul’s letters are not light reading. But it lands. You close the book with something to believe, to repent of or to do. Speculation never lands, and its favourite questions are the ones God chose not to answer.

Should I stay in a hard church? Paul asked Timothy to stay in a difficult place, a word to those of us who leave too quickly: a church with problems may be exactly where God wants a faithful member. But Timothy stayed to correct error, with an apostle’s authority behind him; this is no rule to stay anywhere at any cost. If the gospel itself has been abandoned and the leaders will not hear correction, or if you or your children are being harmed and the church will not act, leaving is not unfaithfulness. Take counsel from mature believers before you decide, and leave, if you must, without bitterness.

Uncertain wording. What exactly these “myths and endless genealogies” were is not known, because Paul describes the error only by its fruit. It had a Jewish flavour (v. 7; Titus 1:14), and most likely it was elaborate speculation built on the Old Testament family trees and legends; some think it also included speculation about chains of spiritual beings between God and the world, of the kind later developed in Gnosticism.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV (“godly edifying”), read oikodomē, edification, in place of oikonomia; the better reading is stewardship.
verseByVerse.note: Ephesus was the leading city of the province of Asia, where Paul had spent about three years.

verseByVerse.quote: The aim of our charge is love that issues from a pure heart and a good conscience and a sincere faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole point of Paul’s charge is love, flowing from a pure heart, a good conscience and a sincere faith. Sound doctrine exists to produce a certain kind of person, not to win arguments.

The aim of our charge is love. The word for aim is telos: the goal, the point of the whole exercise. Not correct opinions, a settled congregation or the defeat of the opposition, but love (agapē), in sharp contrast with the speculations of verse 4, which produced quarrels. That is a startling thing to write at the head of a letter about to spend six chapters on doctrine and church order. Paul is telling us what doctrine is for, and so how to test it: not merely whether it is true, though it must be, but what it grows, speculation and controversy or people who love.

A pure heart. Love flows from three springs, and each guards against a false kind of love. Pure (katharos) means clean, unmixed; the heart is the centre of the person, thought, desire and will together. Without a pure heart you get love as a performance, done for an audience or for what it returns.

What a pure heart looks like. Pure here means not sinless but undivided. An impure heart loves, but it is also after something: thanks, admiration, control, the feeling of being needed. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8); the “double-minded” are to purify their hearts (James 4:8); David prayed, “unite my heart to fear your name” (Psalm 86:11). This side of glory our motives are never wholly clean, so a pure heart is a direction and a fight, not an achievement. God creates it (Psalm 51:10) and cleanses it by faith (Acts 15:9), chiefly by showing us Christ, until he matters more than what we get from serving. Before you serve, ask quietly, “Who is this for?” And sometimes do good where no one will ever know it was you.

A good conscience. Conscience (syneidēsis) is the faculty that sits in judgment on our own actions. A good conscience does not accuse us, because we have been cleansed by Christ’s blood (Hebrews 9:14) and are walking in obedience. At verse 19 a wrecked conscience is what sinks a man; the false teachers had consciences seared as with a hot iron (4:2). Without a good conscience you get love as compensation: the busy kindness of someone trying to make up for a guilt he will not face.

A sincere faith. Sincere (anypokritos) means without a mask; the hypokritēs was the actor on the Greek stage. Paul uses the same phrase of the faith that lived first in Timothy’s grandmother and mother (2 Timothy 1:5). Without it you get love as religion: the correct behaviour of a person who does not actually trust God.

Real faith and masked faith. Masked faith says the right words while the person underneath leans on something else: money, reputation, their own decency, the approval of family or church, often so long that the mask feels like our face. Real faith is not the same as strong or doubt-free faith; the father who cried, “I believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24) had it. It is faith that rests its weight on Christ, and it shows in what you do when trusting God costs something, where you run when you are afraid, whether you pray when nobody is watching (Matthew 6:6), and what you hold on to after you have failed: your own record, or his blood. Weak faith that is real saves, because Christ saves, not the strength of our grip. The cure for a mask is honesty: tell God what you are really trusting, and ask him to turn you to his Son.

Three springs, one source. The heart is what I want, the conscience how I stand regarding what I have done, faith whom I rely on, and each can fail on its own. Yet all three are God’s gift. He does not only command love; he is love, and he has shown it. The pure heart he asks for, he creates; the good conscience he requires, he cleanses with his Son’s blood; the sincere faith he looks for, he gives. Hebrews joins all three: “let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience” (Hebrews 10:22). Draw near to Christ, and all three springs are refreshed together.

Love with a face. Paul does not leave the word undefined. Ten verses later he names the love this charge exists to reproduce: “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners” (1:15). “By this we know love,” John writes, “that he laid down his life for us” (1 John 3:16). A man whose doctrine of the cross is accurate but who is cold toward people has learned what happened at the cross without learning to love as Christ loved there.

In everyday life. Recall the last theological conversation that grew heated, and test it by the three springs. Did I want God’s glory and the other person’s good, or to win? Was I arguing loudly about one thing to avoid facing another? Was I performing? Then do one thing verse 5 would recognise: write to that person, pray for them, or ask their forgiveness for the tone if not the content.

What it does not mean. It does not mean doctrine is unimportant so long as people love. Love here is the fruit of sound teaching, not a replacement for it: the same chapter will hand two men over to Satan for false teaching.

Deeds, not creeds? Many would gladly keep verse 5 and drop the rest of the letter, since doctrine only divides. But that is a creed of its own, with firm beliefs about God (that he cares mainly about kindness, if he is there at all) and about us (that we can love well without help). History does not bear it out. The sociologist Rodney Stark argued in The Rise of Christianity that when epidemics swept the cities of the Roman Empire, many who could afford to fled, while Christians stayed to nurse the sick because they believed that God had loved them first and that death was not the end. Love that costs that much needs a reason that large. Paul’s doctrine is not a fence around love but its root: “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners” (v. 15).

Does love mean I should never confront false teaching? No. This verse stands in the middle of a command to stop false teachers, and explains it. Error harms people, and love will not stand by while sheep are harmed; the father who lets his child drink poison because correcting him feels unkind does not love him. What love changes is the manner: gently, patiently, without quarrelling, in the hope that God may grant repentance (2 Timothy 2:24–25). And it changes the aim. You are not trying to win; you are trying to heal.

How can I have a good conscience when mine keeps accusing me? A good conscience is not one that has never been guilty but one that has been cleansed. Bring the specific thing to God, confess it plainly, and believe that the blood of Christ purifies our conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:14). Where you have wronged someone, put it right as far as you can. Then refuse to keep paying for what Christ has paid for, and keep your conscience tender by obeying it quickly the next time it speaks.

How to answer the accuser. If the accusation returns after you have confessed, it is no longer your conscience speaking. Conscience, working rightly under God’s Word, is specific: it names a particular thing, leads you to Christ, and points you to something you can do. The accuser is vague and total (“You are hopeless. God must be tired of you”), drags up what has been confessed, and drives you away from God. Do not answer him from your improvement, because you will lose; answer from Christ’s blood. Tell God: I did that, Christ died for exactly that, I have confessed it, and you have promised to be faithful and just to forgive (1 John 1:9). “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies” (Romans 8:33). That is how the saints win: “they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb” (Revelation 12:11). Then do not stay to listen. Thank God, and go and do the next thing he has given you to do.

verseByVerse.quote: Certain persons, by swerving from these, have wandered away into vain discussion, desiring to be teachers of the law, without understanding either what they are saying or the things about which they make confident assertions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some teachers missed love’s target and wandered into empty talk, wanting the standing of teachers of the law without understanding the law they pronounced on.

By swerving from these. To swerve (astocheō) is to miss the mark. The image is an archer, and the target was named in verse 5. These men did not attack the target from outside; they aimed at it and missed, a more uncomfortable diagnosis than malice, because it can happen to anyone who stops checking where he is pointing.

Vain discussion. Wandered away (ektrepō) is used of turning off a road, and in medical writers of a limb wrenched out of joint. Vain discussion (mataiologia) is empty talk: not necessarily false, but empty. Like a dislocated limb, their teaching still moved, but it could no longer bear weight.

Desiring to be teachers of the law. Teachers of the law (nomodidaskaloi) is the word used of the Jewish teachers of the law (Luke 5:17; Acts 5:34). The order of the sentence is the whole diagnosis. First comes the desire to be a teacher; a subject was needed, and the law provided one. These men wanted the standing that comes with teaching and then went looking for something to teach, which is not confined to the first century.

Confident assertions. They do not understand their own words, nor the matters they pronounce on; yet the verb (diabebaioomai) means to insist strongly. Certainty without understanding is the reliable mark of this kind of teacher. Confidence in the truth is not the fault; Paul can say, “I know whom I have believed” (2 Timothy 1:12). But genuine understanding usually makes a person more careful, not less. The more a man truly knows of God, the more often he says, “I do not know.”

The one Teacher. There is one Teacher who never spoke a word he did not understand, and who never sought the standing his teaching earned. The crowds marvelled that he taught as one who had authority, and he used that authority to wash feet and to die for the men who had been listening.

Paul had been this man. Before Damascus, Saul of Tarsus was as confident in the law as any man of his generation (Galatians 1:14; Philippians 3:5–6), and he understood neither what he was saying nor the things he asserted, because the law he taught was pointing to the Christ he was hunting. What cured him was not a better argument but a meeting: the risen Jesus spoke his name. It is still the only cure for certainty without understanding, and it lets Paul write of these men with severity but without contempt.

Is it wrong to want to teach? No: to aspire to oversight is to desire a noble task (3:1). The difference is in what is wanted. One man wants the work: to feed people, to make Christ known, to see a church grow in love. Another wants the platform: to be listened to, quoted, deferred to. You can usually tell which you are by what happens when someone else is asked instead of you, and by whether you will learn before you teach (James 3:1). A good teacher is first a good listener, to Scripture and to wiser people.

How do I know if I am confident without understanding? Three signs. You find it easier to explain why others are wrong than to explain the passage in front of you. You have never seriously read the best case for the view you oppose. And you are rarely heard to say, “I am not sure,” or, “I was wrong about that.” The remedy is not timidity but to sit longer with the text before you speak, to check your reading against the faithful teachers of the church, and to hold firmly what Scripture says plainly and lightly what it does not.

verseByVerse.quote: Now we know that the law is good, if one uses it lawfully,
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s law is good, provided it is used for the purpose he gave it. The fault lay not in the law but in teachers who used it for what it was never meant to do.

The law is good. Paul guards against a misunderstanding: that the problem is the law itself, and the sooner the church is clear of the Old Testament the better. Marcion drew that conclusion in the second century; Paul heads it off at once. The law, here especially its moral commands, is good (kalos): excellent, beautiful, “holy and righteous and good” (Romans 7:12), because it reflects the character of the God who gave it.

If one uses it lawfully. There is a deliberate play in the Greek: nomos used nomimōs. The law must be used as the law itself intends. The false teachers were using it as a source of speculation, or perhaps as a ladder for earning God’s favour; its proper use here is to expose and restrain the sin of the lawless (vv. 9–10).

The remedy for bad use is good use. The instinct when something good is handled badly is to withdraw it, as some churches have done with election, with the law, with the Holy Spirit. Paul does not answer the abuse of the law by abandoning it; he explains what it is for. Good use always costs more effort than avoidance.

Where the lawful use leads. A law used lawfully does not leave a man admiring his own record; it sends him to a Saviour. The commandment that promised life proved to be death to Paul (Romans 7:10), and it drove him to Christ, who is “the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:4): the goal the law was leading to. The false teachers made it a puzzle and so never arrived there.

What it does not mean. Not that we are saved by keeping the law (Galatians 2:16). Justification is acquittal in God’s court: the sinner is pardoned and accepted because Christ’s obedience and death, every commandment kept perfectly and gladly, are counted as ours (Romans 4:5; 2 Corinthians 5:21). Nor is the law bad because it cannot save. The fault lies in us: our sinful nature left the law too weak, and what it could not do, God did by sending his own Son (Romans 8:3).

If I am not under the law, why should I read it? You are not under it as a covenant of works, a way of earning life, but you are still under God, and the law tells you what he loves. A believer reads the commandments as a child reads a letter from his father: not to find out how to be adopted, but to learn how to please the one who already adopted him. Christ fulfilled the law (Matthew 5:17), and the Spirit writes it on our hearts (Jeremiah 31:33). The commandments that once condemned you now describe the family likeness the Spirit is forming in you.

Do I need to keep the food laws, festivals and sacrifices? No. They belonged to the ceremonial law, a shadow of the things to come whose substance belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:16–17). The sacrifices pointed to his one sacrifice and ended when it was offered (Hebrews 10:1–14). The food laws marked Israel off from the nations, and Christ has made the two one (Mark 7:19; Ephesians 2:14–15). You read those chapters to see Christ in them, not to obey them as rules. The moral law is different, grounded in God’s own character and in creation, and repeated throughout the New Testament. The Sabbath commandment needs a word of its own. This commentary holds that its rest is fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 4:9–10), so that Christians gladly set the Lord’s Day apart for worship and rest as a gift, not under rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience on it (Romans 14:5); many godly brothers in the Westminster and 1689 tradition hold it as a continuing Sabbath, and they are to be honoured.

Where Christians differ: what is the place of the law for Christians? Some say the Old Testament law has no role for Christians at all; others make it a way of earning favour with God. Faithful Christians weigh this differently, and some who love the gospel are wary of any talk of law for believers because they fear it breeds legalism. This commentary’s view: The Reformed tradition, following Scripture, speaks of three uses of the moral law. First, it shows us our sin and drives us to Christ (Romans 3:20; Galatians 3:24). Second, it restrains evil in society (the use in view here, vv. 9–10). Third, it guides believers in grateful obedience (Romans 13:8–10; Ephesians 6:2). The ceremonial laws are fulfilled in Christ and no longer binding (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 10:1–14); the civil laws of Israel expired with Israel’s state, though their principles of justice remain instructive. The moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, remains God’s will, but it is never the way of justification.

verseByVerse.quote: understanding this, that the law is not laid down for the just but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and sinners, for the unholy and profane, for those who strike their fathers and mothers, for murderers, the sexually immoral, men who practice homosexuality, enslavers, liars, perjurers, and whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law is aimed at sinners, and Paul’s list of them follows the Ten Commandments, ending with whatever contradicts healthy teaching.

Not laid down for the just. Laid down (keitai) is a legal term: enacted, on the statute book. Paul does not mean a righteous person may ignore God’s commands, but that the law as accuser is not aimed at people already doing what it requires. Those justified in Christ do not live under its condemnation (Romans 8:1), though they delight in its moral content (Romans 7:22).

The lawless and disobedient. The list falls into two halves that track the two tables of the Ten Commandments, duties toward God and duties toward neighbour. The first six words come in three pairs describing sin against God: those who reject authority, those without reverence for God, and those who treat sacred things as common.

Who strike their fathers. Now the second table, in the order of the commandments. Those who strike their fathers and mothers break the fifth commandment at its most violent extreme (Exodus 21:15; see “Uncertain wording” below). Murderers follow: the sixth.

Men who practice homosexuality. The seventh commandment, broadened to all sexual sin. The sexually immoral (pornoi) are those who engage in any sexual relations outside marriage. Men who practise homosexuality translates arsenokoitai, a compound of male and bed, which Paul may have coined from the Greek translation of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13: arsenos koitēn, a male bed. It refers to same-sex sexual acts, not only to exploitative forms, and the historic Christian reading should be stated plainly rather than hidden or softened.

Enslavers. The eighth commandment in its most extreme form. Enslavers (andrapodistai) are kidnappers and slave-traders, men who steal human beings to sell them, a crime the law punished with death (Exodus 21:16). The worst theft is to steal not a purse but a person. Writing inside an empire built on slavery, Paul calls slave-trading contrary to sound doctrine, which condemns the Atlantic slave trade too, carried on for three centuries by men professing Christ against the plain words of this verse.

Liars, perjurers. The ninth commandment, false witness. Perjurers (epiorkoi) are those who swear falsely, the lie told under oath where justice depends on the truth.

Sound doctrine. The list gives examples and is not complete: “whatever else”. Sound (hygiainousa, related to our word hygiene), a phrase these letters keep repeating, is a medical word: healthy, wholesome (6:3; 2 Timothy 1:13; Titus 1:9). Paul’s standard for teaching is not merely accuracy but health; false doctrine spreads like gangrene (2 Timothy 2:17). And these sins are contrary not to good manners but to sound doctrine: what a church believes and how its people live cannot be separated.

Where Paul put it. The list must be read where Paul put it, five verses before he calls himself the foremost of sinners. It names whom the law puts on trial, and the answer includes the writer. Any use of verse 10 that leaves the user feeling comfortable has misread the paragraph it sits in.

A list of people Christ came for. Six verses on, the same pen writes that “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners” (1:15), using the very word that stands in this list (v. 9). Every kind of person named here is the kind the Son of God came for. The law charges the lawless so that the gospel can declare them not guilty, and it can do so only because Christ became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). He kept every one of these commandments: he honoured his mother from the cross, gave life and took none, was pure, stole nothing and gave everything, never once lied. And the man who was all the law requires was numbered with the lawless, so that the lawless who trust him could be numbered with the just.

What if I am a Christian who experiences same-sex attraction? Then you are not in this list for your temptations; you are in Christ, and the list is about practice. Being tempted is not sin: our Lord was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). Your calling is every Christian’s, to say no to sexual sin and yes to Christ, whether in faithful celibacy or, for some, in marriage to someone of the opposite sex. That is costly, and the church must not pretend otherwise. It must be a family to you: open homes, friendships deep enough to carry the weight, no jokes or contempt tolerated. Many faithful believers walk this road, and Christ is not ashamed to call them brothers and sisters.

Did the Bible approve of slavery? Not of the slavery most people picture: the Atlantic trade was the man-stealing this verse condemns. Servitude among Israelites was mostly a way of working off debt, limited in time and protected by law (Exodus 21:2; Deuteronomy 15:12–15; 23:15–16). The law also allowed foreigners to be held permanently (Leviticus 25:44–46), a hard text Christians should not hide: like divorce, it was an institution the law regulated and restrained because of hardness of heart rather than one it created (Matthew 19:8). Paul did not lead a revolt against Roman slavery, which would have been swiftly crushed, but he planted the gospel that dissolved it: masters and slaves equal in Christ (Galatians 3:28), a runaway sent back as a beloved brother (Philemon 16), slaves told, on the most likely reading, to gain their freedom if they could (1 Corinthians 7:21). The Christians who fought to end the trade were reading these verses rightly.

Where Christians differ: same-sex relationships. Some argue that Paul condemned only exploitative or abusive practices, such as pederasty, and not loving, committed same-sex relationships. Many who argue this are moved by love for gay friends and family, and the question deserves care. This commentary’s view: The word arsenokoitai comes from the Levitical prohibition, which concerns the act itself, regardless of the relationship. Romans 1:26–27 describes mutual desire, not only exploitation. Scripture consistently teaches that sexual union belongs to the marriage of one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4–6): Jesus roots marriage in creation itself, God making them male and female, not in the customs of a culture. This is held with compassion: same-sex attraction is a real struggle for many, it is not itself the same as acting on it, and all of us stand in this list as sinners. The hope is the same for all: “And such were some of you. But you were washed” (1 Corinthians 6:11).

Uncertain wording. The two words behind “those who strike their fathers and mothers” (patrolōais kai mētrolōais) can mean either father-killers and mother-killers or those who beat their parents; the KJV has “murderers of fathers”, the ESV “strike”. Either way it is the fifth commandment broken at its most violent.
verseByVerse.note: The list follows the order of the Ten Commandments, from the first table (God) to the second (neighbour).

verseByVerse.quote: in accordance with the gospel of the glory of the blessed God with which I have been entrusted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All sound teaching is measured by the gospel, which displays the glory of the supremely happy God and was entrusted to Paul, not invented by him. The law exposes sin; the gospel announces the remedy.

In accordance with the gospel. This is the standard against which the whole chapter has been measuring. What is sound doctrine (v. 10)? Whatever agrees with the gospel.

The gospel of the glory. The KJV renders it the glorious gospel, but literally it is the gospel of the glory: the gospel whose content is God’s glory. And the glory is seen in a face: “the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God” (2 Corinthians 4:4). At the cross you see God’s holiness, which would not overlook sin, and his love, in which he paid for it himself, both at full strength at once (Romans 3:25–26).

The blessed God. A phrase Paul uses only in this letter (here and 6:15). The word is makarios, the word that opens the Beatitudes: happy, supremely fortunate. Applied to God it means he is perfectly and self-sufficiently happy, the Father delighting in the Son and the Son in the Father in the fellowship of the Spirit from all eternity. His joy was full before the first morning of creation, and out of that fullness he sent his Son, not to fill an emptiness in himself but to bring us into the fellowship he had always enjoyed.

Entrusted. The verb is the language of a deposit placed in someone’s keeping, the idea he will press on Timothy: “guard the deposit” (6:20). Paul did not devise this message and does not own it (Galatians 1:11–12), and only someone who knows that can safely correct anybody else’s doctrine. That word is the turning point of the paragraph. Paul has been describing men who wanted to be teachers. Now he remembers that he was made one.

Is it irreverent to call God happy? No; it is Paul’s own word, and it guards against two errors. One pictures God as stern and joyless, so that the Christian life becomes keeping a grim master satisfied. The other pictures him as needy, as if he made us because he was lonely. He is holy and he is happy, and these are not in tension: his joy is joy in what is good. That is why his commands are not burdensome, why his presence is fullness of joy (Psalm 16:11), and why the faithful servant is told to enter into the joy of his master (Matthew 25:21).

verseByVerse.ref: 1:12–17 – Christ Jesus Came to Save Sinners
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If Christ saved Paul, he can save anyone. Paul thanks Christ for taking a blasphemer, persecutor and violent man and making him a servant, by mercy and overflowing grace (vv. 12–14). A trustworthy saying puts the gospel in one sentence: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and Paul is the foremost (v. 15). His conversion was a display of Christ’s patience for all who would believe, and the memory breaks into praise to the King of the ages (vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Present Tense of Verse 15

‘Of whom I am the foremost’, not was (see the note on v. 15).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The persecutor became the pattern (v. 16): Christ's patience with him is the outer limit that no later case exceeds.

Now: The doxology of verse 17 comes from a man remembering his own conversion and unable to finish the sentence without worship.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank him who has given me strength, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he judged me faithful, appointing me to his service, though formerly I was a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent opponent. But I received mercy because I had acted ignorantly in unbelief, and the grace of our Lord overflowed for me with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul thanks Christ, who took a violent persecutor, showed him mercy, flooded him with grace and made him a servant of the gospel. This is the heart of Paul’s answer to the men who wanted to be teachers of the law (v. 7): the most zealous teacher of the law in his generation tells what actually happened to him.

Who has given me strength. The first thing Paul thanks Christ for is strength. The verb (endynamoō) means to put power into. Paul’s ministry was not his own achievement but Christ’s power in him (Philippians 4:13).

He judged me faithful. Not because Paul had earned it; he was a persecutor. The Lord does not find faithful men; by grace he makes them, and then he entrusts them with his work.

Appointing me to his service. Service (diakonia) is ministry, the word from which deacon comes. It was a gracious appointment, given on the Damascus road: “he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name” (Acts 9:15; 26:16).

Formerly a blasphemer. Three words, and they escalate. Blasphemer: he had spoken against the name of Christ, and had tried to force others to do it (Acts 26:11). Persecutor: he had gone house to house dragging off men and women to prison (Acts 8:3). Insolent opponent is hybristēs, related to our word hubris: the violent man who takes pleasure in humiliating people. It is the ugliest of the three, and Paul chose it about himself.

I received mercy. He was shown pity: the verb (eleeō) is passive. He did not find mercy, earn it or ask for it. He was not seeking Christ; he was seeking Christians. Christ did not wait for Saul to soften; he met him at full speed on the road to Damascus, with letters of arrest in his bag.

Ignorantly in unbelief. This is not an excuse; he has just used three brutal words about himself. He thought he was serving God (Acts 26:9; Romans 10:2). The Old Testament made provision for sins committed unwittingly, and none for sins committed “with a high hand”, in open defiance (Numbers 15:27–31). Paul was on the first side of that line: catastrophically wrong, and sincerely so. Not innocent. Reachable. Jesus prayed for his crucifiers in the same terms: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34).

Grace overflowed. Overflowed is an enormous verb: super-abounded (hyperpleonazō). Where his sin had been extreme, grace was more extreme: “where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20).

Faith and love. Faith and love were not what Paul contributed in response; they arrived in the flood. Faith in place of his unbelief; love in place of his violence. Both are found in Christ Jesus: joined to him by faith, as a branch draws its life from the vine, we receive what is his (John 15:4–5). Here is the answer to verse 5, where love from sincere faith was named as the goal. Such love is not produced by teaching alone. It is poured in by grace.

In everyday life. Name the most hostile person you know toward Christ, and pray for more than their restraint: pray that Christ would do to them what he did to Saul. Then thank him, specifically, for what you were when he found you.

What it does not mean. Not that Paul’s ignorance earned God’s mercy. Ignorance is not innocence; Paul still calls himself the foremost of sinners (v. 15). It means only that his sin was not the deliberate, knowing rejection of the Spirit that Jesus calls unforgivable (Mark 3:28–29). The mercy was God’s free choice. His call did not merely invite Saul; it brought him. God spoke, and the dead heart answered (Galatians 1:15–16).

Could I have committed the unforgivable sin? If you are worried that you have, you have not. The sin Jesus warned of (Mark 3:28–30) was committed by men who watched the Spirit’s work in Christ and deliberately called it the devil’s, so hardened that they had no desire to repent. It is a settled, knowing hostility to Christ, not a single dreadful thought, a terrible season of backsliding, or a past as violent as Paul’s. The very fear that you have gone too far is evidence that the Spirit is still at work in you. Paul blasphemed, persecuted and enjoyed hurting people, and he was received. Come to Christ now: he does not cast out anyone who comes (John 6:37).

Can God really use someone with my past? Yes. God did not merely forgive Paul but put him in the front line, among the very people he had hunted. Some offences do have lasting consequences, and roles such as eldership require a good reputation over time (3:2, 7).

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the gospel in one sentence, worth trusting with your whole weight: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and Paul counts himself the worst of them.

The saying is trustworthy. Trustworthy (pistos) is the same word as “faithful” in verse 12. This is the first of five such sayings in the Pastoral Letters (3:1; 4:9; 2 Timothy 2:11; Titus 3:8), and the phrase appears to mark a line already well known in the churches, which Paul now endorses with his apostolic authority.

Full acceptance. Wholehearted reception: not only agreed with but embraced, the way a starving man does not merely agree that bread is nourishing.

Came into the world. He was somewhere else first. In passing, Paul says that Christ existed before he was born (John 1:9), and that he became man: the eternal Son did not stop being God, but took a real human body and soul, so that one person is truly God and truly man (John 1:14; Philippians 2:6–7). He walked into a world of sinners, not to inspect them but to save them.

To save sinners. Not merely to teach or to set an example, but to rescue from sin and its penalty (Matthew 1:21; Luke 19:10). And sinners: not the promising, not the religious, not the nearly good (Mark 2:17). The only qualification is the one thing everyone has.

What it means to be a sinner. Most people hear the word as a label for someone else. In the Bible sin is first not a broken rule but a broken relationship: “Against you, you only, have I sinned” (Psalm 51:4), the heart turning from God to lean its whole weight on something else. Timothy Keller, drawing on Kierkegaard in The Reason for God, described sin as trying to build your identity, worth and security on anything other than God. That is how Paul can call himself the foremost of sinners after years of blameless law-keeping (Philippians 3:6): his religious record was what he had built on, and it made him a persecutor. You can sin by breaking the rules, and by keeping them so as to need no Saviour. Christ came for both, and “gave himself for our sins to deliver us” (Galatians 1:4), so that the heart can rest on him at last. See Sin in the Theological Dictionary.

The foremost. Then Paul adds words of his own. Foremost (prōtos) is first, chief, worst. And the tense is the thing: not “I was”, but “I am”. Decades into his apostleship, this is still his settled estimate of himself. Mature believers see their sin more clearly, not less: over the years Paul called himself “the least of the apostles” (1 Corinthians 15:9), then “the very least of all the saints” (Ephesians 3:8), and now the foremost of sinners.

Nearness to light. This is not humility put on for show, nor a measured claim to be the worst man who ever lived. The nearer a man comes to the light, the more dust he sees on himself. John Bunyan took the title of his spiritual autobiography from this verse: Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners. And John Newton, the slave-ship captain who became a minister of the gospel, is remembered as saying near the end of his life that his memory was nearly gone, but he remembered two things: that he was a great sinner, and that Christ was a great Saviour.

How Paul uses it. Paul is about to discipline two men (v. 20), and he does it from this position. A man who genuinely considers himself the foremost sinner in the room can correct other people without contempt.

In everyday life. When you next find yourself despising someone, the political opponent, the neighbour, the church member who has failed publicly, or catch yourself defending your record before God or anyone, say this verse under your breath with your own name in it. It changes the tone of what you say next. And if you carry a sin you think too heavy for this verse, read it again: it does not say that Christ came to save sinners, except the worst. The man who called himself the worst wrote it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Christ came to save every person, so that all will be saved in the end; he came to save sinners, and those he came to save he actually saves (Matthew 1:21; John 10:11, 27–29).

Isn’t it unhealthy to call myself the worst of sinners? Not when it is said the way Paul says it, in the same breath as “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners”. Self-hatred looks at sin and stops there, ending in despair or self-punishment. Paul looks at his sin in order to look at his Saviour, and it ends in a doxology two verses later. Nor is it a false humility that refuses to see God’s work in you: Paul also says he worked harder than all the apostles, though it was not he but the grace of God (1 Corinthians 15:10). The healthy Christian holds both: I am a great sinner, and I am greatly loved. Each truth keeps the other from going wrong.

What if I do not feel that bad? The question is not how you compare with Paul, but how you stand before God. A respectable sinner is still a sinner, and the danger of feeling “not that bad” is that you never come to Christ as one who needs saving. Paul’s first opinion of himself was that he was blameless (Philippians 3:6); that was his worst condition, not his best. The door of this verse is marked “Sinners”, and the only people who cannot go through it are those who think the sign does not apply to them.
verseByVerse.note: The first of five “trustworthy sayings” in the Pastoral Letters.

verseByVerse.quote: But I received mercy for this reason, that in me, as the foremost, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life. To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ saved the worst sinner on purpose, to show every future believer how far his patience reaches, and the memory makes Paul burst into praise. God had a reason for choosing such an enemy, and the reason was you.

His perfect patience. Perfect patience (tēn hapasan makrothymian) is the whole extent of his long-suffering, the slowness to boil that endures provocation. Christ was patient with Saul for the whole time Saul was doing his worst, and that patience gives time for repentance (Romans 2:4).

An example. An example (hypotypōsis) is a pattern, an outline drawn so that others can see the shape of a thing. If Christ’s patience stretched to a man who hunted his people and tried to make them curse his name, nobody who comes after can reasonably say their case is too hard. Whatever sin anyone brings, Christ has already been patient with worse.

Eternal life. Not simply living for ever; in one sense everyone will exist for ever (Matthew 25:46). Eternal life is the life of the age to come, God’s own life shared with us: “And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3). It is above all a relationship, and it does not wait until we die: whoever believes “has passed from death to life” (John 5:24). It begins when someone trusts Christ and is completed at the resurrection. And it comes to “those who were to believe in him”: Saul had zeal, learning and religion, and no life until he met Christ. Paul later calls it “that which is truly life”, and tells Timothy to “take hold” of it (6:12, 19). Take hold of it today by speaking to the God you will spend eternity with.

To the King of the ages. Then the sentence breaks into a doxology, a burst of praise. It springs not from thinking about God in the abstract but from Paul’s memory of his own conversion, a fair test of whether we have understood the gospel or merely learned it. King of the ages: he reigned before the first age began and will reign when the last has ended, and he rules every age between, including this troublesome one in Ephesus, and yours.

Immortal, invisible, the only God. Immortal (aphthartos) is incorruptible, unlike everything else Timothy is dealing with, his own frail body included. Invisible: no one has ever seen God in his essence (John 1:18; 1 Timothy 6:16). That is the difficulty of pastoral work: the one you serve cannot be seen, while the opposition is entirely visible. The only God (Deuteronomy 6:4): in a city whose economy ran on the temple of Artemis, that is not a philosophical statement but a stand.

Forever and ever. Literally “to the ages of the ages”, one of the strongest phrases Greek has for endlessness. And “Amen” means “so be it”. Paul expects the congregation to say it back.

Is it fair that a man like Saul should be forgiven? No, and that is the point: mercy is never fair, or it would not be mercy. But it is not unjust either. God did not pretend Saul’s violence had not happened. Every blow he struck at Christ’s people was a blow at Christ himself (Acts 9:4), and Christ bore the punishment for it on the cross, so that God is just when he forgives (Romans 3:26). The objection often hides the elder brother’s complaint that the prodigal gets a feast he did not earn (Luke 15:28–30). Nobody at that feast earned it. The only people who stay outside are the ones who insist on being paid what they deserve.

What if I was converted quietly as a child? Is my story worth anything? Yes. Paul’s story is the outer limit, set there so that the worst may hope. But a child brought up in the faith and kept from great sins has received just as much mercy, only earlier, before the damage could be done. Being kept is as much grace as being rescued, and your story displays Christ’s patience in a different way: with all the small, stubborn sins of a long ordinary life, and faithfulness through every year of it.

If God is invisible, how can I know him? Because the invisible God has made himself known. The only Son, himself God and at the Father’s side, has made him known (John 1:18). Christ is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15), and whoever has seen him has seen the Father (John 14:9). You meet him in the Scriptures, which testify to Christ, and know him by faith, through the Spirit who opens the eyes of your heart. God’s invisibility is not his absence but his greatness: he is not one more object in the world and cannot be captured in an image, but he has come close in his Son.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add “wise” (“the only wise God”), probably borrowed from Romans 16:27; the earlier reading is “the only God”.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The gospel is a charge to be guarded in a fight, and the fight is lost first in the conscience. Paul hands the charge on to Timothy, reminding him of the prophecies spoken over him, so that he may wage the good warfare with faith and a good conscience (vv. 18–19a). Hymenaeus and Alexander threw conscience away and wrecked their faith, and Paul has put them out of the church in the hope that they will learn not to blaspheme (vv. 19b–20).
verseByVerse.theology:
Which Goes First: Conduct or Doctrine

In verse 19 conscience is thrown away first, and faith is wrecked as a result; and even the severest discipline is meant to restore (see the note on vv. 18–20).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Timothy was to fight by the prophecies once made over him (compare 4:14).

Now: Shipwreck is what happens when a man keeps sailing while ignoring what his conscience tells him about the rocks.

verseByVerse.quote: This charge I entrust to you, Timothy, my child, in accordance with the prophecies previously made about you, that by them you may wage the good warfare, holding faith and a good conscience. By rejecting this, some have made shipwreck of their faith, among whom are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan that they may learn not to blaspheme.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy must fight the good fight by holding on to faith and a good conscience, because men who threw their conscience away have wrecked their faith.

This charge I entrust. Paul returns to where the chapter began. Entrust (paratithēmi) is to deposit with someone for safekeeping. As the gospel was entrusted to Paul (v. 11), he entrusts the charge to Timothy, who must entrust it to faithful men who will be able to teach others also (2 Timothy 2:2).

The prophecies. Spirit-given words of the apostolic age had marked Timothy out for his ministry, probably spoken when the elders laid hands on him (4:14; 2 Timothy 1:6). We are not told what they said, but he is to fight by them, to use them as ammunition on hard days. When a man wonders whether he should be doing this at all, one answer is to remember what was said when he began. Such words belonged to that founding time; today the church recognises a call to ministry by gifts, character and fruit, tested by Scripture (see “Where Christians differ” below).

The good warfare. Wage warfare (strateuomai) is to serve as a soldier, a note that will return (6:12; 2 Timothy 2:3–4). Ministry here is not administration but a campaign against an enemy, fought in the strength Christ gives (v. 12). He is the captain of the good warfare, who fought the battle that mattered on the cross and won it.

What the good fight is. It has two fronts. Outwardly, it is the fight to keep the gospel true and pass it on unchanged: “Fight the good fight of the faith” (6:12; compare 2 Timothy 4:7). Inwardly, it is the fight against sin in yourself, holding faith and a good conscience (v. 19), two of the springs of verse 5 and the very things the shipwrecked men threw away. The enemy is not the people around you: “we do not wrestle against flesh and blood” (Ephesians 6:12). It is the devil, the world’s pull and our own sinful desires, and the weapons are the Word, prayer, faith and a clean conscience. It is good because the cause, the captain and the outcome are good. We fight from Christ’s victory, not for it.

Shipwreck. Rejecting (apōtheomai) is deliberately pushing aside, and “this” is the good conscience. Paul, who had been shipwrecked three times (2 Corinthians 11:25), uses a vivid image: they threw their conscience overboard, and their faith broke up on the rocks.

The conscience goes first. The order is one of the most practical things in the chapter. Paul does not describe men who reasoned their way out of Christianity and then began living badly, but men who kept doing what they knew to be wrong, and whose doctrine followed their conduct onto the rocks. Sooner or later, a man who lives wrongly changes his beliefs to excuse his life. Not everyone who leaves the faith takes this road, and honest doubts deserve honest answers; but some who say they lost their faith for intellectual reasons lost their conscience first.

Hymenaeus and Alexander. Two names, after a whole chapter of “certain persons”. Hymenaeus later taught, with Philetus, that the resurrection had already happened, and upset the faith of some (2 Timothy 2:17–18). Alexander may be the coppersmith who did Paul great harm (2 Timothy 4:14), though the name was common.

Handed over to Satan. The phrase is used elsewhere of putting someone outside the church’s fellowship (1 Corinthians 5:5): out of the sphere where God’s people gather under Christ’s protection, and back into the domain of darkness (Colossians 1:13). This is excommunication, the most serious act of church discipline. It is not a sentence to hell.

Learn not to blaspheme. The stated purpose changes how the whole sentence reads. Learn (paideuō) is to be trained, as a child is trained: the aim is to correct, not merely to punish, and life outside the church might bring them to repentance. Blasphemer is what Paul called himself in verse 13, before he received mercy. Their false teaching was blasphemy because it treated the name of the holy God as a common thing, inside his own house. Paul hands them over hoping that what happened to him will happen to them.

A defeated enemy on a short chain. Handing a man over to Satan could only do him good if Satan is not free, and he is not. At the cross Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities (Colossians 2:15). The devil still prowls, but inside the limits his conqueror sets (2 Corinthians 12:7–9), and even the enemy’s ground can become a school in which Christ teaches a blasphemer to stop.

Not one link was strong in itself. The gospel has come down to us through a long chain of trembling hands, Paul to Timothy, Timothy to faithful men, and on through every century, and not one link was strong in itself. Christ kept it. Even his discipline is mercy, a hand reaching after the wanderer, and the blasphemer who wrote these lines is the proof that it can bring him home.

In everyday life. Is there one thing you have been doing that you know is wrong and have stopped thinking about? That is where shipwrecks start. Name it to God today, at the cross, and if it involves another person, put it right this week. A sin you hate and keep fighting is a different thing: the fight itself is the Spirit’s work, and the conscience that grieves over it is still afloat.

How do I know I am fighting it? Not by never falling, but by never making peace. You are in the fight if you feel the struggle (a dead fish floats with the current; only the living swim against it); if you keep coming back to Christ after you fall; if you refuse to call a known sin “just how I am”; if you keep using his means, the Word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and the church; and if you hold on to the gospel when it costs you. You are drifting when you no longer mind a sin you once grieved over, avoid the Word because it disturbs you, or adjust what you believe to fit how you want to live. Then the way back is short: come to the captain, confess it, and pick up your weapons again.

Were Hymenaeus and Alexander true believers who lost their salvation? Arminian Christians, who hold that a true believer can finally fall away, read “made shipwreck of their faith” that way. The more likely reading is that they held the faith outwardly but never truly trusted Christ; as John says of such people, “if they had been of us, they would have continued with us” (1 John 2:19). Paul’s discipline was meant to bring them to repentance, that they might learn not to blaspheme. The warning is for every believer to hold faith and a good conscience.

What if I am afraid my own faith could be shipwrecked? The fear itself is a good sign; the men in this verse were not afraid but careless. Christ keeps his sheep, and no one will snatch them out of his hand (John 10:28), and he keeps them by means, one of which is this warning. So do what verse 19 says: when your conscience accuses you, do not argue with it or bury it, but take the thing to the cross. Keep near the Word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and the church, and tell a trusted believer when you are drifting. Ships rarely sink in one wave; they take on water slowly, and someone who loves you can see the list before you can.

What does church discipline look like today? It begins quietly, as Jesus taught: a private word, then one or two others, and only then the church (Matthew 18:15–17). Most discipline ends at the first step, with repentance and restoration. Excommunication is the last step, for serious, unrepented sin or persistent false teaching, carried out by the church under its elders, not by individuals. The person is no longer received as a member or at the Lord’s Table. It does not mean hatred or shunning in every form: you may still greet them, and you should pray for them and call them back, warning them as a brother (2 Thessalonians 3:14–15). And it must never be used to silence the victims of abuse or to protect leaders; that is a perversion of it.

Where Christians differ: do prophecies like these continue today? Charismatic and Pentecostal Christians see the prophecies over Timothy as a model for prophetic words in churches today. This commentary’s view: The New Testament prophets belonged to the foundation-laying era of the church, alongside the apostles (Ephesians 2:20), when Scripture was still being given. With the completion of the canon, God guides his church through the sufficient written Word, not through new revelations (Hebrews 1:1–2; Jude 3). This is held charitably: brothers who differ often love Christ deeply, and God still guides through his Word, wise counsel, providence, and the inward witness of the Spirit to Scripture. But no word claiming to be prophecy may add to or stand alongside Scripture.

Uncertain wording. The phrase translated “the prophecies previously made about you” could also mean prophecies that “pointed the way” to Timothy, marking him out for this work. Either way the sense of the verse is the same.
verseByVerse.note: To hand someone “over to Satan” means putting him out of the church, in the hope that he will be brought to repentance.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope,<sup>2</sup>To Timothy, my true child in the faith: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.<sup>3</sup>As I urged you when I was going to Macedonia, remain at Ephesus so that you may charge certain persons not to teach any different doctrine,<sup>4</sup>nor to devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies, which promote speculations rather than the stewardship from God that is by faith.<sup>5</sup>The aim of our charge is love that issues from a pure heart and a good conscience and a sincere faith.<sup>6</sup>Certain persons, by swerving from these, have wandered away into vain discussion,<sup>7</sup>desiring to be teachers of the law, without understanding either what they are saying or the things about which they make confident assertions.<sup>8</sup>Now we know that the law is good, if one uses it lawfully,<sup>9</sup>understanding this, that the law is not laid down for the just but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and sinners, for the unholy and profane, for those who strike their fathers and mothers, for murderers,<sup>10</sup>the sexually immoral, men who practice homosexuality, enslavers, liars, perjurers, and whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine,<sup>11</sup>in accordance with the gospel of the glory of the blessed God with which I have been entrusted.<sup>12</sup>I thank him who has given me strength, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he judged me faithful, appointing me to his service,<sup>13</sup>though formerly I was a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent opponent. But I received mercy because I had acted ignorantly in unbelief,<sup>14</sup>and the grace of our Lord overflowed for me with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.<sup>15</sup>The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost.<sup>16</sup>But I received mercy for this reason, that in me, as the foremost, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life.<sup>17</sup>To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.<sup>18</sup>This charge I entrust to you, Timothy, my child, in accordance with the prophecies previously made about you, that by them you may wage the good warfare,<sup>19</sup>holding faith and a good conscience.
