By rejecting this, some have made shipwreck of their faith,<sup>20</sup>among whom are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan that they may learn not to blaspheme.

keyVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost.
keyVerse.note: This is the gospel the whole chapter guards, and the measure of all teaching (v. 11). It answers the false teachers by turning from speculation to a rescue, and from the law’s list of sinners (vv. 9–10) to the Saviour who came for them. And Paul puts his own name at the head of that list, which is why he can correct others without contempt, and why no reader is beyond hope.

1.reflection:
Paul says the aim of his charge is love from a pure heart, a good conscience and a sincere faith (v. 5). How would our church life, and our conversations about doctrine, change if we measured teaching by what it grows? Which of the three springs is weakest in you?

Verses 9–10 list the sins the law exposes, and verse 15 says Christ came to save sinners, with the writer at their head. Why does that matter? How should it shape the way we speak about people whose sins differ from ours?

Paul calls Christ’s patience with him an example “to those who were to believe in him for eternal life” (v. 16). Whom do you find it hardest to believe Christ could save, yourself included? What does Paul’s story say to that?

Hymenaeus and Alexander rejected a good conscience and made shipwreck of their faith (v. 19). What small compromises let water into a life? What keeps a conscience clean, and who could help you notice the list before you do?

2.title: One Mediator, Many Prayers
2.overview:
Where we are. After Timothy’s charge against the false teachers (chapter 1), Paul begins to set the household of God in order (3:15), starting with the church at worship and going on, in chapter 3, to its leaders.

The message. The church’s prayers must be as wide as God’s saving desire, because there is one God and one mediator, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom. Everything else flows from that single door into God’s presence: men come through it with hands cleansed of anger, women with lives adorned by good works rather than wealth, and the gathered church keeps the order God set at creation, in which its teaching and governing belong to qualified men. A restriction on a role is never a verdict on a person’s worth.

Why it was said. The false teaching at Ephesus (see the introduction) seems to have been narrow towards outsiders and quarrelsome within; it had a hearing among some women and apparently forbade marriage (4:3). A small church under Nero could easily have turned in on itself, praying only for its own and fighting over words.

How the chapter makes its case. Prayer for everyone, rulers included (vv. 1–2), is grounded in God’s heart: he desires all people to be saved (vv. 3–4), has given one mediator who paid the ransom (vv. 5–6), and sent Paul to the Gentiles to prove it (v. 7). Then the assembly: men pray without anger (v. 8); women are adorned with good works, not display (vv. 9–10); women learn, but do not teach or exercise authority over men in the church (vv. 11–12), on grounds taken from creation and the fall, not Ephesian culture (vv. 13–14). A hard promise about childbearing closes the chapter (v. 15).

Where it leads. The centre of the chapter is “the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all” (vv. 5–6): God and man in one person, still bearing our nature before the Father. He prayed for those who crucified him, and he is the last Adam, who did not stand silent when the serpent came for his bride but gave himself up for her. Even the hard last verse turns towards him, the Child born of a woman who crushed the serpent’s head.

For us. Pray for everyone, even those hardest to pray for, because God’s desire is wide and the way to him is open through Christ alone. Come to worship reconciled, and let your life, not your wealth, be what people notice. And read verses 11–15 with the gospel in front of you: in the household of God order serves love, and every member is equally a child at the Father’s table.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The church must pray for everyone, because God’s saving desire reaches everyone and the way to him is open through one mediator. Paul calls for every kind of prayer for every kind of person, rulers included, so that believers may live quiet and godly lives (vv. 1–2). Such prayer pleases God, who desires all people to be saved (vv. 3–4), for there is one God and one mediator, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom (vv. 5–6). Paul’s own commission as teacher of the Gentiles is the proof that God meant it (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology:
‘Desires All People to Be Saved’

Verse 4 has been read as all kinds of people, or as God’s revealed will set beside his decreed will (see the note on vv. 3–4 and its box). Either way there is one mediator, and his ransom is a substitute’s (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Under Nero, the church was told to pray, and give thanks, for kings (v. 2; compare Jeremiah 29:7).

Now: The aim is modest: a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified (see the note on vv. 1–2).

verseByVerse.quote: First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church’s first duty in worship is to pray for everyone, even the rulers who may persecute it. Paul asks for quiet, not power: room for Christians to live godly lives where their neighbours can see them.

First of all. The first item, first in importance, is not strategy against the false teachers but prayer for outsiders. A church that fights error but does not pray for the world has already lost what the narrow-minded false teachers wanted it to lose: its care for outsiders.

Four kinds of prayer. The words overlap. Supplications (deēseis) are requests arising from need; prayers is the general word; intercessions (enteuxeis) was used of bringing a petition before a king on someone’s behalf; and thanksgivings is the surprising one, since those to be given thanks for include Nero. Together they describe not a brief nod to the government before the real business, but the church on its knees, bringing the world before the throne.

For all people, for kings. Because Paul at once names kings, he means all kinds and classes of people, not least those we might leave out. Kings includes the emperor, Nero (AD 54–68); high positions are governors, magistrates and officials. A church in Ephesus is to pray, and give thanks, for the man who would shortly use Christians as living torches in his gardens, and under whom, as the early church remembered, Paul himself would be executed. It matches Romans 13:1 and Jeremiah’s word to the exiles: “seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf” (Jeremiah 29:7). God’s people have usually lived under governments they did not choose, and this is the standing instruction. On leadership and submission in every sphere, see on Ephesians 5:21.

A peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified. Peaceful is free from outward disturbance; quiet is settled within. The aim is modest: not influence for the church but room to worship and for the gospel to spread, a smaller ambition than a modern church often has for its nation, and Paul thought it enough. Godliness (eusebeia), reverent devotion to God shown in life, is a key word of these letters: peace is asked not for comfort but so that Christians can be holy in public, where their neighbours can see it.

The setting. The false teachers seem to have been exclusive and contentious, influential among some women (5:13–15; 2 Timothy 3:6–7), and opposed to marriage (4:3) (see the introduction). The whole chapter answers them: pray for everyone; stop quarrelling; let women learn but not take over the teaching office; honour marriage and motherhood.

Praying for the power that judged him. The church’s Lord stood before a Roman governor, Pontius Pilate (6:13), was condemned by Roman authority and nailed up by Roman soldiers, and he prayed for the men who did it (Luke 23:34). A church that prays for Nero is doing what its Master did. And it prays through him: its intercessions reach God only because there is one mediator (v. 5), who lives for ever to intercede for his people. Our prayers for rulers are heard because he prays for us.

A royal priesthood praying for Nero. The Lord who rules the kings of the earth is never threatened by them. He turned the heart of Cyrus, humbled Nebuchadnezzar, and used a Roman census to bring his Son to Bethlehem. So the church praying for Nero in a house in Ephesus was not a frightened minority pleading for its life but a royal priesthood interceding for the world, under a King whose kingdom no emperor could touch.

In everyday life. Pray today, by name, for your head of state, your local leaders, and one public figure you find hard to like. Pray for their good and their salvation, and thank God for one specific good thing that has come through them.

What do I actually pray for a ruler I think is wicked? Pray what Paul prays. For their salvation first: Nero was beyond the church’s reach but not beyond God’s, and the prayer that a persecutor might be converted was answered spectacularly in Paul himself. For wisdom and justice in their decisions; for restraint on their evil and protection for the weak who suffer under it; for peace, so that the church can worship and the gospel can run. And give thanks for whatever good they do, and for the order even a bad government preserves. You can pray all this without pretending to admire them.

Does praying for rulers mean I must never oppose them? No. Praying for a ruler is not agreeing with him. Christians may vote, campaign, protest lawfully and speak out against injustice, as the prophets confronted kings and Paul appealed to Caesar for his rights (Acts 25:11); where a ruler commands what God forbids, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). But prayer changes the spirit in which we do it. It is very hard to hate a man you have prayed for by name every week, and very hard to put your hope in politics once you have spent time before the King of the ages.
verseByVerse.note: Christians were to pray for rulers such as Nero, under whom they would later suffer.

parallels.desc: seek the welfare of the city

verseByVerse.quote: This is good, and it is pleasing in the sight of God our Savior, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s saving desire reaches all kinds of people, so the church’s prayers must reach that far too. Praying for everyone pleases God because it matches his own heart.

Who desires all people to be saved. All people is the phrase of verse 1. God is not grudging toward sinners; his heart is open to all kinds of people, including kings who persecute and Gentiles whom the false teachers may have excluded. Beside this stands Scripture’s equally clear teaching that God chooses and that his purposes do not fail: he does not merely wish; he saves. Everyone who will stand before his throne, from every tribe and language and people and nation, will be there because this God desired it, accomplished it, and gave his Son to make it so.

Two ways of speaking about God’s will. The distinction between what God commands and what he has decreed (see the box below) was not invented for this verse. The cross was the most wicked act ever committed, forbidden by God’s law, yet it was exactly what his hand and plan “had predestined to take place” (Acts 4:27–28). God genuinely commands all people everywhere to repent (Acts 17:30) and has purposed to save a people he will not lose. We cannot see how this fits together in the mind of God; we are asked to believe both, and to pray accordingly.

The knowledge of the truth. Knowledge (epignōsis) is full knowledge; the truth is the gospel (2 Timothy 2:25; Titus 1:1). God saves people by bringing them to know the truth, and he brings the truth by sending people to tell it, which is why prayer and preaching go together.

The desire with tears in it. To see what God’s desire for the lost looks like, look at his Son. Jesus wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41–42) and said, “How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” (Matthew 23:37). The same Lord said he would lose none of all that the Father had given him (John 6:39). Both are true in one Christ, and his tears show most clearly that God’s call is sincere.

In everyday life. Paul tells a small, harassed congregation that nobody is beyond their prayers: not the magistrate who fined them, the emperor, or the neighbour who reported them. Think of the person you have quietly decided will never be saved. You were once as far off, and someone prayed for you. Begin again today, and add one name from a group your church usually forgets.

If God has chosen whom he will save, why should I pray and evangelise? Because God ordains the means as well as the end: he saves people through the prayers and preaching of his church, as he grows crops through farmers. Paul believed in election more firmly than anyone and was the early church’s great missionary; election gave him confidence that his preaching would not be wasted (Acts 18:9–10; 2 Timothy 2:10). You do not know who God’s elect are, and are not meant to. You are meant to pray for everyone, tell everyone, and trust God to use it.

How can I be sure the offer includes me? Because it is addressed to you. The gospel does not say, “Christ died for the elect; find out if you are one.” It says, “Come, believe, repent,” and “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:13). You never have to look into God’s secret decree to know whether you may come; you look at his open invitation and take him at his word. Everyone who has ever come to Christ has been received, and you will not be the first to be turned away.

Where Christians differ: if God desires all to be saved, why are not all saved? Arminian Christians argue that God wills to save every individual equally and that his grace enables everyone to believe, so that the difference lies in each person’s free response. Universalists argue that, since God desires it, all will eventually be saved. This commentary’s view: Universalism contradicts Scripture’s plain teaching on final judgment (Matthew 25:46; 2 Thessalonians 1:9). As for the Arminian view, Scripture distinguishes what God desires in the sense of what pleases him and what he commands (his revealed will) from what he has decreed will happen (his decretive will). God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 18:23; 33:11) and sincerely calls all to repent; yet he has, for wise and holy reasons, chosen to save some and not all (Romans 9:18; Ephesians 1:4–5). Two further points help. First, all people here means all kinds of people, including rulers and Gentiles (vv. 1–2, 7), as all often means in Scripture (Titus 2:11; compare Revelation 5:9). Second, God’s desire is the ground for the church’s universal prayer and preaching: we do not know who the elect are, so we pray for and preach to all, knowing that God is pleased to save through that means. The Reformed view does not make God less loving; it makes him the sovereign author of every salvation. Arminian brothers and sisters hold their view out of a real concern for God’s love and human responsibility, and they preach the same crucified Christ; the difference is serious, but it is a difference within the family.

verseByVerse.quote: For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all, which is the testimony given at the proper time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one God has given one go-between for all kinds of people: the man Christ Jesus, who paid for their freedom with himself. That is why the church can pray for everyone.

For there is one God. Here is the reason for praying for all, in a compact, balanced form that suggests a confession the churches used. “One God” echoes the Shema, Israel’s daily confession (Deuteronomy 6:4), and lands with force in a city whose riot in Acts 19 was a two-hour chant: “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” Since there is only one God, he is the God of Gentiles as well as Jews (Romans 3:29–30), of rulers and slaves alike, so the church must pray for every group.

One mediator. A mediator (mesitēs) brings two estranged parties together: here a holy God and the sinners separated from him. “One” excludes every other candidate: angels, the intermediary beings the false teachers seem to have been fascinated by, Mary, the saints, a priest, the church itself. Christ alone (John 14:6; Acts 4:12): the single point of access is a person. The eternal Son took our flesh so that one of us could stand in the gap, and he stood there not to bargain for us but to give himself as the price.

The man Christ Jesus. Not the Son, not the Lord: the man (anthrōpos). To represent humans, the mediator had to be truly human; to bring us to God, he had to be truly God (Hebrews 2:14–17; John 1:1, 14). And he remains a man now, in heaven, in the risen body that showed Thomas the marks of the nails (John 20:27), and he always lives to make intercession for us (Hebrews 7:25). He bears our nature and our name before the Father, and he has never lost one of those he bought.

Who gave himself as a ransom for all. He was not taken; he handed himself over, with authority to lay his life down and take it up again (John 10:18). The ransom was a gift, not a seizure. The word (antilytron, not found in any earlier Greek writing that survives) joins a ransom price (lytron), the word Jesus used of himself (Mark 10:45), with in place of (anti): a ransom price paid in place of another. Jesus did not merely pay for us; he stood where we were standing. It is penal substitution: he bore in our place the penalty God’s holy justice required for our sin, to set us free (Isaiah 53:5–6; 1 Peter 2:24).

The testimony given at the proper time. The testimony (martyrion) is evidence put on record. Christ’s giving himself is God’s public evidence of what he is like and what he wants, that he “desires all people to be saved” (v. 4): you do not have to guess at God’s heart towards sinners, for the evidence is a cross (Romans 5:8). At the proper time (kairois idiois) is literally “at its own appointed seasons”. History was being brought, after centuries of promises, to the fullness of time (Galatians 4:4), and now the testimony is carried to each nation by preaching (Titus 1:3), as the next verse says. So when you speak of Christ you pass on God’s testimony, not a private opinion; and when you doubt whether God is for you, go back to the evidence he has given.

To whom was the ransom paid? Not to the devil, as some early writers suggested, as if God owed Satan anything, but to the justice of God. Our debt was to his broken law, and the penalty was death (Romans 6:23). Christ paid it by bearing that penalty himself, so that God could be both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). The Father did not extract the price from an unwilling Son, nor did the Son buy a reluctant Father’s love. The Father so loved the world that he gave, and the Son gave himself: the whole Trinity planned and paid the ransom.

Can I pray to Mary or the saints to help me? No, and you do not need to. They were sinners saved by the same mediator, nowhere promised to hear our prayers, and Scripture never directs a single prayer to anyone but God. Nor do you need anyone to soften Christ toward you, because he is not hard. He is a high priest who sympathises with our weaknesses and invites us to draw near to the throne of grace with confidence (Hebrews 4:15–16). Ask fellow believers to pray for you, as Paul did; but bring your prayers to God through Christ alone.

Is it not arrogant to say there is only one way to God? It would be, if Christians claimed to have found the way by being cleverer or better. The claim is the opposite: none of us could find it, so God opened one himself, at the cost of his Son. Every view of salvation draws a line somewhere; even the belief that all roads lead to God shuts out those who think otherwise. And if there were another way, the cross would have been needless (Galatians 2:21). So the gospel is narrow in its door and wide in its welcome: there is one mediator, and anyone at all, of any nation or past, may come through him by faith (Romans 10:13–14).

Where Christians differ: for whom did Christ die? Many hold that Christ died for every individual equally, making salvation possible for all. This commentary’s view: In context all means all kinds of people (vv. 1–2, 7), and Christ’s ransom actually frees those for whom it was paid; yet his death is sufficient for the whole world, the gospel is offered sincerely to every person, and those who differ preach the same Saviour.

verseByVerse.quote: For this I was appointed a preacher and an apostle (I am telling the truth, I am not lying), a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s own commission to the Gentiles is the proof that God meant the ransom for all kinds of people. Paul swears to it because this was the contested ground of his ministry.

Preacher and apostle. A preacher (kēryx) is a herald, who announces a king’s decree in the public square and has no licence to edit. An apostle is an authorised messenger. A teacher explains and instructs over time. Together they describe the whole task.

Appointed. Appointed (tithēmi) means set or placed. Set that against 1:7, where the troublemakers were “desiring to be teachers of the law”. One man was placed; the others placed themselves. So Paul can insist on his credentials and call himself the foremost of sinners in the same letter: he is not defending a position he took for himself.

I am not lying. The solemn assertion (like Romans 9:1) backs his claim to be teacher of the Gentiles. These were the fighting words of his ministry; the Jerusalem crowd listened to him until the word “Gentiles”, and then shouted for his death (Acts 22:21–22). The man who calls himself the foremost of sinners does not much mind what people think of him. He minds a great deal that they believe the Gentiles are truly included, and if you are not Jewish, he was fighting for you.

A teacher of the Gentiles. This was Paul’s special calling (Galatians 2:7–9): the persecutor became the Gentiles’ teacher, and a message from a corner of Judea has reached the ends of the earth. In faith and truth could mean faithfully and truthfully, or teaching the faith and the truth; either way, not in speculation, which is what the rivals dealt in (1:4). The apostolic office itself was unique and foundational: the apostles were witnesses of the risen Christ, sent by him in person (Acts 1:21–22; 1 Corinthians 9:1), and the church is built once for all on their foundation (Ephesians 2:20), so the office has not continued.

The herald’s voice is Christ’s. A herald speaks in another’s name. Writing to this same church, Paul said that Christ “came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near” (Ephesians 2:17). The Gentiles of Ephesus never saw Jesus in Galilee, yet Christ preached to them, because when his herald announced the ransom, the King himself was speaking (Acts 26:16–18).

In everyday life. The gospel reached you along a chain of heralds that runs back to Paul. Give thanks for the last link in that chain, and think of the nations that have come to your own street: the family from overseas, the international student, the colleague from another faith.

Does God still call people to preach? Yes, though not as apostles. The church still needs heralds and teachers, and God still gives them (Ephesians 4:11; Romans 10:14–15). A call to preach is not normally a voice or a vision but a desire for the work, the gifts and character Scripture requires (3:1–7), and the recognition of the church, which tests a man and sets him apart. If you sense that desire, ask your elders to test you, and take every opportunity to serve and learn. And whether or not you are called to preach, you are called to speak of Christ to the people around you.

verseByVerse.ref: 2:8–15 – Men and Women in the Assembly
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the church gathers, men and women are each to bring a life that fits the gospel, and to keep the order God set at creation. Men are to pray with hands not clenched in anger (v. 8); women are to be adorned with good works rather than display (vv. 9–10). Women are to learn, while the teaching and governing office is kept for qualified men (vv. 11–12), on grounds Paul takes from creation and the fall, not from local custom (vv. 13–14). The section ends with a hard promise about childbearing, anchored in continuing faith (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Contested Passage, Read Slowly

The key word of verse 12 is authentein, to exercise authority (see the note on vv. 11–12). Paul grounds the restriction in the order of creation, an order that concerns role, not worth (see the note on vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The braided hair, gold and pearls of verse 9 brought social rank into the assembly (see the note on vv. 9–10).

Now: On why a restriction on a function is never a verdict on a person, see the note on vv. 11–12.

verseByVerse.quote: I desire then that in every place the men should pray, lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Men are to lead the church in prayer, coming with hands that are holy and not clenched in anger against a brother. Paul’s first instruction to Christian men is not to take charge but to pray.

I desire then that in every place the men should pray. Desire (boulomai) is an apostolic instruction, not a preference, and “then” draws it from what precedes: since there is one mediator, here is how the church is to pray. Every place is wherever the church gathers (1 Corinthians 1:2), echoing Malachi’s promise that in every place incense will be offered to God’s name among the nations (Malachi 1:11). This is not a local Ephesian arrangement but Paul’s expectation for every church, which matters for how his instructions to men and women are read. The men (tous andras) are males specifically: they are to lead the congregation in public prayer.

Lifting holy hands. The posture is the ordinary one of the ancient world, standing with hands raised and open (1 Kings 8:22; Psalm 141:2), and nothing here forbids kneeling. The weight falls on holy (hosios): hands lifted to God must be clean. God told Israel that when they spread out their hands he would hide his eyes, because their hands were full of blood (Isaiah 1:15).

Without anger or quarreling. What makes the hands unholy here is the state of a man’s relationships. Anger (orgē) is settled resentment; quarrelling (dialogismos) is disputing, or the inner turmoil of a man going over his case against someone. The false teaching had stirred up controversy (1:4; 6:4–5), and men were apparently carrying it into worship. Scripture always joins the two: “First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5:24); husbands are to live with their wives in an understanding way, “so that your prayers may not be hindered” (1 Peter 3:7). If a man’s praying feels obstructed, the first place to look is not his technique but whether there is somebody he is angry with.

The one who can ascend the hill. “Who shall ascend the hill of the LORD?” asks Psalm 24, and answers: “He who has clean hands and a pure heart” (Psalm 24:3–4). Only one man has fully answered that description, our high priest, “holy, innocent, unstained” (Hebrews 7:26). Men can lift their hands not because they have qualified themselves but because the one mediator has opened the way: because his hands were pierced, ours are washed. Holy hands are not hands that never sinned; they are hands cleansed by him and no longer clenched against a brother.

May women pray aloud in church? Yes. Paul assumes that women pray and prophesy in the gatherings at Corinth (1 Corinthians 11:5), and the women were praying with the apostles before Pentecost (Acts 1:14). This verse lays a particular duty on the men: to lead in prayer, with clean hands. A church where only women pray has not obeyed it, and a church where women are silenced from praying has misread it.

What if I want to be reconciled and the other person refuses? Then do what lies with you, and leave the rest with God: as far as it depends on you, be at peace (Romans 12:18). Go to them, admit your part without excusing it, forgive from the heart whether or not they ask, and refuse to nurse the grievance or spread it. If they still will not be reconciled, your hands can be holy though the relationship is broken, because what defiles them is your anger, not their refusal. Keep praying for them. And if the conflict involves abuse or danger, reconciliation does not mean putting yourself back in harm’s way; forgiveness and safety can go together.
verseByVerse.note: Standing with raised hands was a common posture for prayer.

parallels.desc: the lifting up of my hands

verseByVerse.quote: likewise also that women should adorn themselves in respectable apparel, with modesty and self-control, not with braided hair and gold or pearls or costly attire, but with what is proper for women who profess godliness—with good works.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christian women are to make themselves beautiful with good works, not with displays of wealth or with immodesty. Paul is not against beauty; he changes what it is made of.

Women should adorn themselves. “Likewise” ties this to verse 8: as the men’s temptation in the assembly is anger, the women’s is display. Adorn (kosmeō, whence cosmetic) is to make beautiful; respectable (kosmios), from the same root, is orderly. Modesty (aidōs) is reserve, the instinct not to draw improper attention; self-control (sōphrosynē) is the settled self-mastery prized in Greek moral thought: inner qualities expressed outwardly.

Braided hair and gold. Elaborately braided hair threaded with gold and pearls took slaves and hours to produce, and it existed to announce wealth and rank (compare 1 Peter 3:3–4). The issue is social rank carried into the church’s gathering: a poor woman, perhaps a slave, entering a room where wealth was advertised knew exactly where she stood (compare James 2:1–4; 1 Corinthians 11:21–22).

With good works. This is the point. A woman who claims to worship God should be known for kindness, hospitality and service, like Dorcas, who was full of good works and acts of charity (Acts 9:36–39). Paul does not tell them to look poor but to change what they are adorned with, and that is a levelling standard: a wealthy woman can outspend a poor one on pearls, but nobody can outspend anybody on kindness. He has replaced the currency of the room with one everybody can trade in.

Adorning the Saviour’s teaching. Paul uses this verb in Titus, where slaves are to adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour (Titus 2:10). Good works make the beauty of Christ visible in a city that knew only the beauty of money, and they are his gift: we are created in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:10). The Saviour who had no form or majesty that we should look at him (Isaiah 53:2) is still shown to the world in the plain kindnesses of his people.

The clothes of the wedding. God himself is the great adorner. He clothed Adam and Eve after their shame, and he has clothed his people with the robe of Christ’s righteousness. The church is being made ready as a bride, and her fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints (Revelation 19:8). A woman adorned with good works is already wearing the clothes of the wedding.

What it does not mean. It does not forbid all braiding, jewellery or nice clothes; Rebekah received gold jewellery as a sign of God’s blessing (Genesis 24:22). The issue is extravagant display, status-seeking and immodesty.

How do I decide what is modest and appropriate? Ask three questions. What is it saying? If the honest answer is “look how wealthy I am” or “look at my body”, it says the wrong thing in the house of God. Whom does it serve? Clothing that makes a poorer sister feel shabby, or pulls attention from worship, does not serve the church. What does it cost, in money and time? If your appearance absorbs more of both than your good works, the balance is wrong. Within those questions there is freedom, and cultures differ: do not judge other women by your preferences, or make rules Scripture has not made.

Does this make women responsible for men’s lust? No. Every man is responsible for his own eyes and heart; Jesus put the guilt of the lustful look on the man who looks (Matthew 5:28), and Job made a covenant with his eyes (Job 31:1). A woman is never to blame for a man’s sin against her, and no one may excuse harassment or abuse by pointing at what a woman wore. Paul’s concern is different: that a Christian woman should aim not to draw attention to herself, by wealth or by immodesty, but to adorn the gospel with a godly life. Modesty is a woman’s gift to God and to the church, not a fence she must build around men.

verseByVerse.quote: Let a woman learn quietly with all submissiveness. I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; rather, she is to remain quiet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Women are to be taught as disciples, but the authoritative teaching and governing of the gathered church belong to qualified men. These contested verses should be read with the actual words in front of us, and with care for the many Christian women who read them with a lump in the throat.

In the flow. Paul is still ordering the gathered church: who learns and who teaches when it meets (chapter 3 goes on to the men who hold the teaching office). The question was live in Ephesus (see the setting at vv. 1–2), but Paul’s reasons (vv. 13–14) rest not on that situation but on creation.

Let a woman learn. Learn (manthanō, be a disciple) is a command, not a grudging permission, and in the first century a generous one: women were often not taught the law at all, and some rabbis spoke with contempt of teaching it to a woman. Whatever else this passage does, it puts women in the class rather than outside the door, as Jesus did when Mary sat at his feet and he said she had chosen the good portion (Luke 10:38–42).

Quietly, with all submissiveness. In quietness (en hēsychia), the same root as the quiet life of verse 2, is not absolute silence but a receptive, peaceable attitude. Submissiveness (hypotagē) is ordering oneself under, the posture of any learner: submission to the teaching and to the church’s order under the elders, not of every woman to every man.

I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority. Permit is present tense: as my settled practice. Teach (didaskō) in the Pastoral Letters is the authoritative teaching of doctrine in the church, the work of elders (2 Timothy 2:2), and teaching and exercising authority together describe the eldership: teaching and governing (3:2, 5; 5:17). Paul is forbidding women to hold that office in the gathered church. (On the rare word for exercise authority, see “Uncertain wording” at the end of this note.)

The scope. The scope is narrower than it is often made: the gathered assembly (v. 8) and two functions, authoritative teaching and governing. Paul is not saying that women may not speak (1 Corinthians 11:5) or teach anyone at all, that they are more easily deceived by nature, or that every woman must submit to every man.

Every disciple sits at one Teacher’s feet. Jesus told his disciples they have one teacher, and they are all brothers (Matthew 23:8). An elder teaches not his own word but Christ’s, as an under-shepherd answerable to the chief Shepherd (1 Peter 5:1–4). The woman who learns and the man who teaches are disciples of the same Lord, and the authority Paul restricts is a stewardship, never a possession to boast of.

In everyday life. If you are a woman, use your gifts in every way Scripture opens to you. If you are a man in leadership, train women to serve, ask their counsel, and honour them publicly.

What of a woman teaching a Sunday school class, leading a Bible study or reporting on mission? Complementarians draw the line at the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the gathered church, and churches apply it with some differences. Women may teach women and children (Titus 2:3–4), share their testimony, and explain the faith in many settings, as Priscilla did privately with her husband (Acts 18:26). Many churches also welcome women to teach mixed groups under the elders’ oversight, as long as they are not exercising the elder’s authority. The aim is to honour both the gifts God gives women and the order he has set.

Doesn’t this make women second-class Christians? No, and a church where it feels that way has misunderstood it: a restriction on a function is not a verdict on a person. In the work of salvation the Son willingly submits to the Father, and he is not less God, equal with the Father in nature and glory (1 Corinthians 11:3; 15:28; Philippians 2:6); church members submit to their elders, and they are not lesser Christians (Hebrews 13:17). The New Testament is full of women honoured for their faith and service: the women who stayed at the cross when most of the men fled, and were first at the empty tomb; Lydia, whose home became the church at Philippi; Phoebe, bearer of the letter to the Romans; Priscilla, often named before her husband; the women who laboured beside Paul in the gospel (Philippians 4:3). Eldership is one calling. The church depends on a thousand others, and on the women who fill them.

What about Deborah, Phoebe and Junia? Deborah was a prophetess and judge at a time when, as the story itself notes, the men were failing to lead (Judges 4:4–9); she is honoured, but Israel’s priesthood remained male, and her story is not about the eldership. Phoebe was a servant (diakonos) of her church, likely a deaconess, and Paul commends her warmly (Romans 16:1–2); that service is not the teaching and governing office of elder. Junia (Romans 16:7) is well known to the apostles, or among them; even if she is called an apostle, the word there has the broader sense of a sent messenger or missionary, not one of the Twelve or Paul. None of them overturns the reason Paul gives, which is rooted in creation.

What if a man uses these verses to control or abuse? Then he is defying them. Paul has just told men to lift holy hands without anger; he requires elders to be gentle, not violent or quarrelsome (3:3); he tells husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). Headship in Scripture is self-giving love and responsibility, never domination, and this passage concerns the office of elder; it does not put every woman under every man. Abuse is never tolerated: a woman being harmed should seek safety and tell the authorities and her church leaders, and a church that protects an abuser or tells his victim to submit to him has betrayed Christ.

Where Christians differ: may women be pastors and elders? Egalitarians (Christians who hold that every church office is open to women and men alike) argue that this verse addressed a temporary situation in Ephesus (uneducated women spreading false teaching), so that once women are educated, they may teach and lead equally. They also point to Galatians 3:28, to the women who prophesied and laboured beside Paul, and to the debated meaning of authenteō, and many hold their view precisely because they want to honour both Scripture and the gifts God gives to women. This commentary’s view: The complementarian view is the natural reading. Paul grounds the restriction not in local culture or women’s lack of education but in the order of creation (v. 13) and the account of the fall (v. 14), which apply to all times and places. The same principle appears elsewhere (1 Corinthians 11:3; 14:33–35; Ephesians 5:22–33), and the qualifications for elders assume men (3:2; Titus 1:6). This does not mean women are inferior: men and women are equally made in God’s image (Genesis 1:27), equally heirs of grace (1 Peter 3:7), and equally gifted for ministry. Women may teach other women (Titus 2:3–5) and children (2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15), share the gospel, explain Scripture privately (Acts 18:26), serve as deaconesses or in a diaconal role, and exercise a vast range of gifts. The restriction concerns the office of elder: authoritative teaching and governing of the whole church. Egalitarian brothers and sisters are not enemies of the Bible; this commentary simply judges that Paul’s appeal to creation reaches beyond Ephesus.

Uncertain wording. Exercise authority translates authenteō, a rare word found only here in the New Testament, and its exact shade is debated. Some argue it carries a negative sense, to domineer or usurp, so that Paul forbids only overbearing authority; that is a serious reading held by serious Christians. Two things weigh against it. Much of the wider evidence for the word in that period, on many scholars’ reading, points to plain authority, though the evidence is debated. And in sentences built like this one, the two activities joined by “or” are normally either both good or both bad; since to teach is a good thing throughout these letters, Paul is restricting the thing itself, not an abuse of it. The likely meaning is simply to have or exercise authority.

verseByVerse.quote: For Adam was formed first, then Eve; and Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and became a transgressor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul grounds his instruction in how God made the first man and woman and in what went wrong at the fall, not in the customs of Ephesus. So it reaches every church.

For Adam was formed first, then Eve. “For” introduces Paul’s grounds for verse 12, and they decide how far it reaches: not Ephesian culture or the education available to women, but Genesis. Formed (plassō) is moulded, as a potter shapes clay (Genesis 2:7). God made Adam first, and then Eve from him and for him as his helper (Genesis 2:18–23; 1 Corinthians 11:8–9). This reason comes from before the fall: God’s good design, not a result of sin or culture.

Order, not worth. Both are made in the image of God (Genesis 1:27), and in Christ “there is no male and female” (Galatians 3:28). And “helper”, which Genesis uses of Eve, is used most often in the Old Testament of God himself (Psalm 33:20; 121:1–2): not the title of a servant but of one who brings what is lacking.

Adam was not deceived. Paul uses deceived (apataō) of Adam and a stronger form (exapataō, thoroughly deceived) of Eve; his second reason comes from the fall (Genesis 3:1–6, 13). It is not a claim that women are more gullible: Paul nowhere says that, men are deceived all the time (2 Timothy 3:13), and elsewhere he lays the fall squarely at Adam’s door (Romans 5:12–19; 1 Corinthians 15:22). What happened in the garden was a reversal: the serpent bypassed Adam’s headship and approached Eve, and she was deceived; Adam was with her (Genesis 3:6), said nothing, and sinned with his eyes open, which made his sin, if anything, worse. Both failed, and the church should not repeat that reversal.

The man who did not stand by. Paul calls Adam “a type of the one who was to come” (Romans 5:14): a pattern, in advance, of Christ. The first man stood silent while his wife listened to the serpent; the last Adam stepped between his bride and the enemy and took the blow himself. He loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). The first man hid among the trees; the second was lifted up on a tree in her place. That is headship done perfectly: not passivity and not domination, but a husband who protects at the cost of his life.

Met by the serpent, and not deceived. The Son of God met the same serpent, not in a garden but in a wilderness, and was not deceived. Where Eve was talked out of trusting God’s word, he answered every lie with what is written; where Adam said nothing, he spoke the truth and kept it. The serpent’s first lie was that God was holding back something good. At the cross God held back nothing, not even his own Son (Romans 8:32), and the transgression that began with a lie believed was carried away by the one who is the truth.

In everyday life. Men, notice where Adam was standing while his wife was deceived. Godly headship is not control but the courage to protect, to speak and to take responsibility. Ask where you have been silent when you should have spoken. Where you have failed, the last Adam did not: his perfect obedience is counted as yours, and his Spirit gives the courage you lack.

Isn’t the appeal to creation just Paul’s culture talking? That is exactly what Paul rules out by going to Genesis. Asked about divorce, Jesus did the same: “from the beginning it was not so” (Matthew 19:8). Going back to creation is the Bible’s way of saying that this is not a custom of the time but how God made things. Had Paul argued from Ephesian conditions, his instruction would lapse when they changed; he argued from the way God made the first man and woman, and that has not changed.

How can there be order without inferiority? Look at Christ. The Son is equal with the Father in every way, God from God, yet he delights to do the Father’s will: “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29). He is not less for obeying, nor was he less than Joseph and Mary when as a boy he submitted to them (Luke 2:51). Order is the way love arranges itself in a family. The world assumes that whoever leads is worth more and whoever follows is worth less; the gospel has overturned that reckoning: “The greatest among you shall be your servant” (Matthew 23:11).

verseByVerse.quote: Yet she will be saved through childbearing—if they continue in faith and love and holiness, with self-control.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Women are not saved by bearing children; a Christian woman’s salvation is lived out within her God-given calling, of which motherhood is the chief example, as she goes on in faith, love and holiness. This is one of the genuinely difficult verses of the New Testament.

Yet she will be saved through childbearing. This cannot mean that women are saved by having babies: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and there is one mediator (1:15; 2:5). “Saved” is Paul’s normal word for salvation. “She” at first refers to Eve, and through her to women generally; the change to “they” shows he means Christian women. Childbearing (teknogonia) stands for the calling of bearing and raising children. The likeliest sense is that a woman works out her salvation, and shows it is genuine, by embracing her God-given role rather than reaching for the role of elder (for other readings, see “Uncertain wording” at the end of this note). That fits the context: the curse on Eve touched childbearing (Genesis 3:16), and the false teachers were apparently forbidding marriage (4:3). A woman is not saved by escaping her circumstances but within them, and the work of bearing and raising children can be offered to Christ as service (Colossians 3:23).

If they continue. The real anchor is not “if they bear children” but “if they continue” in faith. To continue (menō) is to abide, the word Jesus used: “Abide in me” (John 15:4). Salvation is by grace through faith (Ephesians 2:8–9), so these are not payments but what a saved life goes on showing, and perseverance in them is the evidence of genuine salvation (Colossians 1:22–23), exactly what Paul asks of everybody in this letter.

Faith, love, holiness and self-control. In an ordinary week: faith goes on trusting Christ, not yourself, for your standing with God, especially on the days you have done badly. Love is not first a feeling but steady care that seeks another’s good at cost to yourself, patient, kind, not insisting on its own way (1 Corinthians 13:4–5). Holiness (hagiasmos, sanctification) is the Spirit’s slow remaking of someone already forgiven (2 Corinthians 3:18), putting off old habits and putting on new ones (Colossians 3:5–14) in speech, purity and honesty with money; it is his work, done through our effort, not instead of it. Self-control (sōphrosynē, as in verse 9) is a sound mind governing appetite, tongue, temper and spending, instead of impulse, mood or fashion.

What grace grows. None of these earns salvation; they are what grace grows. “For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age” (Titus 2:11–12). Ask which one most needs his help this week, and ask him for it. The study Love: The Greatest Commandment says more about love.

Not through her labour but through his. The woman who was deceived was given a promise in the same breath as her sentence: her offspring would crush the serpent’s head. Through the long line of mothers from Eve to Mary the Saviour came, born of a woman, carried and nursed and raised by a woman. He has redeemed the curse at its root, and every woman who trusts him will be brought safely home, not through her own labour but through his.

In everyday life. If you are a mother, see your work as holy service to God: the meals, the patient answers to the same question, the prayers at the bedside are where your faith is being worked out. And thank a mother in your church this week, especially one who is weary.

Where does this leave me if I am single or cannot have children? Exactly where it leaves every believer: saved by Christ, and called to continue in faith, love and holiness. Motherhood is a central example of a woman’s calling, not a condition of salvation. Some of the church’s most fruitful women were unmarried, and Paul commended singleness as a gift that frees a person for undivided devotion to the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:32–35). Many childless women are spiritual mothers to dozens. If your childlessness is a grief, it is a real one, and Scripture does not dismiss it: Hannah wept before the Lord, and he heard her. But you are not less in his eyes, and your calling is just as real.

Does “if they continue” mean I could lose my salvation? No. The condition describes what true faith does, not a test it might fail. Those whom God has justified he will also glorify (Romans 8:30), and he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6). But he brings it to completion through our continuing, and warnings like this are among the means he uses to keep us. The person anxious to continue in faith is the person God is keeping; the one who should fear is the one who has stopped caring.

Uncertain wording. How childbearing relates to being saved is genuinely unclear, and there are three main readings. (1) Women will be kept safe physically through childbirth; but saved is normally spiritual in Paul, and many godly women have died in childbirth, which no reading of this verse may treat as a sign of God’s displeasure. (2) Women will be saved through “the childbearing”, the birth of the Messiah, the offspring of the woman promised in Genesis 3:15; this reads beautifully after verses 13–14, though the Greek “the” need not carry that weight. (3) Women will work out their salvation within their God-given role, as explained above. The third fits the context best, and the second can be combined with it: the Child born of a woman reversed the curse, and in him women’s ordinary calling is redeemed.
verseByVerse.note: One of the harder verses in Paul. Suggested readings include: kept safe through childbirth; saved through the Childbirth, the birth of Christ; or saved while fulfilling her calling. It cannot mean earning salvation.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people,<sup>2</sup>for kings and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way.<sup>3</sup>This is good, and it is pleasing in the sight of God our Savior,<sup>4</sup>who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.<sup>5</sup>For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus,<sup>6</sup>who gave himself as a ransom for all, which is the testimony given at the proper time.<sup>7</sup>For this I was appointed a preacher and an apostle (I am telling the truth, I am not lying), a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth.<sup>8</sup>I desire then that in every place the men should pray, lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling;<sup>9</sup>likewise also that women should adorn themselves in respectable apparel, with modesty and self-control, not with braided hair and gold or pearls or costly attire,<sup>10</sup>but with what is proper for women who profess godliness—with good works.<sup>11</sup>Let a woman learn quietly with all submissiveness.<sup>12</sup>I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; rather, she is to remain quiet.<sup>13</sup>For Adam was formed first, then Eve;<sup>14</sup>and Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and became a transgressor.<sup>15</sup>Yet she will be saved through childbearing—if they continue in faith and love and holiness, with self-control.

keyVerse.quote: For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all, which is the testimony given at the proper time.
keyVerse.note: Everything in the chapter flows from this confession. Because there is one God and one way to him, the church prays for all people, men come to prayer with clean hands, and women and men alike learn at the feet of one Teacher. The only go-between is a man who is also God, and he did not bargain for us but gave himself as the price.

2.reflection:
Paul puts prayer for everyone, rulers included, “first of all” (vv. 1–2). Who are the people, in public life or nearer home, you find hardest to pray for? What would it look like to pray for their good and their salvation this week?

Verses 5–6 say there is one God and one mediator, who gave himself as a ransom. How does knowing that the only go-between is a man who still bears our nature change the way you come to God in prayer?

Paul says that anger and quarrelling make lifted hands unholy (v. 8), and that display can crowd out good works (vv. 9–10). Where do these temptations show themselves when we gather, and how can we help one another away from them?

Verses 11–15 are hard for many readers. How does Paul’s appeal to creation, and the picture of Christ as the last Adam who gave himself for his bride, help us hold together equal worth and different callings? How could our church honour the gifts of its women more fully?

3.title: The Household of God
3.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 2 set the church’s worship in order. Chapter 3 names who may lead God’s household, then states the purpose of the whole letter (vv. 14–15) and crowns it with a hymn to Christ (v. 16): it is the hinge of 1 Timothy.

The message. The church is the household of the living God, holding up his truth for the world to see, so those who lead and serve in it must live that truth. God asks first not for talent or a following but for tested, visible godliness, at home, in the church and before outsiders; only one requirement, “able to teach”, is a skill. And the truth the household holds up is not finally a system but a person.

Why it was said. False teachers had risen from within the church at Ephesus, as Paul had warned (Acts 20:30), perhaps some of its elders (see the introduction). They were confident talkers, quarrelsome and eager for gain (1:6–7; 6:4–5). Timothy needed to know whom to trust with the flock, and Paul could not be sure when he would come (vv. 14–15).

How the chapter makes its case. The overseer’s work is noble (v. 1), but he must be above reproach in marriage, mind, table and teaching (v. 2), free from drink, violence, quarrelling and greed (v. 3), proven at home (vv. 4–5), mature, and well regarded outside the church (vv. 6–7). Deacons serve rather than teach but meet the same standard and are tested first; so are the women of verse 11; and faithful service brings great confidence (vv. 8–13). Then Paul says why it matters: the church is God’s household and the pillar of the truth, and that truth is sung in six lines about Christ (vv. 14–16).

Where it leads. The chapter that begins with job descriptions ends with a song, because the ordinary machinery of a church exists to hold up one glorious person where the world can see him: he was “manifested in the flesh”, and “taken up in glory” (v. 16). Every quality in the lists he alone has had perfectly: the gentle chief Shepherd who never loved silver, faithful to his one bride, the Son over God’s house, the Servant who came not to be served but to serve. Elders and deacons are only his under-shepherds.

For us. Choose leaders for character, not charisma, test them before you trust them, and pray for them. Use the lists as a mirror, for they describe what grace grows in every Christian. Belong to a local church and bear weight in it. And when church life feels like rotas and meetings, remember what it is for: to hold up Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wanting to be an overseer is good, because the work is noble; but the man must already be what he will call the flock to become. Paul affirms the desire (v. 1), then sets out what an elder must be: above reproach, with grace visible in his marriage, mind, table and teaching (v. 2); free from the vices that ruin leaders under pressure (v. 3); proven in caring for his own household (vv. 4–5); neither a new convert nor a man with a bad name outside the church, for the devil sets snares for both (vv. 6–7). Almost all of it is character, tested at home, over time, and in the eyes of outsiders.
verseByVerse.theology:
Character, Not Competence

Of some fifteen requirements only one, ‘able to teach’, is a skill (see the notes on v. 2 and v. 3).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: ‘Overseer’ and ‘elder’ name one office (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5–7).

Now: Verse 7 gives outsiders a say (see the note on vv. 6–7).

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy: If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wanting to be an overseer is a good desire, because the work itself is noble. Paul commends the wish, then sets a high bar for the man who has it.

The saying is trustworthy. The second of the five trustworthy sayings in these letters (1:15; 4:9), most likely introducing what follows, though some take it back to 2:15.

Overseer and elder. In the New Testament, overseer (episkopos, from which comes bishop) and elder (presbyteros, from which comes presbyter) appear to be two names for one office: Paul tells the elders of Ephesus that the Spirit has made them overseers (Acts 20:17, 28), and Titus 1:5–7 moves between the two words. Elder stresses maturity; overseer, watching over the flock. Churches were led by a plurality of elders (Acts 14:23; Philippians 1:1); one bishop over several churches came in the second century.

If anyone aspires. Two verbs, both positive. Aspires (oregō) means to stretch toward something; desires (epithymeō) is to set one’s heart on it. Paul does not treat the wish as suspicious, as though the only safe candidate were the man who has to be dragged to it. It is not pride to want the office, if the motive is to serve Christ and his people.

A noble task. A work, not a title or a rank: hard labour (5:17; 1 Thessalonians 5:12), not a platform, which is why everything that follows concerns character rather than ability. And where leadership could bring danger rather than prestige, the desire was a mark of devotion: when persecution came, leaders were often the first to suffer, as James was in Jerusalem (Acts 12:1–2).

Keeping the office. Ephesus was full of men who wanted the standing of a teacher (1:7). Paul does not abolish the position. He keeps the office, affirms the desire and raises the bar, a better answer to the abuse of authority than pretending authority should not exist. On leadership in the home, the church, work and the state, see on Ephesians 5:21.

A flock bought with blood. Why is the work noble? Because of whose flock it is. Paul told the elders of this very church “to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood” (Acts 20:28). The overseer watches over people for whom Christ died, which makes the job both splendid and frightening. And the office is itself a gift of the risen Lord, who gave shepherds and teachers to his people (Ephesians 4:8, 11): to desire it is to ask to become one of Christ’s gifts to his church, a noble thing to want, and a humbling one. Christ is the chief Shepherd and the true Overseer of our souls (1 Peter 2:25). He did not merely desire the noble task; he laid down his life to do it, and he still watches over every sheep the Father gave him.

In everyday life. Pray for your elders by name. Much of their work is invisible: the hospital visit at night, the couple in crisis, the hours over a passage you will hear in forty minutes on Sunday. Send one of them a note this week to say you are praying for him, naming one thing he has done that helped you.

What does an elder actually do? He shepherds the flock: knowing the people, praying for them, visiting the sick, warning the wandering, comforting the grieving (Acts 20:28; 1 Peter 5:2–3). He teaches, in public and in private, and guards the church from error (Titus 1:9). With his fellow elders he leads in the decisions that shape the church’s life (5:17), and he will give an account for the souls in his care (Hebrews 13:17). He is not a board member who attends meetings but an under-shepherd of Christ’s sheep.

How do I know whether I should aspire to this? Examine the desire: do you want to care for people and feed them God’s Word, or to be recognised? Hold your life honestly against the list that follows, and ask those who know you well to do the same. Men who will make good elders are usually doing elders’ work already without the title: opening their homes, teaching a group, visiting the lonely, praying for the flock. Tell your elders of the desire, ask them to watch and test you, and be content to wait. The call is confirmed by the church, not by the man alone.

Where Christians differ: how should the church be governed? Episcopal churches have bishops over priests and deacons (three orders); congregational churches vest final authority in the members; presbyterian churches govern through elders in local sessions and wider courts. Each reads the New Testament honestly, and each has produced faithful churches. This commentary’s view: The New Testament knows two ongoing offices in the local church: elders (overseers), who shepherd, teach and govern, and deacons, who serve practical needs (Philippians 1:1). Each church should be led by a plurality of qualified elders, men who meet these qualifications (Acts 14:23; Titus 1:5). Apostles were a unique, foundational office that has ceased. Within this, churches differ charitably on how much authority the congregation holds and how churches relate to one another.
verseByVerse.note: “Overseer” and “elder” appear to be two names for the same office.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore an overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach,
verseByVerse.commentary:
An overseer must be a man no one can fairly accuse, with grace visible in his marriage, his mind, his home and his teaching. Above reproach is the heading; the rest of the list shows what it looks like.

Above reproach. Must (dei): requirements, not ideals. Above reproach (anepilēmptos) means nothing in his life an accuser could take hold of: not sinless, which would empty every pulpit, but with no glaring, ongoing pattern of sin that could fairly be charged against him. Only one item, “able to teach”, is a skill; a church that chooses leaders for their gifts or their following has turned Paul’s priorities upside down.

The husband of one wife. Most likely a man sexually faithful to his wife, devoted to one woman (see “Uncertain wording” below). It concerns present character rather than an audit of his history: a marriage in which nobody can point to unfaithfulness. A widower who remarried is plainly not excluded, and a man divorced long ago, before he came to Christ, may qualify if his past is not a present scandal: a man’s history is neither irrelevant nor unforgivable. The qualifications also assume that elders are men, as 2:12 does.

Sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable. Sober-minded (nēphalios) is clear-headed: a shepherd who is not awake cannot see the wolf. Self-controlled is of sound judgment (2:9; Titus 1:8), not driven by moods or appetites. Respectable is orderly (the word of 2:9): his days, finances and commitments are in order, and people can rely on him.

Hospitable. Literally a lover of strangers (philoxenos). Inns had a bad name, and travelling Christians depended on the hospitality of believers’ homes (Romans 12:13; 1 Peter 4:9), so an elder’s family shared the cost of his office. A flock is mostly shepherded around tables, and a closed home cannot do it.

Able to teach. The one gift, and what distinguishes elders from deacons: able to instruct in sound doctrine and rebuke those who contradict it (Titus 1:9). Not every elder must be a gifted preacher, but every one must be able to teach, whether a congregation or a troubled man across a kitchen table.

A life the flock can follow. An elder is an example to the flock (1 Peter 5:3), and the sheep learn their Shepherd partly by watching his under-shepherds (1 Corinthians 11:1). A gifted man of poor character teaches one thing with his mouth and another with his life, and the flock usually believes the life. Only one man has had every one of these qualities perfectly. He was faithful to his one bride, the church, and gave himself up for her; he was clear-headed in the wilderness, self-controlled under every provocation, and hospitable to sinners at his table. An elder’s life is meant to show, in small and imperfect measure, what he is like.

What it does not mean. It does not require elders to be married or have children; it describes how they behave if they are. Nor are these qualities for elders only: every Christian is called to them, and elders must model them.

In everyday life. Use this list as a mirror. You will not meet it perfectly; Christ has, in your place, and his Spirit is growing these qualities in you. Which is he growing now? If hospitality, invite someone to eat with you this week whom you would not normally invite.

Does a terrible past before conversion disqualify a man? Not in itself: a former persecutor wrote these words. Above reproach describes present life and reputation, not a record with nothing in it. What matters is whether he has been changed, whether the change has been tested over time, and whether his past still brings reproach on the church. Some offences, such as the abuse of children, rightly bar a man permanently, because the trust the office needs cannot be restored and the vulnerable must be protected. The church must judge with grace and wisdom.

Does this list mean the church is to be led by the respectable? No. It describes a man in whom grace has done visible work, not one who never needed it. A heart proud of its own record is rarely gentle, teachable or safe with other people’s failures (vv. 3, 6), and the man who wrote this list called himself the foremost of sinners (1:15). The list is for office, not for belonging: everyone enters the church the same way, as a sinner received through Christ. Elders show what that grace produces.

Where Christians differ: may a divorced and remarried man be an elder? Some churches forbid it absolutely; others ignore the question. This commentary’s view: The phrase concerns present faithfulness and character, not merely marital history. A man who was divorced on biblical grounds (adultery or desertion by the other spouse, Matthew 19:9; 1 Corinthians 7:15) and has since lived faithfully may be considered. But a man whose divorce was sinful, especially if recent, or whose marriage history brings reproach, would not be above reproach. Each case requires wise judgment by the church.

Uncertain wording. “The husband of one wife” is literally “a one-woman man” (mias gynaikos andra), a compressed phrase and the most argued-over in the list. Four meanings have been proposed: (1) not a polygamist; (2) not remarried after divorce or the death of his wife; (3) married; (4) sexually faithful to his wife, devoted to one woman. Polygamy was rare in the Greek world, against the first; Paul urges younger widows to remarry (5:14), against the second; he was apparently unmarried himself and commends singleness (1 Corinthians 7:8), against the third. The fourth fits best.

verseByVerse.quote: not a drunkard, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An overseer must not be ruled by drink, temper, argument or money, but must be gentle.

Not a drunkard. Drunkard (paroinos) is literally “beside wine”: one who lingers over it. This letter tells Timothy to take a little wine (5:23); what is ruled out is the man whose drink governs his evenings.

Not violent but gentle. Violent (plēktēs) is a striker, a bully. Against it Paul sets epieikēs (Philippians 4:5): gracious, forbearing, the man who does not insist on the last inch of what he is owed. An elder deals with people patiently, not domineering over those in his charge (2 Timothy 2:24–25; 1 Peter 5:3).

Not quarrelsome. Not a fighter, here with words. Ephesus was full of vain discussion (6:4–5), and the church might seem to need a leader who could out-argue the talkers. Paul says the opposite: a man who enjoys the fight is disqualified, however right he is. An elder must still refute error (Titus 1:9); the difference is between a contentious spirit and a faithful defence.

Not a lover of money. Money runs through this letter: godliness as a means of gain (6:5), the love of money as a root of all kinds of evils (6:10). Elders may be paid (5:17–18), but they must not be in it for money. A man who loves money will eventually be bought, and everyone will find out what the price was.

What they have in common. Each of the four is a way of handling pressure or appetite badly, and each is invisible to a congregation until it is too late. You can assess a man’s preaching in twenty minutes; these take years to see. Ask his wife, his children and the people who have disagreed with him.

The gentleness of Christ. Paul appealed to the Corinthians “by the meekness and gentleness of Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:1), using the noun of this word. The Lord of glory came gentle and lowly in heart. He would not quench a smouldering wick, a faith barely alight (Matthew 12:20); he restored Peter with questions by a charcoal fire rather than a rebuke (John 21:15–17); when he was reviled he did not revile in return. And the one man who never loved silver was sold for thirty pieces of it by a man who did. His gentleness is the strength of a King with nothing to prove, and it is how he shepherds us still. An elder is to be gentle because the church already has a Shepherd who is.

What if my pastor is harsh, controlling or a bully? Then he is failing one of the plainest requirements of his office, and it must not be excused as strong leadership. A man who manipulates, intimidates, shames people from the pulpit or punishes disagreement is domineering over the flock (1 Peter 5:3). If it is a single incident, speak to him privately and humbly. If it is a pattern, take it to the other elders, or to whatever wider body your church answers to. If you have been harmed, you are not being disloyal by speaking up, and abuse of any kind, spiritual, emotional or physical, must never be covered up to protect a leader’s reputation. The flock belongs to Christ, not to the shepherd.

Should Christians drink alcohol at all? Scripture permits it and warns against its abuse. Jesus made wine at a wedding, and wine gladdens the heart (Psalm 104:15). But drunkenness is sin (Ephesians 5:18), and wisdom may call for abstinence: a history of addiction, drink as a destroyer in your family, a friend who is struggling, or simply a weaker brother (Romans 14:21). Many godly Christians abstain, and many drink moderately. Neither should judge the other, and both should watch that it never becomes their master.

verseByVerse.quote: He must manage his own household well, with all dignity keeping his children submissive, for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man who cannot lead his own family with dignified, loving care is not fit to care for God’s family.

He must manage his own household well. Manage (proistēmi) is to lead and to care for, the word used of elders who rule well (5:17). The household included family, servants and property.

With all dignity. Probably the father’s manner: he keeps order with dignity, not by shouting or force. A house kept in line by fear would meet the letter of this requirement and fail its spirit; Paul has already ruled out the violent man (v. 3). This concerns children still at home.

For if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God’s church? The argument runs from lesser to greater, and assumes what the modern church often forgets: that home and congregation are the same kind of thing. Both are households, and Paul will call the church the household of God ten verses later (v. 15).

Care for. Paul does not ask how a man will manage God’s church but how he will care for it (epimeleomai), the word used of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:34–35). Church leadership is not corporate management but tender care.

The Son over the house. Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant, but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son (Hebrews 3:5–6). An elder is never the master of the church, only a steward in the Son’s house. And the house has a Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named. He rules it with perfect dignity and tenderness, never harsh, never neglectful, disciplining his children for their good and running to meet the prodigal on the road. He has never once mismanaged it. Every earthly father, and every elder, is learning to do in small what he does perfectly.

What it does not mean. Not perfect children, nor disqualification because an adult child has chosen to rebel: children have their own wills, and Scripture nowhere promises that a good father’s children will all believe. It means a pattern of godly, loving leadership.

The place where character is known. The principle reaches everyone. Public competence is easy to manufacture for a few hours a week; nobody sustains a performance before the people who see him tired. Ask how a man’s children speak of him when he is not in the room.

In everyday life. Fathers: is your leadership at home marked by dignity and care, or by harshness or neglect? Lead out of the Father’s patience with you, not fear of failing; his Spirit gives what you lack. Children learn what God the Father is like by watching their fathers, so this week apologise to one of yours for something you got wrong.

Have I failed if my child has walked away from the faith? Not necessarily, and do not assume it. Every parent fails, and it is right to confess those failures to God and, where it helps, to your child. But a child’s faith is not manufactured by parenting; it is the gift of God. Adam and Eve had a perfect Father and walked away. Keep loving your child, keep the door open, keep praying, and do not turn every conversation into a sermon. Many prodigals have come home years later, remembering a father or mother who never stopped loving them. Leave the outcome with God, who loves your child more than you do.

verseByVerse.quote: He must not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit and fall into the condemnation of the devil. Moreover, he must be well thought of by outsiders, so that he may not fall into disgrace, into a snare of the devil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An overseer must be mature enough not to be swollen by office, and well enough regarded outside the church that his life does not undo his message. Each requirement carries a warning: the devil brings leaders down through pride and through disgrace.

He must not be a recent convert. Recent convert (neophytos) is newly planted, our neophyte: however gifted, not yet tested. The church at Ephesus was about ten years old; in Crete, where the churches were all new and every believer a recent convert, Paul omits this requirement (Titus 1:5–9).

Puffed up with conceit. Puffed up (typhoō, related to a word for smoke) is swollen larger than the substance warrants. Give a new believer standing quickly, and you may be endangering him rather than honouring him.

The condemnation of the devil. The sin that ruined the devil was pride, and a man promoted before he is ready is being walked along the same road (on the phrase, see “Uncertain wording” below).

Well thought of by outsiders. The most surprising qualification: the opinion of non-Christians, who see the man when he is not being religious. They need not approve of his beliefs, for the gospel will always offend; but they must not be able to say he is dishonest, cruel or unreliable.

A snare of the devil. Snare (pagis) is a bird-trap (2 Timothy 2:26). A leader with a bad reputation outside the church is already caught: everything he says about Christ is discounted by those who know what he is like. The enemy appears throughout this letter (1:20; 2:14; 4:1); these qualifications are part of the good warfare of 1:18, and an unready or disreputable leader is a gap in the wall.

Thirty quiet years. The Son of God, sinless from the cradle, spent some thirty years in a carpenter’s home, increasing in wisdom and in stature, before his public ministry began (Luke 2:52; 3:23). Even then, the Spirit first led him into the wilderness, where the devil offered him every shortcut to glory and he refused them all (Luke 4:1–13). If the Lord of the church was content to wait for his Father’s hour, his under-shepherds can wait for theirs. And because the Son humbled himself, the devil’s condemnation will never touch those who are hidden in him.

In everyday life. What would your neighbours and colleagues say about you if the subject came up? Be the one who pays on time, keeps his word, and treats the cleaner with the same respect as the director.

How long is a recent convert? Scripture gives no number of years, wisely, because people mature at different speeds. The question is whether a man’s faith has been tested by time and trouble, his character seen under pressure, and his humility under correction.
