In an established church that usually means years, not months; Paul himself spent years in relative obscurity before his great missionary work began (Galatians 1:17–18; 2:1).

Should a famous convert be put on the platform straight away? No, and churches do great harm when they do. A celebrity who comes to Christ is a cause for joy, and his testimony may be told. But a pulpit, a book contract or a leadership role before his roots have grown is exactly what this verse forbids, and many such men have fallen publicly, to the gospel’s shame and their own harm. Love him by letting him be an ordinary church member for a good long while: learning, serving, being known.

Uncertain wording. “The condemnation of the devil” may mean the condemnation the devil himself received, or the accusation he brings against a fallen leader; the Greek allows either. Most take the first, since pride brought the devil down.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those who serve the church’s practical needs must be as trustworthy as those who teach it. Deacons must be dignified, honest in speech, free from drink and greed, and hold the faith with a clear conscience (vv. 8–9), and they are tested before they serve (v. 10). The women of verse 11, deacons’ wives or women deacons, meet the same standard, and deacons must be faithful in marriage and home (v. 12). Faithful service is promised not promotion but a good standing and great confidence in Christ (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology:
Wives, or Women Deacons?

The gynaikas of verse 11 may be deacons’ wives (so the ESV) or women serving as deacons (compare Phoebe, Romans 16:1). The passage does not settle it; the standard of character is the same either way.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: On what is missing from the deacons’ list, see the note on vv. 8–10.

Now: Test first, then appoint (see the note on vv. 8–10).

verseByVerse.quote: Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for dishonest gain. They must hold the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience. And let them also be tested first; then let them serve as deacons if they prove themselves blameless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who serve the church’s practical needs must be as trustworthy as those who teach it, and proven before they are appointed.

Deacons likewise. Deacons (diakonoi) are servants. The office is often traced to Acts 6:1–6, where seven men handled the distribution to widows so that the apostles could devote themselves to prayer and the word. Deacons serve rather than teach, so “able to teach” is missing from their list; everything else is just as demanding.

Not double-tongued. Dignified is serious, worthy of respect. Double-tongued is literally two-worded (dilogos): saying one thing in one house and another in the next, a real danger for men who move between households hearing everybody’s business.

Not greedy for dishonest gain. Deacons handled the church’s money and gifts to the poor, often with no one checking the accounts. The disciples once had a treasurer, Judas, who helped himself to what was put into the bag (John 12:6).

The mystery of the faith. Mystery (mystērion) is a truth once hidden, now revealed. Deacons need not expound the faith, but they must hold it with a clear conscience, the letter’s steady link between belief and behaviour (1:5, 19). A man may distribute bread faultlessly while hiding a sin he has not dealt with, and Paul will not have it.

Tested first. Tested (dokimazō) is the assayer’s word for testing metal: not necessarily a formal probation, but an observed track record. Blameless (anenklētos) is unaccused. Paul’s order is: observe the man, then appoint him. The reverse order has brought many churches to grief.

The mystery is a person. Paul names the mystery at the end of the chapter, in a hymn about Christ (3:16): not a secret doctrine for insiders but the open secret of the Son of God made man, crucified, raised and reigning. A deacon who holds this faith is holding on to Christ himself, and every deacon who carries a meal or keeps an honest ledger is following the steps of a Servant-King, who emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and has been highly exalted.

In everyday life. Deacons serve quietly. Look for one practical need in your church that nobody has noticed, and meet it without telling anyone.

What do deacons do in a church today? Whatever practical service frees the elders to pray, teach and shepherd. In many churches deacons care for the poor, manage finances and buildings, organise care for the sick and elderly, welcome newcomers, run the practical side of the Lord’s Supper and baptisms, and coordinate volunteers. Scripture leaves room for the details to vary. The spirit does not: deacons serve so that the Word can run and no one in need is forgotten, as in Acts 6, where widows were being overlooked.

Is serving less spiritual than teaching? No. The word deacon means servant, and the Lord of the church took that title for himself: “I am among you as the one who serves” (Luke 22:27). The seven in Acts 6 had to be full of the Spirit and of wisdom, to wait on tables. Carrying meals to a widow, fixing a leaking roof, counting the offering honestly and driving an old man to church are as much the work of Christ as preaching, and often how the gospel becomes visible to a watching world.
verseByVerse.note: Deacons (“servants”) cared for the church’s practical needs.

verseByVerse.quote: Their wives likewise must be dignified, not slanderers, but sober-minded, faithful in all things. Let deacons each be the husband of one wife, managing their children and their own households well. For those who serve well as deacons gain a good standing for themselves and also great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The women who serve, whether deacons’ wives or women deacons, must be as trustworthy as the men, and all who serve faithfully gain a firm standing and a bold faith in Christ.

Their wives likewise. The Greek says simply “women” (gynaikas), so the verse may describe deacons’ wives or women deacons (see “Uncertain wording” below). Either way, they are held to the deacons’ own standard, quality for quality.

Not slanderers. Slanderers (diaboloi) is the word used of the devil, whose name means accuser. Careless talk about people is given the devil’s own title, which should sober anyone who has ever enjoyed passing something on.

Faithful in all things. The woman to whom you could give the keys, the money and the secret, and sleep well.

Husband of one wife. The same requirements as for elders (vv. 2, 4).

A good standing. A promise rather than a requirement: a good step (bathmon kalon), good ground to stand on, respect in the church.

Great confidence. Confidence (parrēsia) is boldness, freedom of speech, as of Peter and John before the council (Acts 4:13). Paul promises deacons not promotion but this: assurance before God and boldness before others. A man or woman who has carried food to widows for years, quietly and honestly, gains a settledness in the faith that study alone never produces.

Boldness that rests on Christ. The confidence lies in the faith that is in Christ Jesus (compare Ephesians 3:12): a faithful deacon grows bold not by admiring his record but by watching Christ, year after year, keep his promises in the homes of the poor and the sick.

Christ’s name is Advocate. The accuser spreads what will wound. Christ is our Advocate, speaking for us before the Father, covering our sins rather than exposing them. He knows every secret of every household in his church, yet has never betrayed a confidence or brought up again a sin he has forgiven. He is faithful in all things, and the accuser’s whispers fall silent before the one who has answered every charge against his people with his own blood.

So may my church have women deacons? It may, and many faithful churches do; others keep the office for men and have women serve alongside in diaconal work without the title. Within a few generations the church had women formally serving in this way, caring for women in need, visiting the sick and assisting at the baptism of women. The work matters more than the title. If your church is divided on the question, do not let it become a cause of quarrelling; Paul has just said that a quarrelsome man is unfit to lead.

How do I share a prayer need without gossiping? Ask three questions. Is it mine to tell? If it was told you in confidence, it is not, and asking for prayer does not change that. Would they be glad to hear me telling it? If not, keep it between you and God. And is my aim that this person be helped, or that I be the one who knows? Often the best prayer request is the vaguest: “Please pray for a friend going through a hard time.” Gossip disguised as concern is still gossip, and the devil’s name is on it.

Where Christians differ: may women serve as deacons? Some say the diaconate is for men only; others allow women deacons. This commentary’s view: Either reading of verse 11 is within faithful bounds. Since deacons do not hold the authority to teach and govern the church (2:12), women may serve in a diaconal capacity, as Phoebe did. Churches should decide wisely and charitably, without treating the question as a test of orthodoxy.

Uncertain wording. The Greek word (gynaikas) means either wives or women, and there is no word for “their”, so the verse is genuinely ambiguous. Serious Christians hold two readings: (1) the wives of deacons, who would assist their husbands in ministry; or (2) women deacons, often called deaconesses. For the second: “likewise” introduces a new group, as in verse 8; the qualities match the deacons’ own point for point; no qualifications are given for elders’ wives, which would be odd if deacons’ wives needed them; and Phoebe, “a patron of many”, is called a diakonos of the church at Cenchreae (Romans 16:1–2). For the first: the verse sits inside the deacon paragraph, and verse 12 returns to male deacons as husbands of one wife. The ESV reads “their wives”, with a note that the word can mean “women”.
verseByVerse.note: “Their wives” may also be translated “women,” that is, women deacons; the Greek can mean either.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: All of this matters because the church is God’s household and holds up his truth, and that truth is Christ. Paul states why he writes: so that Timothy may know how to behave in the household of the living God, the pillar and buttress of the truth (vv. 14–15). Then he shows what the pillar holds up, in an early hymn that runs from Christ’s coming in the flesh to his being taken up in glory (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology:
Pillar and Buttress

The church does not create the truth; it holds it up where it can be seen (see the note on vv. 14–15). And in the hymn of verse 16 God is doing all of it (see the note on v. 16).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In a city proud of Artemis’s hundred-odd columns, house churches are called the pillar of the truth.

Now: The question to ask of a church is whether it is holding up Christ (see the note on vv. 14–15).

verseByVerse.quote: I hope to come to you soon, but I am writing these things to you so that, if I delay, you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul writes so that the church will know how to live as what it is: the household of the living God, holding up his truth for the world to see. This is the purpose of the whole letter.

I am writing these things. Paul intends to come, but he may not, and the letter stands in for his presence, now for the whole church in every generation.

The household of God. Chapter 3 has been building to this: the overseer must manage his own household because the church is one. A household in that world was not a nuclear family but kin, servants and dependants, with an order to it and a head. The church is that, and it is God’s: God as Father, believers as brothers and sisters, elders as stewards (Titus 1:7).

The church of the living God. “Living” has a sharp edge in Ephesus, whose great temple housed an image that could not move, said to have fallen from the sky, and whose craftsmen made a living selling silver shrines of it (Acts 19:23–41). The true God is alive and present among his people, and the Thessalonians turned to him from idols, “to serve the living and true God” (1 Thessalonians 1:9). And the living God is holy: “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Hebrews 10:31), which is why Paul cares how people behave in his house: it is not a club with rules but the dwelling of the Holy One.

A pillar and buttress of the truth. A pillar (stylos) holds a thing up where it can be seen; a buttress (hedraiōma) keeps it from shifting. The temple of Artemis, according to Pliny, had 127 columns, each sixty feet high; Paul takes the vocabulary of the most famous building in Asia and gives it to a congregation meeting in houses.

The right way round. The church does not create the truth or make it true. A pillar does not make the roof; it holds it up where people can see it. The truth stands on its own; the church holds it visibly in place, as the false teachers of chapter 1 were failing to do.

A temple with a cornerstone. Paul had told the Ephesians what this temple stands on: the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20–22). The living God does not live in a marble shrine but among forgiven people, joined to his Son. And the truth the pillar holds up is not finally a system but that same Son, who said, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). A congregation is not chiefly a service provider, a campaign or a community centre; it is a pillar of the truth to the degree that it lifts Christ up where the town can see him. The temple of Artemis lies in ruins, a single reconstructed column standing in a marsh; the household of the living God still stands in every nation, because the one it rests on is alive.

In everyday life. Think of your church as it really is, weak points and awkward people included. Christ has built you into this house; are you bearing weight in it, or watching from the forecourt?

Why do I need to belong to a local church? Because this is the home God has made for you, and you cannot belong to a household by yourself. The New Testament knows nothing of Christians who believe privately and belong nowhere: every command about loving one another, bearing burdens, submitting to elders, using gifts and sharing the Lord’s Supper assumes you are in a church. Online sermons can feed you, but they cannot know you, visit you when you are ill, correct you when you wander or need your gifts. Find a church where the Bible is taught faithfully, join it, and commit yourself to its people.

What if my church is a poor pillar? Every church is imperfect, and Timothy’s was troubled by false teachers. Do not leave over preferences, disappointments or ordinary weakness; pray, serve, and be part of the remedy. But if a church has abandoned the gospel itself, denying the truths about Christ that the church has always confessed, or refusing to submit to Scripture, it has stopped being a pillar of the truth, and you should find one that still is. The question is not whether the church is impressive but whether it is holding up Christ.

Where Christians differ: does the church stand above Scripture? Roman Catholic teaching uses this verse to argue that the church, through its teaching office, is the infallible guardian and interpreter of truth, and that Scripture and tradition together form the rule of faith. This commentary’s view: The church supports the truth; it does not create it or stand over it. The truth is God’s Word, which the church receives, guards and proclaims (2 Timothy 1:13–14; Jude 3). When a church departs from Scripture, it ceases to be a pillar of truth, as the false teachers in Ephesus showed. Scripture alone is the final authority over the church (sola Scriptura, by Scripture alone). Roman Catholic Christians who see it otherwise often love the church’s long history deeply, and that love is right; the question is only whether the church is the roof or the pillar.

verseByVerse.quote: Great indeed, we confess, is the mystery of godliness: He was manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The truth the church holds up is Christ himself, and Paul sums him up in a hymn that runs from his coming in the flesh to his reign in glory.

Great indeed, we confess, is the mystery of godliness. We confess (homologoumenōs) is by common confession, undeniably. Mystery is a truth once hidden and now revealed, and this one produces godliness. The opening may be a deliberate contrast with the two-hour cry in the theatre at Ephesus: “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” (Acts 19:28, 34). The mob shouted the greatness of a goddess who could not hear them. The church confesses the greatness of a Saviour who came.

A hymn. What follows is almost certainly an early hymn or creed: six lines, each opening with a verb in the same form, perhaps in three pairs contrasting earth and heaven. Every verb is passive: Christ is the subject throughout, and God is doing all of it.

He was manifested in the flesh. The truth at the centre of godliness is a person. “He” is literally “who” (see the textual note below). Manifested is made visible, which means he existed before he appeared; and in the flesh, true human nature, not a costume (John 1:14). The line rules out the two errors the early church had to fight: that he was not truly divine, and that he was not truly human.

Vindicated by the Spirit. Vindicated (dikaioō) is declared righteous, shown to be in the right. Condemned by a Jewish council and a Roman court, he was “declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection from the dead” (Romans 1:4): God’s higher court overturned their verdict (on the phrase, see “Uncertain wording” below).

Seen by angels. Angels appear at every turning point of his life, from the announcement to the empty tomb and the ascension (Acts 1:10–11), and they long to look into this salvation still (1 Peter 1:12).

Proclaimed among the nations. The message went to the whole world; Paul himself had been appointed its herald to the Gentiles (2:7).

Believed on in the world. Not merely proclaimed but believed, the least likely line of all. A crucified provincial was announced to the empire, and people believed it, though there was no army, no money and no prestige behind the message, only witnesses who had seen him alive and held to it under threat of death (1 Corinthians 15:3–8), and the Spirit opening hearts. The church in Ephesus existed because that line came true, and every believer today is more evidence of it.

Taken up in glory. The word used of the ascension (Acts 1:2, 11). The hymn ends where he now is, reigning at the Father’s right hand, from where he will come again.

What it is all for. This is why a chapter on the unglamorous machinery of a church ends here: the rules about drink and quarrelling exist so that the pillar stands straight and Christ can be seen from the street.

In everyday life. When you are weary of the meetings, the rotas and the disagreements about small things, read the six lines aloud slowly, and take one line a day this week into your prayers.

What is godliness, and how does a hymn about Christ produce it? Godliness (eusebeia) is the whole person living before God’s face in reverence, love and obedience, and it grows from this mystery and from nothing else. You do not become godly by trying harder to be religious, as the false teachers taught, but by beholding Christ. As we see the glory of the Lord, we are transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another (2 Corinthians 3:18). The incarnate, risen, ascended Christ is not only the object of your faith but the pattern and power of your new life.

Uncertain wording. “Vindicated by the Spirit” renders a compressed phrase, literally “in spirit” or “in the Spirit” (en pneumati), set against “in the flesh”. It may mean that the Holy Spirit vindicated him, above all by raising him (Romans 1:4; 8:11), or that he was vindicated in the realm of the Spirit, his risen life, as against his earthly life in the flesh (compare 1 Peter 3:18). The two overlap, since the Spirit raised him to that life, and the ESV’s “by the Spirit” gives the likely sense.

Textual note. Many later manuscripts (followed by the KJV) read “God was manifest in the flesh” (theos) instead of “He who was manifested” (hos). In ancient manuscripts, the abbreviation for God (ΘΣ) looked very like “who” (ΟΣ) with a small line added. The earliest and best manuscripts read “who”, and this is the more likely original. The deity of Christ does not depend on this verse; it is clearly taught elsewhere (John 1:1; Romans 9:5; Titus 2:13; Hebrews 1:8), and the hymn itself assumes his pre-existence.
verseByVerse.note: Probably an early Christian hymn or creed, with six lines in three pairs. “He” is literally “Who” in Greek; some manuscripts read “God,” others “Which” (ESV note).

3.text: <sup>1</sup>The saying is trustworthy: If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task.<sup>2</sup>Therefore an overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach,<sup>3</sup>not a drunkard, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money.<sup>4</sup>He must manage his own household well, with all dignity keeping his children submissive,<sup>5</sup>for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?<sup>6</sup>He must not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit and fall into the condemnation of the devil.<sup>7</sup>Moreover, he must be well thought of by outsiders, so that he may not fall into disgrace, into a snare of the devil.<sup>8</sup>Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for dishonest gain.<sup>9</sup>They must hold the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience.<sup>10</sup>And let them also be tested first; then let them serve as deacons if they prove themselves blameless.<sup>11</sup>Their wives likewise must be dignified, not slanderers, but sober-minded, faithful in all things.<sup>12</sup>Let deacons each be the husband of one wife, managing their children and their own households well.<sup>13</sup>For those who serve well as deacons gain a good standing for themselves and also great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.<sup>14</sup>I hope to come to you soon, but I am writing these things to you so that,<sup>15</sup>if I delay, you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth.<sup>16</sup>Great indeed, we confess, is the mystery of godliness: He was manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory.

keyVerse.quote: if I delay, you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth.
keyVerse.note: Paul here tells Timothy why he is writing, and it explains the whole chapter: leaders must be tested and trustworthy because the church is God’s own household, set to hold up his truth where the world can see it. The very next verse names that truth, and it is Christ.

3.reflection:
Almost every qualification for an overseer concerns character, and only one is a skill (vv. 2–7). Why do you think God puts character first? In what ways are churches, and we ourselves, tempted to value gifts, confidence or a following more?

Paul ties a leader’s fitness to his conduct at home, and calls the church the household of God (vv. 4–5, 15). What difference does it make to think of your church as a family rather than an organisation or a service you attend?

Faithful deacons are promised not promotion but “great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus” (v. 13). Where have you seen quiet, faithful service strengthen someone’s faith? What unnoticed need in your church could you meet?

Read the six lines of verse 16 aloud together. Which line moves you most, and how does seeing Christ like this produce godliness rather than mere rule-keeping?

4.title: A Good Servant of Christ Jesus
4.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 3 ended with the church as “a pillar and buttress of the truth” and a hymn to Christ “manifested in the flesh” (3:15–16). Chapter 4 turns to the lies that attack that truth, and then to the kind of minister who will hold it up.

The message. What God made is good, and godliness does not come by refusing his gifts but by receiving them with thanks and training the soul on his word. Against a religion of refusal, which the Spirit unmasks as demonic in origin, Paul sets the doctrine of creation, the habit of thanksgiving, and a pastor whose ordinary faithfulness is God’s means of bringing a church safely home: reading Scripture aloud, teaching, living what he teaches, and watching his own life and doctrine to the end.

Why it was said. The false teachers at Ephesus forbade marriage and certain foods (see the introduction), and their severity looked impressive, the way strict religion usually does. The man sent to resist them was young for the task, facing older men who were inclined to look down on him (v. 12). He needed to know that the error was not merely mistaken but spiritual in its roots, and that the answer to it was not a cleverer strategy but steady, visible faithfulness.

How the chapter makes its case. The Spirit foretold the apostasy, and named its source: deceiving spirits speaking through men with seared consciences (vv. 1–2). Their rules forbid what God created to be received with thanksgiving (v. 3), but everything God made is good, made holy by his word and prayer (vv. 4–5). Timothy’s answer is to set these truths before the church, keep feeding on them, refuse the myths and train for godliness, which holds promise for this life and the next (vv. 6–8), because our hope is in the living God, the Saviour of all, especially of those who believe (vv. 9–10). He is to be an example despite his youth (vv. 11–12), give himself to the public reading, preaching and teaching of Scripture, use the gift the elders recognised (vv. 13–14), and keep watch over himself and the teaching, for that is how God saves both preacher and hearers (vv. 15–16).

Where it leads. The teaching that despises the body is answered by the Son of God who took one, ate at tables, gave thanks over bread and then gave himself. He is the reader in the synagogue at Nazareth whose Scriptures were about himself, and the Chief Shepherd who kept perfect watch over his life and teaching and persisted to the end, saving not himself but all who believe. The chapter that begins with demons ends with a young man reading the Bible aloud to a congregation, and that is the whole strategy of God against the lie.

For us. Receive God’s ordinary gifts, food, marriage, rest and pleasure, with thanks rather than suspicion or greed. Train for godliness by small, steady means, keep your conscience tender, and value the public reading and preaching of Scripture in your church. Pray for those who teach you, that they may watch their lives and their doctrine, and watch your own.

verseByVerse.ref: 4:1–5 – Some Will Depart from the Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What God made is good, and is to be received with thanks; teaching that forbids it comes from a lie. The Spirit foretold that some would abandon the faith, led by deceiving spirits through men whose consciences no longer feel (vv. 1–2). Their rules forbid marriage and foods (v. 3). Paul answers with creation: God made these things to be received with thanksgiving by believers, nothing he made is to be rejected, and the word of God and prayer make an ordinary meal holy (vv. 4–5).
verseByVerse.theology:
False Teaching That Restricts Rather Than Permits

The Ephesian error was ascetic: it made holiness a matter of giving things up, and impressed by how much it gave up. Paul answers it with Genesis 1 (see the notes on vv. 3 and 4–5).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A conscience is seared one small step at a time (see the note on vv. 1–2).

Now: Giving thanks at the table sets an ordinary meal apart for God (see the note on vv. 4–5).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Spirit expressly says that in later times some will depart from the faith by devoting themselves to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, through the insincerity of liars whose consciences are seared,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit has warned that some who profess the faith will abandon it, led by deceiving spirits speaking through men who have silenced their own consciences. False teaching is not only bad reasoning: behind ordinary persuasion there can be a will set against God.

The Spirit expressly says. Explicitly, in plain terms (rhētōs), as the Spirit had said through Jesus (Mark 13:22) and through Paul (Acts 20:29–30). There is comfort in that. Apostasy has never taken the church by surprise: its Lord told his people in advance, so that when it happens it shows not that he has lost control but that he spoke the truth. Some depart, but none whom the Father gave to the Son is lost.

In later times. Not a distant final period. The New Testament treats the whole time between Christ’s two comings as the last days (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2), and the prophecy was being fulfilled in the room where the letter was read, as it has been in some room in every generation since.

Depart from the faith. A standing away (aphistēmi, the verb behind our word apostasy): not pagans who never believed, but people who had professed the faith, sat in the meetings, perhaps taught in them, and then walked away.

Deceitful spirits and teachings of demons. The men in Ephesus were church people with opinions about genealogies and diet, yet Paul says something else was in the room: deceiving spirits at work behind the teachers (2 Corinthians 11:13–15; 1 John 4:1–3). Satan’s great weapon has always been the lie: he is a liar and the father of lies (John 8:44).

The insincerity of liars. The demonic works through ordinary channels: no possession, no darkened room. Insincerity (hypokrisis) is the actor behind a mask: men saying what they know to be untrue, in a normal voice, wearing the face of piety. The devil rarely appears with horns. He far prefers a pulpit.

Whose consciences are seared. Searing is done with a hot iron (kaustēriazō), and there are two pictures in it: a slave branded as someone’s property, and a wound cauterised until the flesh no longer feels. These men have overruled their consciences until the nerve has died, as 1:19 described: first the conscience is pushed aside, then the faith is wrecked. It happens one small overruling at a time, and the frightening part is that by the end it does not hurt.

The setting. The false teaching had an ascetic strand (see the introduction): it treated marriage and certain foods as spiritually dangerous, perhaps mixing Jewish food laws with Greek ideas that matter is inferior to spirit. The teachers may also have believed the resurrection had already happened (2 Timothy 2:18), so that believers should already live like angels, who do not marry (Luke 20:35–36).

The same Spirit who vindicated him. The chapter break hides a link. The Spirit who vindicated Christ “manifested in the flesh” (3:16) now warns against a teaching that despises the flesh. If matter were unclean, the Son of God could not have taken a body, eaten at tables, or been raised bodily from the tomb. Teaching that despises the body is, at bottom, embarrassed by the incarnation.

A dead conscience made to feel again. Against the father of lies stands the God who cannot lie, and against every seared conscience stands the blood of Christ, which purifies the conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:14). It does what no surgeon can: it makes a dead conscience feel again.

In everyday life. Keep your conscience tender by confessing sin quickly. Notice the small things you have learned to overrule: the unkind remark, the figure rounded in your favour, the thing you watch that you would not watch with your pastor in the room. Go to God about them while they still sting, because the sting is a mercy.

Can a genuine Christian be deceived like this? A true believer can be misled for a season, especially on secondary matters: the Galatians were bewitched for a while (Galatians 3:1), and Peter had to be corrected (Galatians 2:11–14). But Christ’s sheep will not finally be snatched from his hand (John 10:27–29); the false christs would lead astray the elect “if possible” (Mark 13:22), and it is not. So the right response is watchfulness, not anxiety: stay close to Scripture and a faithful church, and keep your conscience soft. Those are the means by which God keeps his own.

How can I tell if a teaching comes from deceitful spirits? Not by how spiritual it sounds or how sincere the teacher seems, for hypocrisy is exactly the disguise Paul names. Ask three questions. What does it say about Jesus Christ: does it confess him come in the flesh, truly God and truly man, the only Saviour (1 John 4:2–3)? What does it do with Scripture: submit to it, or add to it, subtract from it, or claim a secret key to it? And what does it do to grace: rest everything on what Christ has done, or quietly move the weight onto what you must do or avoid? Teaching that makes Christ smaller, the Bible thinner or grace conditional is not from the Spirit of truth.

Is talk of demons not just an old way of describing bad ideas? Jesus spoke of the devil as a real person who lies and murders (John 8:44), and cast out demons as a sign that the kingdom of God had come (Luke 11:20). Yet Paul’s demons are undramatic: they work through sermons, opinions and diets, not séances. Behind ordinary persuasion there can be a will set against God. Wave that away and we have not become wiser than Jesus, only easier to deceive. The remedy is not fear but Christ, who disarmed the powers at the cross (Colossians 2:15).

verseByVerse.quote: who forbid marriage and require abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The false teachers forbade marriage and foods, the two most bodily of God’s gifts, though God made both to be received with thanks by his people. Paul answers their religion of refusal not with a compromise but with the doctrine of creation.

Who forbid marriage. We assume false teaching will be permissive; this kind impressed by how much it gave up. It treated marriage as unspiritual, against the God who said it is not good for the man to be alone (Genesis 2:18–24) and calls the marriage bed undefiled (Hebrews 13:4).

Abstinence from foods. Probably specific foods were treated as impure, on the old and durable idea that the material world is the problem. Marriage and food are the two most bodily things there are, so both had to go (compare Colossians 2:21). Such rules pull at the heart: they give you something to measure and be proud of, and put holiness within your own control. That is why they impress, and why they are do-it-yourself salvation, with no power to hold back our sinful desires (Colossians 2:23).

That God created to be received with thanksgiving. Paul goes straight to creation. God made food (ktizō, created; Genesis 1:29–31; 9:3), and that clause dismantles the whole system: refusing what he made on purpose is not superior spirituality but an insult to the Giver, and declining a gift made for you is not humility. He made it to be received (metalēmpsis, a sharing, a partaking) meta eucharistias, with thanksgiving: the word behind Eucharist, an old name for the Lord’s Supper, as though every meal were meant to be a small thanksgiving service.

By those who believe and know the truth. Believers know that Christ has declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19; Acts 10:15). And more: an unbeliever can eat and marry with great pleasure, but he cannot receive them as gifts, because he does not know there is anyone to thank. The Christian alone can taste the bread and see the hand that gave it.

What marriage and bread were made to show. The false teachers banned the two things God has used most plainly to picture his Son. Marriage was made from the beginning with Christ in view: its union “refers to Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:31–32). And bread is the sign Christ chose for his body given for us (Luke 22:19). To forbid them as unspiritual is to tear down God’s pictures of his Son’s love and sacrifice. The demons forbid; God gives. When Adam and Eve took the one tree, he did not withdraw the rest. The Lord came eating and drinking (Luke 7:34), and on the night he was betrayed, the Son through whom every grain of wheat was made took bread, gave thanks for it, and then gave himself, so that the hungry might eat and live for ever. A religion of refusal cannot follow a Saviour who gives.

What it does not mean. It does not forbid voluntary fasting, or personal abstinence for health, conscience or love for a weaker brother (Romans 14:21). The error is making abstinence a rule that defines holiness.

I am single, and not by choice. Is this verse saying I am missing out on God’s best? No. Paul is attacking teachers who forbade marriage as unholy, not saying every Christian must marry or that the unmarried are second class. Neither your singleness nor your longing for marriage, a desire for a good thing God made, is a spiritual failure: bring the longing to him honestly. Jesus was unmarried, and so, at least in his ministry, was Paul. Your life is not on hold: you have real freedom to serve (1 Corinthians 7:32–35), a family in the church (Mark 10:29–30), and the same full inheritance in Christ as any married saint. God’s best for you is himself, and he is not rationed by marital status.

Are there modern versions of this error? Yes, rarely in religious language: the Christian circle where what you do not eat, drink or own becomes the badge of seriousness; the hint that married people are less devoted; the wellness gospel that treats certain foods as defiling rather than merely unhelpful. Self-denial for love of Christ and neighbour is good. Self-denial as a ladder to holiness, or a way to look down on others, is the Ephesian error in modern dress (Colossians 2:20–23).

Where Christians differ: is celibacy holier than marriage? Some traditions require celibacy of clergy, or have treated virginity as a higher spiritual state. This commentary’s view: Celibacy is a gift for some, and can free a person for undistracted service (1 Corinthians 7:7, 32–35; Matthew 19:12). But marriage is equally honourable and holy (Hebrews 13:4), and neither state is more meritorious before God. Forbidding ministers to marry contradicts this passage and 3:2, where an elder may plainly be married. The Reformers applied this verse to compulsory clerical celibacy, and rightly: singleness freely chosen for the kingdom is good; a rule forbidding ministers to marry is not.

verseByVerse.quote: For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving, for it is made holy by the word of God and prayer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything God made is good, and becomes holy for our use when we receive it with thanks, through his word and prayer. Paul does not divide foods into clean and unclean; he divides the ways of receiving them, with thanks or without.

For everything created by God is good. Paul echoes Genesis 1, where God pronounces what he made good, and then very good (Genesis 1:31), a verdict never withdrawn. The fall brought a curse (Romans 8:20) that spoiled how the world works and how we use it; it did not change who made it. A religion that treats the physical as unspiritual is at odds with the Bible’s first page; with its last, where the new creation has rivers and fruit and a city; and with its middle, where the Son of God took a body and kept it.

Nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving. No food is unclean in itself (Romans 14:14), but the condition is not a formality. The same meal eaten with gratitude and eaten greedily are two different acts.

Made holy by the word of God and prayer. Set apart for God’s use by two ordinary instruments: the word of God, perhaps the Genesis verdict just cited, and prayer, thanks before eating. So saying grace, the habit children learn first and adults do without thinking, is a holy act that sets an ordinary meal apart for God (1 Corinthians 10:31).

The harder way. Paul’s alternative is neither to refuse God’s gifts nor to grab them, but to take them and say thank you, which means thinking about God at the moment you are most likely to forget him. It is easy to remember God in a hospital. It takes grace to remember him at a feast.

Good because it is his. All things were created through the Son and for him (Colossians 1:16), so the goodness of bread, wine, marriage and morning light is Christ’s own workmanship. Before he fed the five thousand he said a blessing over five loaves (Mark 6:41), and every Christian grace at a table follows him. He is not the reluctant God of the ascetics, grudging every pleasure, but the overflowing Father who invented taste and colour, friendship and marriage, bread and wine, and gave them away.

What it does not mean. It does not mean anything is acceptable if we say grace over it; sin cannot be sanctified by prayer. Nor does it override love (1 Corinthians 8:13).

In everyday life. Take one ordinary pleasure today, the first cup of coffee, a walk in the light, an evening with your wife or husband, and receive it deliberately from God. A gift received tastes different from a thing merely taken.

Isn’t Christianity against pleasure? Many assume so; the Victorian poet Swinburne addressed Christ as the “pale Galilean” and complained that the world had grown grey from his breath. Yet here it is the false teachers who say no to marriage and food, and the apostle who says yes. And a culture that prides itself on enjoying the world often enjoys it least, because it asks of pleasure more than pleasure can give: when a meal, a body or a romance has to be your salvation, it buckles under the weight. C. S. Lewis, in The Screwtape Letters, has his senior devil grumble that the Enemy is a hedonist at heart: every real pleasure is God’s invention, and hell can only spoil them. Thanksgiving is the hinge. Someone who receives a gift from a Giver can enjoy it without needing it to be God, and find in the Giver himself the joy the gifts point to: “in your presence there is fullness of joy; at your right hand are pleasures forevermore” (Psalm 16:11).

Does this cover things like alcohol, or food I struggle with? It covers what God made, received rightly. Wine is among God’s gifts (Psalm 104:15; John 2:1–11), so total abstinence cannot be a test of holiness; but receiving with thanksgiving rules out drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18), and gluttony too. If something has become your master, it is not being received as a gift, and the wise thing may be to put it down altogether (1 Corinthians 6:12). That is freedom, not asceticism, as long as you do not make your choice a rule for everyone else (see the note on v. 3).

Is saying grace just a habit, or does it really matter? It matters, and this verse is why. Thanksgiving is not a superstition that makes food safe, and God does not need the words. But by it you confess, before him and whoever is at the table, that this came from his hand and not merely from the shop or your wages. If grace has become mechanical, do not stop; change it: name one thing on the table, or one mercy of the day. Children who hear you thank God for specific gifts will learn that the whole world is his.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A good servant of Christ Jesus is made by steady faithfulness, not by novelty or severity. He keeps feeding on sound doctrine, refuses the myths and trains for godliness, which holds promise for both lives because it rests on the living God (vv. 6–10). He sets the believers an example despite his youth (vv. 11–12), gives himself to reading, preaching and teaching Scripture and to the gift God gave him (vv. 13–14), and watches his life and doctrine to the end, the means by which God saves him and those who hear him (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology:
Godliness Is Trained For

Godliness is trained for like a body, by repetition (v. 7), and unlike bodily training its results survive the body, with value for this life as well as the next (v. 8). God is Saviour of all as their preserver, and especially of believers (v. 10).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Public reading of Scripture came first (v. 13) in a church where few could read: read, explain, apply.

Now: A young leader earns respect by being an example where nobody is watching (v. 12).

verseByVerse.quote: If you put these things before the brothers, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, being trained in the words of the faith and of the good doctrine that you have followed. Have nothing to do with irreverent, silly myths. Rather train yourself for godliness;
verseByVerse.commentary:
A good servant of Christ sets these truths before the church, keeps feeding on them himself, refuses the myths, and trains himself for godliness. Paul does not only forbid the wrong training; he gives Timothy the right one.

If you put these things before the brothers. To set before, as a host sets food on the table: the verb (hypotithēmi) is gentle. These things are the truths of verses 1–5. Timothy’s task is not to innovate but to serve up what he has been given.

A good servant of Christ Jesus. Servant (diakonos) here means minister. What makes a servant good is not brilliance or a large following but faithfulness in setting the truth before God’s people: a standard any minister can meet and none can exceed.

Being trained in the words of the faith. Trained is a feeding word (entrephomenos), and its form means going on being fed: Timothy is to keep feeding on the truth while he feeds others. A minister who has stopped being fed will shortly have nothing to serve.

That you have followed. Followed closely, the word Luke uses of his own research (Luke 1:3). Timothy had kept close to sound doctrine since childhood (2 Timothy 3:14–15). He was not chasing novelty.

Irreverent, silly myths. Irreverent (bebēlos) is profane, without any sense of the holy; silly (graōdeis) is literally old-womanish, tales told by the fire to keep children quiet. Paul does not stop to argue. Some error should be answered carefully; some should simply be refused a hearing, because it gains weight when treated as worth arguing about. These myths treat holy things as common, and leave a person less in awe of God than they found him.

Train yourself for godliness. Train is the gymnasium word (gymnaze): the disciplined, repetitive, unglamorous work of an athlete. The false teachers had their own rigorous training, in abstinence; Paul calls Timothy to the right kind: Scripture, prayer, worship, fellowship and obedience. Godliness is not a temperament some are born with. It is trained for, as a body is, by doing the same unremarkable things repeatedly, long after they stop feeling interesting. It is reverence for God that reaches into everything: a life that takes God as seriously at the breakfast table and at work as in church, because it knows he is there (Proverbs 3:6).

The mystery of godliness has a name. Paul has just spoken of “the mystery of godliness”, and his next words were about Christ (3:16). The secret of godliness is a person: the athlete trains towards a standard, the Christian towards a Saviour. That is why the myths must go: they offer spiritual exercise with Christ left out, and it builds nothing that lasts. And Christ still sets the truth before us, by his Spirit and through his servants; the bread he serves is himself.

In everyday life. Choose one discipline and practise it this week, small enough to keep and specific enough to check: ten minutes in the Gospel of Mark before breakfast, not a vague intention to read more.

If grace trains me, why do I have to train myself? Because grace does not bypass your will; it works through it. The athlete did not create his muscles or lungs, but he still has to run. It is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure, and that is exactly why you are told to work out your salvation (Philippians 2:12–13). Effort is not the opposite of grace; earning is. You train not to be accepted but because you already are, and because the Spirit has given you the desire. A Christian who waits to feel holy before he prays will wait a long time; one who prays in obedience finds, slowly, that the Spirit meets him there.

What does training for godliness actually look like? Ordinary things, done regularly. Reading the Bible daily, even briefly, with a plan. Praying at a set time and place, using the Lord’s Prayer or the Psalms when your own words dry up. Being in church every Lord’s Day, under the preached Word and at the Lord’s Table, as a fixed point. Memorising Scripture. Keeping close company with believers who will ask how you really are. Obeying in small things: the honest word, the kind act, the temptation refused. None of it is dramatic, and that is the point. Athletes do not train by waiting for big races; they train on wet Tuesdays.

verseByVerse.quote: for while bodily training is of some value, godliness is of value in every way, as it holds promise for the present life and also for the life to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bodily training does some good, but godliness does good in every way, because it carries God’s promise for this life and the next. The comparison is one of scope: godliness profits the whole person, in every sphere and for all time.

While bodily training is of some value. This is not the dismissal it is often taken for. Bodily training, prized in Ephesus with its great gymnasium, is of some value: a genuine concession from a man who has just defended food and marriage against people who despised the physical.

It holds promise for the present life and also for the life to come. It has a promise attached, like a deed. Even the strongest body weakens and dies; training for godliness is the only regime whose results survive the body it was performed in. But do not miss the first half. A life ordered towards God is better now: peace with God, contentment (6:6), wisdom, love and purpose, in the plain sense that self-control beats being ruled by appetite, a clear conscience sleeps better, and love makes richer company than resentment. And it holds promise for eternity, the inheritance and the crown (2 Timothy 4:8): not that godliness earns eternal life, but that eternal life is promised to those whom grace makes godly.

The promise of the life that is in Christ Jesus. Paul uses that phrase at the start of his next letter (2 Timothy 1:1). The promise attached to godliness is life in Christ, begun now as branches live in a vine (John 15:5), and complete when we are with him where he has gone to prepare a place (John 14:2–3). His body was laid in a tomb, and on the third day it rose, never to tire or age or die again. Because he lives, godliness is not a gamble but an investment with a promise attached, signed in his blood.

What it does not mean. It does not mean godliness guarantees health, wealth and comfort in this life. Paul himself suffered greatly (2 Timothy 3:12), and he will guard the promise against those who imagine that godliness is a means of gain (6:5).

In everyday life. Read your diary for a normal week as a training log, and see which part of you gets the best hours. The soul, like the body, answers not to inspiration but to small and steady change: one block of time moved, and kept for a month, will tell.

Should a Christian exercise, then? Yes, with a good conscience. Your body is God’s creation and the Spirit’s temple, and caring for it is stewardship, not vanity: exercise can give you energy to serve, clarity to think, and years to love your family and church. What Paul guards against is the inversion, when fitness or appearance becomes what you really live for, the hours at the gym guarded jealously while prayer and worship are fitted around them. The question is which training is getting the best of you. Keep the body in its place: valued, cared for, and second.

Uncertain wording. Of some value (pros oligon ōphelimos) is literally “profitable for a little”, which can mean a little in extent (it helps some things) or a little in time (it helps for a while). Both suit the contrast with a godliness of value “in every way” and for “the life to come”, and Paul may intend both. Bodily training may also glance at the false teachers’ regimen of self-denial (vv. 3, 7), but the gymnasium language of verses 7–8 makes physical exercise the likelier sense.

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance. For to this end we toil and strive, because we have our hope set on the living God, who is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul labours to exhaustion because his hope is fixed on the living God, who does good to all people and saves, in the full sense, those who believe. The trustworthy saying assures Timothy that godliness is worth everything it costs.

The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance. The third of the five trustworthy sayings in these letters (1:15; 3:1), most likely pointing back to verse 8. It is a seal: this can bear your whole weight.

For to this end we toil and strive. Toil (kopiaō) is labour to the point of weariness; strive (agōnizomai) is the athletic word for contending in the arena. With a plural we, Paul puts himself in the gymnasium beside Timothy.

Because we have our hope set on the living God. The fuel is hope rather than duty, and the tense means we fixed our hope and it remains fixed. A man will work himself to exhaustion for godliness because he expects something from a God who is alive.

Who is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe. A phrase that has caused genuine difficulty. It cannot mean everyone is finally saved, for this chapter has just spoken of men departing from the faith (see the boxes below); nor does “especially” mean that believers merely get a better version of the same thing. Saviour in Scripture covers rescue and preservation as well as eternal salvation. Most likely God is the preserver and benefactor of all people, giving life, breath, rain and food to all (Matthew 5:45; Acts 14:17; 17:25), and the Saviour in the full, eternal sense of believers. That fits the context exactly: against men who despised creation, Paul says the God who feeds and sustains everybody is the God who saves believers, the same generosity going far deeper for those who believe.

The living God has shown his face. The living God is not only the God who exists but the God who acts. The idols of Ephesus had mouths that could not speak and ears that could not hear (Psalm 115:5–6); Artemis had to be carried and defended by her worshippers, but the living God carries his people (Isaiah 46:3–4). We tend to treat him as a memory, someone who acted once in the Bible and has since gone quiet. Yet this letter has said how he saves: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners (1:15), the one mediator (2:5). And the proof that God lives is an empty tomb: Jesus was dead, and now he is “the living one” who holds the keys of Death and Hades (Revelation 1:18). Paul works for someone who is watching, answering and coming.

Rain on the fields of his enemies. He feeds the sparrows and the ungrateful, the farmer who curses him and the child who has never heard his name, because it is his nature to give. And to those who believe he gives what no harvest can grow: forgiveness, adoption, a living hope and an inheritance that cannot fade, bought with the blood of his Son. The God who sends rain on the fields of his enemies sent his Son to die for enemies, and made them his friends (Romans 5:10).

In everyday life. If your effort is running on duty alone, it will run out; lift your eyes to the living God and let hope do what willpower cannot. Pray as to someone who is in the room, and expect him to act, in his way and time. And every good thing in your unbelieving neighbour’s life is a kindness from the God who also offers him eternal life in Christ. Tell him whose kindness it is.

How does this fit with God choosing his people? Comfortably. Election is God’s choosing, before time began, of particular people to be saved in Christ, out of his own love and not for anything in them (Ephesians 1:4–5). Scripture also teaches that God is truly kind to all and sincerely offers Christ to all (Matthew 11:28; 2 Peter 3:9). He gives sun and rain to his enemies, commands all people everywhere to repent, and effectually draws those he has chosen, so that they believe (John 6:37, 44). His general goodness is real goodness, meant to lead people to repentance (Romans 2:4). Election does not shrink God’s kindness to the world; it guarantees that his saving purpose will not fail, which is why Paul could toil so hard.

Where Christians differ: does this verse teach universal salvation? Universalists cite it to argue that God will finally save everyone. This commentary’s view: The verse itself distinguishes between all people and those who believe, which would make no sense if all were saved in the same way, and Scripture plainly teaches that unbelievers will face eternal punishment (Matthew 25:46; John 3:36; 2 Thessalonians 1:9). God is the Saviour of all in that he preserves all, shows kindness to all, and offers the gospel freely to all; he is the Saviour of believers in that he actually rescues them from sin and death for ever.

Uncertain wording. Especially (malista) usually means most of all, which gives the reading above. It can sometimes mean “that is” or “namely”, so that the last phrase defines whom God saves: all people, that is, all who believe. Either way the verse does not teach that all are finally saved.

Textual note. Some manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read “suffer reproach” (oneidizometha) for strive; the earliest read strive, and most modern Bibles follow them.

verseByVerse.quote: Command and teach these things. Let no one despise you for your youth, but set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy must keep teaching with authority, and win the respect his youth could not command by a life the believers can copy. Here Paul turns from Timothy’s message to Timothy himself, and the rest of the chapter stays there: in the household of God (3:15) the truth is never carried apart from a life that matches it.

Command and teach these things. The first verb (parangellō) is to give orders with authority, and the form of both verbs means keep on commanding and teaching. Timothy speaks as Paul’s delegate, and Paul as Christ’s apostle, so the instructions are Christ’s, not Timothy’s own.

Let no one despise you for your youth. To despise (kataphroneō) is to look down on someone as not worth listening to. A man under forty could be called young, and Timothy, probably in his thirties, was young for his task in a culture that gave authority to age, among older men he sometimes had to correct, some of whom fancied themselves teachers of the law (1:7). Paul does not tell him to assert himself or be tougher, nor tell the church to respect him. He tells Timothy to be so plainly worth following that contempt has nothing to feed on.

Set the believers an example. An example is the stamp that leaves its impression (typos, 2 Thessalonians 3:9). Authority in this letter is not claimed; it is displayed. Timothy’s life would win the authority his age could not.

In speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity. The order repays attention. Speech: what he says and how, the most public thing about him (Ephesians 4:29; Colossians 4:6). Conduct: the whole visible manner of life. Love: the goal of all instruction (1:5). Faith: his actual trust in God, and with it his trustworthiness. Purity (hagneia): chastity, moral and sexual purity, especially important for a young man ministering to women (5:2). They run from the most visible to the least, and purity, the private one, is the foundation of the other four: the least visible is where a man’s real character is decided.

A copy of the true pattern. Paul received mercy so that Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example (1:16), and Timothy’s example is to be the same: Christ’s work on show in a man he has laid hold of, which is what makes the standard bearable. And Christ was himself the young man despised by the elders of his own nation, who never once answered contempt with self-assertion.

In everyday life. Take purity seriously where only God sees: the screen at midnight, the private thought life, the friendship that is drifting somewhere it should not. That is where an example is actually made.

Is this only for pastors? It was written to a pastor, but the pattern is for every believer. Everyone is watched by someone: children watch parents, colleagues watch the one who goes to church, younger believers watch older ones. A teenager can be an example to his parents’ friends, a new Christian to someone who has been in church for decades. You do not need a title to be a typos, only a life stamped by Christ, so that it leaves his impression on others.

What if people still look down on me, however I live? Then you are in good company: some despised Jesus, who was without sin. Paul’s instruction does not guarantee respect; it makes sure that if you are despised, it is not for good reason (1 Peter 2:12; 3:16). Keep living faithfully, do not retaliate, and do not try to win standing by louder claims or harsher words. Leave your reputation with God. A consistent life usually earns trust in time, and even when it does not, it pleases the One whose opinion finally matters.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts (followed by the KJV) add “in spirit” after “in love.” The earliest manuscripts lack it.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy was probably in his thirties, young for a church leader in that culture.

verseByVerse.quote: Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, to teaching. Do not neglect the gift you have, which was given you by prophecy when the council of elders laid their hands on you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Until Paul comes, Timothy is to give himself to reading Scripture aloud to the church, urging it and explaining it, and to use the gift God gave him and the elders recognised. Read, explain, apply: the shape of Christian ministry, unchanged in two thousand years.

Until I come. Paul expected to come (3:14), but meanwhile the church had what it needed: the Scriptures and a man to read them.

Devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture. Devote yourself (prosechō) is the word used of those absorbed in myths (1:4) and devoted to deceitful spirits (4:1). Everyone is absorbed in something; Timothy is to be absorbed in Scripture. Public reading (anagnōsis) is reading aloud. Many believers could not read, and copies were scarce and expensive, so hearing the Bible meant one person standing up and reading it to everybody. Paul puts that first: before explanation or application, the text itself. It is the synagogue pattern carried into the church, Scripture read and then explained (Acts 13:15), with the apostles’ letters read alongside the Old Testament (Colossians 4:16; 1 Thessalonians 5:27). A church’s primary act of teaching is letting the Bible be heard.

To exhortation, to teaching. Exhortation (paraklēsis) is urging and applying, calling the hearers to respond; teaching explains what the Scripture means.

Do not neglect the gift you have. Neglect (ameleō) is to let something lie unused. Timothy’s gift (charisma) for preaching and leading can be possessed and yet wasted, like something left in a drawer; elsewhere Paul says to fan it into flame (2 Timothy 1:6).

Given you by prophecy when the council of elders laid their hands on you. Two things happened at Timothy’s commissioning. Prophecies had identified his gift and calling (1:18). And the council of elders (presbyterion, the presbytery), with Paul (2 Timothy 1:6), laid their hands on him: the Old Testament gesture of commissioning and blessing (Numbers 27:18–23; Acts 6:6; 13:3), here the church’s public act of setting a man apart. The gift came from God; the laying on of hands recognised and confirmed it. Timothy did not appoint himself, nor was he appointed by one man alone. A body of men had publicly identified themselves with him: the thing to remember when the work goes badly and a man wonders whether he was ever meant to be doing it.

The reader in the synagogue at Nazareth. Behind this pattern stands a famous scene. Jesus stood up in the synagogue at Nazareth, was handed the scroll of Isaiah, read it aloud, sat down, and said that this Scripture had been fulfilled that day in their hearing (Luke 4:16–21): the sermon on that reading was preached by the One it was about. After his resurrection he showed his disciples the things concerning himself in all the Scriptures (Luke 24:27). So Timothy is not reciting religious literature but reading the book whose subject is Christ, and the reading, exhortation and teaching all exist to set him before the church. When the Word is read, the Shepherd is calling his sheep.

What it does not mean. The mention of prophecy here does not mean new revelation continues today; prophecy belonged to the foundational era of the church (Ephesians 2:20). Many Pentecostal and charismatic believers expect prophecy now, and they are brothers and sisters to be heard with respect; this commentary holds that revelation of that kind ended because Scripture is complete.

In everyday life. Before Sunday, read the passage that will be read in church, and pray for the one who will read and the one who will preach. If there is a gift Christ gave you that you have let slide, pick it up again this week.

How do I know what my gift is, and am I neglecting it? Look where three things meet: what you can do that builds others up, what you are drawn to serve in, and what mature believers recognise in you. That last is this verse’s lesson: Timothy’s gift was recognised by the elders, not self-diagnosed. Gifts are found mostly by serving, not by questionnaires: say yes to needs in your church and see where God blesses the work. You are neglecting a gift if you have quietly stopped using something given for others, through fear, busyness or resentment. Ask an elder or a trusted friend where they see God using you, and start there.

Why does public Bible reading matter if everyone has a Bible now? Because hearing God’s Word together differs from reading it alone: the whole church, young and old, scholar and child, sits under the same word at the same moment, and God addresses his people as a people. It also guards the church, holding the sermon accountable to the text everyone has just heard. Many churches now read a few verses before a long sermon; Paul put the reading first. Listen to it as God speaking, not as a preliminary, and read it well if you are asked to.

Where Christians differ: does ordination convey grace? Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches regard ordination as a sacrament that confers an indelible spiritual character and power, and they treat it with a reverence that is right in itself. This commentary’s view: Ordination is the church’s solemn recognition of a man’s gifts and calling, and its commissioning of him to office, with prayer. The gift is from God; the church recognises it. The laying on of hands is a fitting sign, not a channel that transmits grace by the act itself. Scripture names only two sacraments: baptism and the Lord’s Supper.

Uncertain wording. By prophecy (dia prophēteias) could mean that prophecy was the means by which the gift came, or, more likely, that prophecy accompanied the occasion, pointing out Timothy and his calling (1:18). And the council of elders (presbyterion) is usually taken as the body of elders who laid hands on him, though some read it as naming the purpose of the act, a laying on of hands that set him apart as an elder. Either way the gift was God’s, and the church publicly recognised it.

verseByVerse.quote: Practice these things, immerse yourself in them, so that all may see your progress. Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching. Persist in this, for by so doing you will save both yourself and your hearers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy must give himself wholly to these things and keep watch over his own life and his teaching to the end, because that is the means by which God will save both him and those who hear him. The chapter that began with men departing from the faith ends with a man told to persist.

Practice these things, immerse yourself in them. Practise (meletaō) is cultivate; immerse yourself is literally be in these things, live there. Godliness is not a weekend interest.

So that all may see your progress. Progress (prokopē) is something Paul expects to be visible: the congregation should be able to see that Timothy is a better man than he was five years ago. A minister does not need to appear perfect; he needs to be visibly growing. A leader who cannot be seen to grow is teaching his people that growth stops somewhere.

Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching. Two objects, in that order, and the order is the point: his own life first, his character and walk with God; then his doctrine. A man may guard his theology carefully while his character quietly comes apart, and this letter has shown where that ends: the conscience goes, and the doctrine follows it down (1:19; 4:2). Yet neither can stand in for the other: a sound teacher with an unholy life destroys his message; a holy man with false doctrine misleads. Both must be watched, for life, as Paul told the Ephesian elders (Acts 20:28). And only a man who watches himself first can safely correct anyone else, as chapter 5 will require.

Persist in this. Many begin well. The crown is for those who finish.

You will save both yourself and your hearers. Salvation in the full sense, so it needs stating carefully: there is one mediator (2:5), and no minister saves anybody. Timothy’s perseverance in godliness and sound doctrine is the means by which God will bring him and his hearers through to final salvation; those whom God has chosen persevere because he preserves them through such means (Philippians 1:6; 2:12–13). Timothy is one of the instruments, and the instruction is to stay usable.

Progress towards a person. The progress Paul wants is growth into him who is the head, into Christ (Ephesians 4:15). A minister’s visible growth is Christ becoming more visible in him: more of the Lord’s patience in his answers, more of his humility in his authority. He watches his life so that it looks like Christ, and his teaching so that it tells of Christ.

He saved his hearers, not himself. The God who saves is the God who uses means. He could have saved us by lightning; he chose a Book read aloud, a man who keeps watch over himself, and a people who keep listening. And behind every faithful pastor stands the Chief Shepherd, who kept perfect watch over his life and teaching and persisted to the end, and saved, not himself, for he would not come down from the cross, but all his hearers who believe.

In everyday life. Ask yourself the progress question: what can people see in me now that they could not see five years ago? If the answer is nothing, do not despair: your standing rests on Christ’s perfect watch, not yours, and his Spirit has not stopped working. Begin again today, with the Word and prayer.

If God guarantees that his people persevere, why warn them to persist? Because the warning is one of the ways he guarantees it. God does not keep his people like parcels in a vault, but like a father keeping a child on a mountain path: he holds the hand, and he also says watch your step. The elect will certainly persevere (John 10:28–29), and they will do so by heeding these very exhortations. If the warning makes you watch yourself more closely, that is not a sign you are unsafe; it is the Shepherd’s voice doing its work in you.

What does watching my life and doctrine look like for someone who is not a pastor? For your life: a regular, honest look at yourself before God, asking where you are drifting, what you are hiding and whom you are not loving, and confessing it quickly. For your doctrine: knowing what you believe and why, from Scripture, not absorbing every idea that comes through a feed or a friend. Read a good catechism or confession, ask your pastor questions, and belong to a church where both are taught. And do it with others, because the log is in your own eye: give one or two mature believers permission to tell you the truth.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the Spirit expressly says that in later times some will depart from the faith by devoting themselves to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons,<sup>2</sup>through the insincerity of liars whose consciences are seared,<sup>3</sup>who forbid marriage and require abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth.<sup>4</sup>For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving,<sup>5</sup>for it is made holy by the word of God and prayer.<sup>6</sup>If you put these things before the brothers, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, being trained in the words of the faith and of the good doctrine that you have followed.<sup>7</sup>Have nothing to do with irreverent, silly myths. Rather train yourself for godliness;<sup>8</sup>for while bodily training is of some value, godliness is of value in every way, as it holds promise for the present life and also for the life to come.<sup>9</sup>The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance.<sup>10</sup>For to this end we toil and strive, because we have our hope set on the living God, who is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe.<sup>11</sup>Command and teach these things.<sup>12</sup>Let no one despise you for your youth, but set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.<sup>13</sup>Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, to teaching.<sup>14</sup>Do not neglect the gift you have, which was given you by prophecy when the council of elders laid their hands on you.<sup>15</sup>Practice these things, immerse yourself in them, so that all may see your progress.<sup>16</sup>Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching. Persist in this, for by so doing you will save both yourself and your hearers.

keyVerse.quote: Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching. Persist in this, for by so doing you will save both yourself and your hearers.
keyVerse.note: The chapter opens with those who “depart from the faith” (v. 1) and closes with the call to persist, and this verse is God’s answer to apostasy: a life and a doctrine kept under watch, to the end. Its order, yourself and then the teaching, gathers up the whole second half of the chapter. And it shows how God saves: not without means but through them, a faithful preacher and listening hearers, kept by the Chief Shepherd who kept perfect watch and persisted all the way to the cross.

4.reflection:
The false teachers impressed people by what they gave up (vv. 3–5). Why is a religion of rules and refusals so attractive, and where do you see it in yourself or in Christian circles today? What would it look like to receive God’s gifts “with thanksgiving” this week?

Paul says consciences can be seared, one small overruling at a time (v. 2). What helps keep a conscience tender, and what dulls it? Is there something you have learned to stop noticing?

Godliness is trained for, like fitness, by ordinary means repeated (vv. 7–8). Which part of your life gets your best hours, and what one small, specific discipline could you begin and keep?

Timothy was to watch his life and his teaching, and to give himself to the public reading and preaching of Scripture (vv. 13–16). How can we pray for and support those who teach us, and how should these verses change the way we listen on Sunday?

5.title: Honour and Order in the Family of God
5.overview:
Where we are. After charging Timothy to watch his own life and teaching (4:16), Paul turns in 5:1–6:2 to how “the household of God” (3:15) treats its members: old and young, widows, elders and, in 6:1–2, slaves.

The message. The church is God’s family, and its faith shows in how it treats its own. The chapter’s word is honour: respect for the old, real support for the widow who has no one, generous pay and fair protection for the elder who labours in the word. Yet honour is never a cover: families may not hand their duties to the church, and a leader who persists in sin is rebuked before all. Over it all stands God, who sees what is hidden and judges without favourites.

Why it was said. Timothy was young (4:12); the church’s support for widows was strained and open to abuse; some younger widows had drifted towards the false teachers; and elders were under accusation (see the introduction). Paul equips him for the hardest parts of pastoral work.

How the chapter makes its case. Treat everyone as family (vv. 1–2). Honour widows (vv. 3–16): families first, as godliness (vv. 4, 8), the church for the widow truly alone, whose hope is in God (vv. 5, 16); a roll for older widows of proven service (vv. 9–10), and for the younger, remarriage rather than a pledge they may not keep (vv. 11–15). Honour elders (vv. 17–25): pay those who labour in the word (vv. 17–18), protect them from rumour but rebuke persistent sin openly (vv. 19–20), judge without partiality (v. 21) and appoint slowly (v. 22), since nothing, bad or good, stays hidden (vv. 24–25). It is a chapter of welfare lists, salaries and procedure, and it is full of God: church administration, in Paul’s hands, is theology with its sleeves rolled up.

Where it leads. Each relationship here has its pattern in Christ. He called those who do God’s will his brother and sister and mother (Mark 3:35); from the cross he provided for his widowed mother (John 19:26–27); he washed his disciples’ feet. At his trial no two witnesses agreed, yet the one innocent man was condemned. He is the Judge who will bring every hidden thing to light, and he has already borne the shame of his people’s sins. The church honours its widows and its elders because it is the household of a Saviour who provides.

For us. Look at your church as a family and ask who goes unseen: the widow nobody visits, the parent you have not planned for, the pastor nobody thanks, the quiet servant passed over. The God who sees in secret has never stopped caring for you; care for them.
