verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The church is God’s household (3:15), so its people are to be treated as family. Paul applies this first to the way a young leader corrects and cares for others: older men are appealed to as fathers, not rebuked; younger men are dealt with as brothers; older women are honoured as mothers; and younger women are treated as sisters, with a purity above suspicion. The same family frame governs everything that follows, the care of widows and the honour of elders.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church as Household, in Practice

The church is God’s household (3:15), and here Paul puts that into practice: treat people as what they actually are, fathers, brothers, mothers, sisters (on the two mistakes this rules out, see the note on vv. 1–2).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A young leader not taken seriously is tempted to be harsher than the case requires (see the note on vv. 1–2).

Now: ‘As sisters, in all purity’ gives a relationship rather than a rulebook as the safeguard (see v. 2).

verseByVerse.quote: Do not rebuke an older man but encourage him as you would a father, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in all purity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Treat the members of the church as your own family, older and younger, men and women, and keep every dealing with younger women completely pure.

Do not rebuke an older man. To rebuke here is to strike at, to upbraid harshly (epiplēssō, found only here in the New Testament). Older men may need correcting, but not like this. A young leader not taken seriously (4:12) is tempted to be harder than the case requires, and Paul takes the option away: you shall stand up before the grey head and honour the face of an old man (Leviticus 19:32).

Encourage him as a father. A gentle appeal, as a son speaks to his father. You may correct your father, but carefully, and never in public.

Brothers and mothers. Younger men are brothers, dealt with frankly and affectionately; older women are mothers, honoured. This is the household of God (3:15) in practice, and it rules out both mistakes a young leader can make: the harshness that treats the congregation as subordinates, and the deference that never says anything at all.

In all purity. The phrase is added to one group only, and purity is the word of 4:12. Paul is a realist. A young minister, possibly unmarried, caring for young women is in a situation that has destroyed many ministries, and Paul says so without fuss. Timothy’s dealings with them must be free of any impropriety in thought, word and action, and of anything that could give rise to suspicion. The safeguard is not distance but a relationship: as sisters. A man does not have to invent boundaries with his sister; he already knows what is and is not thinkable. That instinct, with a brother’s protective love, protects the women, protects him, and does not require him to treat half his congregation as a hazard.

The family Jesus named. These family words came first from Jesus. When his relatives came to take him home, he looked at those sitting around him and said that whoever does the will of God is his brother and sister and mother (Mark 3:31–35). The church is a family because it gathers round him: the Son is not ashamed to call us brothers (Hebrews 2:11), the Father has adopted us and given us his Spirit, by whom we cry, Abba (Romans 8:15), and those who have left or lost family are given mothers and brothers and sisters a hundredfold in his house (Mark 10:29–30). That is also why purity is not negotiable: no one may treat a woman as anything less than what she is, a sister of Christ.

In everyday life. Picture your church as the family it is: the widower is your father, the teenager your younger brother, the woman who has been missing for weeks your mother. Phone her.

What if an older person in the church really is in the wrong? Then he must be told, but as a son would tell his father: privately, respectfully, as a concern rather than a verdict, and ready to listen, because age often sees what youth misses. Respect for age never means silence about sin or tolerating harm to others; if the wrong is serious, or he will not listen, involve the elders (Matthew 18:15–17). The gentleness is in the manner, not the content.

What practical safeguards does purity call for? The family instinct comes first, but wisdom adds sensible habits, especially in pastoral care. Avoid meetings that are private and unaccountable: use an open office or a public place, keep a door ajar, let someone know where you are. If pastoral conversations drift into emotional dependence, involve a wise older woman or your wife and step back. Never send a message you would not want read aloud. These habits are not suspicion but love: they protect the vulnerable from harm and the church from scandal, and make sure a sister is always treated as a sister.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Honour the widows who really have no one, and let families care for their own. The church supports widows who are truly alone, while children and grandchildren repay their parents as an act of godliness (vv. 3–4). The widow who sets her hope on God and prays is contrasted with the one who lives for pleasure (vv. 5–6), and a believer who will not provide for his relatives is worse than an unbeliever (vv. 7–8). Only older widows of proven service are enrolled (vv. 9–10); younger widows should remarry rather than take a pledge they may not keep (vv. 11–15). Families carry their own, so the church can carry the women who have nobody (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology:
Family First, and Why

To neglect one’s own relatives is to deny the faith and fall below the decency of unbelievers (v. 8); caring for an ageing parent is not a lesser duty but where godliness is practised (v. 4).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The widows on the church’s list prayed for others night and day (v. 5), and what qualified them was a lifetime of service nobody had recorded (v. 10).

Now: Paul’s remedy for idleness and gossip (vv. 11–13) is ordinary life (see the note on vv. 14–16).

verseByVerse.quote: Honor widows who are truly widows. But if a widow has children or grandchildren, let them first learn to show godliness to their own household and to make some return to their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Widows who are truly alone are to be honoured with the church’s support; but where a widow has children or grandchildren, caring for her is first their duty, and a godliness that pleases God.

The setting. In the ancient world a widow was often destitute. There were no pensions, and a widow without family could face starvation or be driven into prostitution. God himself executes justice for the fatherless and the widow (Deuteronomy 10:18); he is a father of the fatherless and protector of widows (Psalm 68:5), who left her the gleanings of Israel’s fields (Deuteronomy 24:19–21) and sent Elijah to a widow of Zarephath. The early church continued his care (Acts 6:1; James 1:27). But resources were limited and some were abusing the system. Paul is not inventing a policy; he is protecting one.

Truly widows. Honour (timaō) here includes financial support, as in Matthew 15:4–6 and the double honour of verse 17. Truly widows are those genuinely alone (v. 5).

Godliness at home. The family, not the church, is the first line of support. Caring for an ageing mother is not a lesser, secular duty but a place where godliness is practised: the fifth commandment kept (Exodus 20:12), the opposite of the excuse Jesus condemned, when people declared their money Corban, given to God, so as not to support their parents (Mark 7:9–13).

Make some return. The language of repaying a debt: our parents cared for us when we were helpless, and we care for them when they are. It is pleasing in the sight of God, the phrase of 2:3: the changed sheets, the hospital visits and the patient repetition of the same conversation are seen, and welcomed, in heaven.

Godliness at the foot of the cross. The Son of God kept this command. As a boy he was submissive to Mary and Joseph (Luke 2:51). On the cross, bearing the sins of the world, he gave his mother into the care of the beloved disciple, who took her to his own home from that hour (John 19:26–27). In his agony he made some return to his mother. He fulfilled the fifth commandment, and his obedience is counted to believers who have often failed in it. And the God who notices widows came in him to the gate of Nain, where he had compassion on a widow and gave her only son back to her (Luke 7:11–15). Caring for an ageing parent is walking where he walked.

The debts we did not choose. We tend to believe that the only obligations that bind us are the ones we chose, so that what I owe a parent depends on how I feel. But none of us chose to be born, fed, carried and taught to speak. The philosopher Alasdair MacIntyre argued in Dependent Rational Animals that human beings begin and usually end their lives in deep dependence on others, and that a society which forgets this forgets what people are. Paul’s word return cuts across our autonomy, and also across an older, harsher piety that honoured parents out of fear and kept careful accounts. The gospel gives a better motive: every Christian lives on a love he did not choose or earn. “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). People carried by grace can carry their parents, without resentment and without keeping score.

In everyday life. Ask your parents or grandparents what they need this week, and listen to the answer. If they have died, care for someone else’s parent in your church who has no one nearby.

Does this mean I must have my elderly parent live with me? Not necessarily. The command is to honour and provide, and what that requires depends on the parent’s needs, your circumstances and your other duties, including to your spouse and children. For some a parent moving in is the loving choice; for others good professional care is, especially where medical needs are beyond what a family can safely give. What Scripture forbids is not a care home but abandonment: a parent unvisited, unfunded, unknown. Whatever the arrangement, stay involved, contribute, visit, and make sure they know they are loved.

What if my parent was abusive or neglectful? Honour does not require you to put yourself back under harm, pretend the past did not happen, or submit to further abuse. You may need distance and boundaries for your own safety and your family’s, and that is not sin. Even then the gospel may call you, in ways that are wise and safe, to see that your parent’s basic needs are met, perhaps through others, and to pray for them; seek counsel from a wise pastor. God sees the care you never received, and he is a Father who does not fail (Psalm 27:10). Honouring a parent who did not honour you is costly, and there the grace of Christ shows most clearly.

verseByVerse.quote: She who is truly a widow, left all alone, has set her hope on God and continues in supplications and prayers night and day, but she who is self-indulgent is dead even while she lives.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The widow who is truly alone has set her hope on God and spends her days in prayer; the widow who lives for pleasure is dead even while she lives.

Left all alone, has set her hope on God. The verb (memonōmenē), from the root that gives us our word monk, means left alone and remaining alone, with nobody to turn to. She has fixed her hope and keeps it fixed (the same form as in 4:10): every human prop was taken away, and she found she was standing on the Rock.

Night and day. What Paul says of his own prayers (2 Timothy 1:3) and Luke of Anna (Luke 2:37). The church that supports such a widow is not merely giving charity but sustaining an intercessor, and gains far more from her prayers than it gives in money.

Dead even while she lives. Self-indulgent (spatalōsa) is a strong word: living luxuriously, given over to pleasure, with a note of wantonness. Some think a few were even selling their bodies to live. Paul means a widow with freedom and no dependants who has turned that freedom into indulgence, and the church should not fund it. Not dying, but dead, present tense, while the body carries on: Jesus’ verdict on the church at Sardis, which had the reputation of being alive and was dead (Revelation 3:1). Her diary is full, but toward God there is no prayer, no hunger, no love: cut flowers in a vase, still bright for a while, already severed from the root.

What Anna’s prayers were waiting for. The widow Paul describes has a portrait in Luke. Anna, widowed for many years, worshipped in the temple with fasting and prayer night and day, and her hope was answered in a person. When the infant Jesus was carried in, she came up at that very hour, gave thanks to God and spoke of him to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem (Luke 2:36–38). A hope set on God is fixed on the God who has kept his word in Christ. And the woman who is dead while she lives has the remedy every sinner has: God, rich in mercy, makes the dead alive together with Christ (Ephesians 2:4–5).

Two widows. Both have lost a husband and have time on their hands. One spends it praying and is alive; the other spends it on herself and is a corpse that has not noticed. Ask the same of every retirement, every empty evening, every free Saturday: on whom is this time being spent?

How do I continue in prayer like this? Few of us have a widow’s empty hours, but her habit can be learned. Start with a fixed time and place, however short, because what has no time in the day usually happens at no time. Keep a short list of names and needs. Pray Scripture back to God: a psalm, the Lord’s Prayer, a promise you have just read. Let the fixed times spill into the day, a name brought to God the moment it comes to mind. When you miss a week, simply begin again; you are not reporting for duty. Prayer rests on Christ, not on us. He is at the right hand of God, “who indeed is interceding for us” (Romans 8:34), and the Spirit helps us in our weakness (Romans 8:26). A widow on her knees at midnight is joining a prayer already going on in heaven.

I am widowed and lonely. How can I set my hope on God when it hurts this much? Grief is not a lack of faith. The widow in this verse has not stopped feeling her loss; she has taken it to God, night and day. Setting your hope on him means not pretending but telling him the truth and asking for help, as the psalmists do, even in a few words. Let the church carry you: accept the meals, the visits, the invitations, even when it is hard. And know that a widow who prays is not on the edge of the church’s life but at its centre.

verseByVerse.quote: Command these things as well, so that they may be without reproach. But if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These duties must be taught so that Christian families stay above reproach, for a believer who will not provide for his own relatives has denied the faith by his deeds and sunk below the decency of unbelievers.

Without reproach. The word used of overseers in 3:2. No one should be able to accuse widows or their families of neglect or self-indulgence; Christian households lived in a watching city.

Provide for his relatives. One of the fiercest sentences Paul wrote. Provide (pronoeō) means plan for: not crisis rescue but forethought, and the closer the relationship, the greater the duty. That is how God provides. He provided for Adam before Adam knew he needed anything, fed Israel with bread from heaven for forty years, clothes the lilies and numbers the hairs on our heads.

He has denied the faith. Denied (arneomai) is the verb used of Peter in the courtyard (Mark 14:68), here a denial in deeds, not words (Titus 1:16). A man may recite the creed accurately and, by leaving his mother destitute, deny every word of it.

Worse than an unbeliever. Pagans looked after their own, so a Christian who neglects his relatives has fallen below the decency of people with no faith at all. Spirituality is measured here by whether the people related to you have what they need.

The Provider of his own household. Neglect denies the faith because the faith is about a Saviour who provides: God planned for us before the foundation of the world and in the fullness of time sent his Son. Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, and he nourishes and cherishes her (Ephesians 5:25, 29); he has never received his people and then left them to fend for themselves. A believer who leaves his family in want tells a story about Christ that is not true. One who plans and provides for them preaches without a word the faithfulness of the Son over God’s house (Hebrews 3:6). The family table is one of the places where the gospel is either confirmed or contradicted.

In everyday life. Is there an ageing parent whose needs you have not planned for, a sibling quietly struggling, a will you have not written? Provision is forethought. Do one piece of it today.

What it does not mean. Not that a person unable to provide, through illness, poverty or circumstance, has denied the faith; the point is unwillingness. Nor that only men provide (v. 16). Some families are estranged for grave reasons, and some carers are already at the end of their strength. Paul means people who could and do not, and have arranged their religion so as not to notice.

Does this apply to a husband who will not work or support his family? Yes, directly. A man able to support his wife and children who refuses, or spends on himself what they need, is the person this verse describes; Scripture expects able-bodied people to work (2 Thessalonians 3:10). Neither his family nor the church should pretend all is well: the elders should lovingly confront him and, if he persists, treat it as a matter of discipline, while making sure his family is cared for. Financial neglect can also be part of a pattern of control or abuse; where it is, the church must protect the vulnerable, not the abuser.

How do I balance providing for my family with giving to the church and the poor? Begin with Paul’s order: your own household is your first earthly responsibility, and neglecting it is not generosity but disobedience. But provision is not luxury, and Scripture also commands generous giving to God’s work and to the poor (2 Corinthians 9:6–8; Galatians 6:10). Most of us have room for both once wants are separated from needs. Budget, save for your family’s future, and give first rather than from what is left, trusting the God who feeds the sparrows.

verseByVerse.quote: Let a widow be enrolled if she is not less than sixty years of age, having been the wife of one husband, and having a reputation for good works: if she has brought up children, has shown hospitality, has washed the feet of the saints, has cared for the afflicted, and has devoted herself to every good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only widows of sixty or more, faithful in marriage and known for a lifetime of humble service, are to be put on the church’s roll.

Let a widow be enrolled. An actual roll of names: widows supported by the church who in return gave themselves to prayer and service (v. 5), like the recognised order of widows in the early church after the apostles.

Not less than sixty. Past the age of likely remarriage and of earning a living: Paul draws the line where long-term dependence begins, and where she would probably not want to leave the role to remarry (vv. 11–12).

The wife of one husband. Literally a one-man woman, the counterpart of the one-woman man of 3:2, and best read the same way: faithful in her marriage (see the uncertain wording below).

A reputation for good works. A track record known to all, and the list is of unglamorous things: bringing up children, her own or perhaps orphans she took in; hospitality, opening her house, as the overseer must (3:2).

Washed the feet of the saints. Washing feet was the lowest job in the household, given to the least slave, and the one Jesus did in the upper room. Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, he tied a towel round himself, washed his disciples’ feet, and told them that they also ought to wash one another’s feet (John 13:3–5, 14). The Lord of glory set the pattern with a basin, and this widow has spent a lifetime following it. The phrase stands for every kind of humble service, the plainest proof that a woman has learned Christ.

Cared for the afflicted. The sick, the poor, the persecuted: before she needed help she gave it, which is why the church now owes her. Not one item on the list is public or recorded anywhere: she is put on the roll for a lifetime of things nobody wrote down.

Heaven’s list of honour is not the world’s. God does not record the speeches and titles; he records the cup of cold water, the guest welcomed, the night by a sickbed, and forgets none of it (Hebrews 6:10). On the last day the King will read the list aloud, and to women whose names were written nowhere but in his book he will say that what they did for the least of his brothers they did for him (Matthew 25:40). The Lord who served will honour those who served, and their reward will be himself.

In everyday life. The Lord who knelt with a basin for you is at work in you by his Spirit. Take a meal round, welcome a guest, sit with a sick friend. Do one this week, and tell no one.

What it does not mean. Not that the church should refuse help to widows under sixty or without this record; these are criteria for the enrolled list, not for help in need (Galatians 6:10).

Should churches keep a list of widows today? Nothing here requires a formal roll, and pensions and state provision now meet part of its purpose. But the principle remains, real need met first by family and then by the church, often through deacons who know the widows and the needy by name (Acts 6:1–6). And the honour remains: older women who have given a lifetime of quiet service should be valued, visited and drawn on for their wisdom and prayer, not left at the edge.

Uncertain wording. The wife of one husband (literally a one-man woman) is compressed, like its counterpart for overseers in 3:2, and could mean married only once or faithful to her husband. Since Paul urges younger widows to remarry (v. 14), he would hardly bar them later for following his advice, so faithfulness in marriage is the likely meaning.
verseByVerse.note: There seems to have been an official list of widows supported by the church, who in turn served it.

verseByVerse.quote: But refuse to enroll younger widows, for when their passions draw them away from Christ, they desire to marry and so incur condemnation for having abandoned their former faith. Besides that, they learn to be idlers, going about from house to house, and not only idlers, but also gossips and busybodies, saying what they should not.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Younger widows should not be put on the roll, because a lifelong pledge they may later break, and a supported life with nothing to do, would do them harm.

Refuse to enroll younger widows. Refuse is the verb used of the silly myths in 4:7. Paul uses it not because younger widows are less worthy, but for their own good.

When their passions draw them away from Christ. The rare verb (katastrēniasōsin) pictures growing restless against something. The desire for marriage is not wrong (v. 14), but here it pulls them away from a commitment made to Christ.

Abandoned their former faith. This sounds like a condemnation of remarriage, until verse 14 tells these same widows to marry. Most likely enrolled widows pledged themselves to Christ and the church’s service for life, without remarrying (see the uncertain wording below). The problem is the broken pledge, not the marriage: it brings condemnation, here God’s censure, because the pledge was a vow made to God (Numbers 30:2; Ecclesiastes 5:4–5), who is in heaven while we are on earth (Ecclesiastes 5:2) and does not treat our words as lightly as we do. Paul is realistic, not harsh: a woman in her twenties or thirties should not be asked to bind herself for life, because many will not manage it and the failure will damage them. The kindest policy is not to let them make the vow.

They learn to be idlers. The verb is learn: the arrangement itself teaches idleness. Support a young woman with no dependants, work or structure, and she will fill the days somehow, going from house to house, perhaps under the guise of ministry, the route the false teachers also used (2 Timothy 3:6).

Gossips and busybodies. Busybodies (periergoi) are meddlers, Paul’s word for the idle men at Thessalonica (2 Thessalonians 3:11). Saying what they should not may mean spreading the false teaching, or private matters learned in other homes. The diagnosis is not really about women: idleness is never neutral. Take away a person’s proper work and the energy goes into other people’s affairs; the remedy is something real to do.

The pledge Christ never breaks. Our promises to Christ are fragile; his to us are not. God swore by himself to Abraham and has never broken his word. Having loved his own, he loved them to the end (John 13:1); if we are faithless, he remains faithful (2 Timothy 2:13). So a woman who had broken her pledge was not beyond hope: the Lord she failed is the Lord who restored Peter after three denials.

In everyday life. If you have unstructured time, give it somewhere good to go before it finds somewhere bad.

What it does not mean. Not that younger widows are worse people. Nor does condemnation here mean loss of salvation; it is the censure due to a broken vow.

How do I know if I am gossiping? Before you speak about someone absent, ask: Is it true, and do I actually know it? Is it mine to tell? Would I say it the same way if they were standing here? Gossip often wears the clothes of concern (let me tell you so you can pray). If you need help with a situation, go to someone who can help, such as an elder, not to someone who will merely enjoy knowing. And when gossip is brought to you, kindly ask whether they have spoken to the person directly.

Does this teach that Christians should not make lifelong vows? No. Marriage is a lifelong vow, and so is the covenant of church membership. Paul warns against binding people, especially the young, to vows they are unlikely to keep and that Scripture does not require, such as lifelong celibacy, the very thing the false teachers promoted (4:3). Vows to God must be kept (Ecclesiastes 5:4–5), which is exactly why they should not be made lightly (Matthew 5:33–37). Make the promises God asks of you, keep them by his grace, and do not add others he has not asked for.

Uncertain wording. Their former faith (tēn prōtēn pistin) can mean their first faith in Christ or their first pledge. Since Paul urges younger widows to marry (v. 14), he cannot mean that remarriage itself abandons Christ, so most read it as a pledge, made on enrolment, to remain unmarried in the church’s service. Such a pledge is inferred from these verses; the letter does not describe it.

verseByVerse.quote: So I would have younger widows marry, bear children, manage their households, and give the adversary no occasion for slander. For some have already strayed after Satan. If any believing woman has relatives who are widows, let her care for them. Let the church not be burdened, so that it may care for those who are truly widows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Younger widows should remarry and run a household, giving the enemy no opening, and believing families should care for their own widows so that the church can support those who have no one.

So I would have younger widows marry. I would have is a word of direction (2:8): Paul prefers remarriage. Against the false teachers who forbade marriage (4:3), his answer to a pastoral risk is not more restriction but ordinary life. Remarriage after a spouse’s death is lawful (Romans 7:2–3), provided it is in the Lord, to a fellow believer (1 Corinthians 7:39).

Manage their households. A strong word (oikodespotein): to rule the house (compare Proverbs 31:10–31). A modern reader may hear this as small; Paul does not. Running a household is a calling from God with real authority in it, and a far better use of a life than drifting from house to house.

No occasion for slander. Occasion (aphormē) began as a military word for a base of operations: the church is watched, by human enemies or by Satan, and its arrangements can hand them ammunition (3:7). This is not hypothetical: some younger widows had already strayed after Satan (1:6), perhaps into immorality, perhaps after the false teachers (4:1).

Any believing woman. The duty of verse 8 is not the men’s alone. Care for is the word of verse 10: what the widow once did for others, others now do for her.

Let the church not be burdened. Every family that supports its own frees the church’s resources for women who have nobody: not meanness but the arithmetic of love. A congregation that carries people whose families could carry them will run out before it reaches the destitute.

Homes that carry the Saviour’s name. Paul gives Titus the same concern: that the word of God may not be reviled, and that believers may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour (Titus 2:5, 10). The street that never reads Paul can read a home. When Christian homes collapse into idleness and scandal, Christ’s name is mocked; when they flourish, the watching city sees in ordinary kitchens what the Saviour does with lives he has taken in hand. God sets the lonely in families (Psalm 68:6), and over every widow stands the Bridegroom whose Bride will never be widowed, because he died and rose, and is coming back for her.

In everyday life. Is there a widow in your family or church you could help this week? Ask her what would actually help: a lift to the shops, help with paperwork, an evening of company.

What it does not mean. It does not command every younger widow to remarry; singleness remains honourable (1 Corinthians 7:8, 40).

Is it disloyal to my late husband or wife to remarry? No. Death ends the marriage bond (Romans 7:2), and in the resurrection people neither marry nor are given in marriage (Matthew 22:30). Paul here encourages younger widows to remarry, and it was God who said it is not good for the man to be alone (Genesis 2:18). Love for a spouse who has died is not betrayed by a new marriage; a good first marriage often prepares a person to love again. Take time, grieve honestly, seek counsel, marry only in the Lord, and be patient with children or friends whose grief moves at a different pace.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read any believing man or woman. The shorter reading is better attested, and the duty is the same either way.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elders who lead well are to be honoured, protected and held to account, and new ones appointed only with care. Those who labour in preaching and teaching deserve generous support, as the law and the Lord Jesus both say (vv. 17–18). No charge against an elder stands without two or three witnesses, but one who persists in sin is rebuked before all (vv. 19–20), and Timothy is solemnly charged to judge without favouritism (v. 21). He must not lay hands on anyone in haste (v. 22), and in the middle of it all Paul stops to care for his friend’s health (v. 23). Patience is possible because nothing stays hidden: sins and good works alike will come to light (vv. 24–25).
verseByVerse.theology:
A Gospel Quoted as Scripture

Verse 18 introduces both Deuteronomy 25:4 and a saying of Jesus recorded at Luke 10:7 with ‘the Scripture says’ (on what that shows, see the note on vv. 17–18).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: An elder is protected from loose accusations (v. 19), but not from open rebuke if he persists in sin (v. 20); a church needs both verses (see the note on vv. 19–20).

Now: Verse 23 shows Paul correcting a good man who was being stricter with himself than God required, and verse 25 promises that unrecorded goodness cannot stay hidden.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the elders who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching. For the Scripture says, "You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain," and, "The laborer deserves his wages."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elders who lead well, especially those who work hard at preaching and teaching, deserve generous honour, pay included, as both the law and the words of Jesus teach.

The elders who rule well. Honour links these elders to the widows of verse 3. Chapter 3 said what an elder must be; this passage, how the church treats one. Rule (proistēmi) is the household word of 3:4, with a father’s care in it. Not all lead equally well; those who do deserve recognition.

Double honour. Honour included money in verse 3, and both quotations that follow are about paying workers, which settles it. Double probably means ample, or honour in two forms, respect and pay (see the uncertain wording below).

Preaching and teaching. Labour (kopiaō) is work to the point of exhaustion; whatever pulpit work looks like from a pew, it is not restful. All elders must be able to teach (3:2), but “especially” implies that some give themselves particularly to the word, and these deserve support.

Do not muzzle an ox. The first quotation is from the law (Deuteronomy 25:4): oxen treading out the grain must be free to eat as they work. As in 1 Corinthians 9:9–11, if God cares that an ox is fed from its labour, how much more those who labour in the gospel.

The labourer deserves his wages. The second is not from the Old Testament at all, but the words of Jesus recorded in Luke 10:7 (compare Matthew 10:10). On the most natural reading, “the Scripture says” covers both, so Paul sets a saying of Jesus, apparently in its written form in Luke, beside Deuteronomy and calls both Scripture. Some take the second line as a proverb simply added on, and those who date the letter after Paul read it differently. But if Paul wrote it, as this commentary holds (see the introduction), it is one of the earliest signs that the words of Jesus were already received as Scripture, stated without argument. Peter does the same with Paul’s letters (2 Peter 3:16). The voice from Sinai and the voice of the Lord Jesus are bound by the one Spirit into one Scripture, the voice of the same God.

The Lord of the harvest pays his workers. Jesus spoke it as he sent out the seventy-two (seventy in some manuscripts and the KJV), telling them to pray to the Lord of the harvest for labourers and to eat what the houses that received them provided (Luke 10:2, 7). The workers and the harvest were his, and their bread was to come from the people they served. A church that supports its preachers is not hiring staff or doing them a kindness: the risen Lord is feeding the men he sent, through the people he sent them to, and he himself called it wages.

In everyday life. Write your pastor a note naming one specific way God has used his preaching in your life. A single sentence of specific thanks can carry a tired man for a month.

How much should a church pay its pastor? Scripture gives no figure but a spirit: ample, not grudging. A good test is whether he can live without distraction at a level comparable to his people, provide for his family (5:8), offer hospitality (3:2) and buy books, without luxury or anxiety. A church that keeps its minister poor to keep him humble has misread this verse, and so has a minister who demands more than his people can bear. And honour is more than money: respect, prayer, encouragement and a willingness to be taught.

Where Christians differ: teaching and ruling elders. The “especially” implies that some elders laboured in preaching and teaching and some did not, or not to the same degree. Presbyterian churches speak of teaching elders (ministers) and ruling elders; many Baptist and independent churches speak simply of elders, some of whom are set apart and paid to preach. This commentary’s view: both read the verse honestly and agree on what it teaches: there is one office of elder, all elders must be able to teach, and some give themselves especially to the word and should be supported to do it. The finer details of government this text does not settle.

Uncertain wording. Double honour may mean twice the support given to widows (v. 3), twice that of other elders, simply ample support, or honour in two forms, respect and pay. What is clear is that the support is generous, not grudging, and includes money (v. 18).
verseByVerse.note: The two sayings come from Deuteronomy and from Jesus’ words as recorded in Luke, a sign that the Gospels were already being received as Scripture.

parallels.desc: You shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain

verseByVerse.quote: Do not admit a charge against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses. As for those who persist in sin, rebuke them in the presence of all, so that the rest may stand in fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An accusation against an elder must be established by two or three witnesses, but an elder who goes on sinning is to be rebuked publicly, so that others take warning.

A charge against an elder. A man in public office is a target; accusations cost the accuser nothing and can end a ministry before anything is established. So Timothy is not to act on one person’s word.

Two or three witnesses. The law’s rule (Deuteronomy 19:15), applied by Jesus to church discipline (Matthew 18:16) and by Paul (2 Corinthians 13:1): not indifference to wrongdoing but ordinary justice. A church that ignores it will destroy good men on rumour.

Those who persist in sin. But the protection is no shelter for sin. The verb’s form means those who keep on sinning after being dealt with, most likely elders, though perhaps any member. This is not a first response.

In the presence of all. Rebuke (elenchō) means expose, convict, reprove; in the presence of all means before the church, or possibly before the other elders. A leader’s sin affects the whole church, so the correction is equally public. That reverses the instinct to protect the institution by settling it quietly and moving the man on. It is sobering, not cruel: it comes only after private warnings have been refused, and it aims at the man’s repentance and the flock’s safety, not his ruin (Galatians 6:1).

That the rest may stand in fear. Leaders are accountable (James 3:1). Hold the two verses together: an elder is hard to accuse, and his office is no place to hide. A church that keeps only verse 19 makes leaders untouchable; one that keeps only verse 20 lets any grievance ruin a man.

The trial where the rule was broken. At the trial of Jesus the chief priests sought testimony against him and found none; many bore false witness, and their testimony did not agree (Mark 14:55–59). The one wholly innocent man was condemned in the end for his own confession that he is the Christ (Mark 14:61–64). A church that refuses to condemn on rumour honours a Lord who knows false accusation from the inside; one that openly rebukes persistent sin honours him too, for he is the church’s holy Head. He was also openly shamed: stripped, mocked and lifted up in the presence of all, as if he were the one who had persisted in sin. He bore that public rebuke for the hidden and the open sins of his people, so that those who come to him may stand before God without fear, and need never hide again.

What it does not mean. Not that elders are above correction; the opposite. Nor that a report of abuse may be dismissed for lack of witnesses (see below), for civil authorities must be involved in criminal matters (Romans 13:1–4). The principle is careful justice, protecting both the accused and the vulnerable.

I have been harmed by a church leader and there were no other witnesses. Will I be believed? You should be heard, carefully and seriously, and this verse must never be used to silence you. The rule of two or three witnesses concerns what establishes a charge, not whether a report may be made or investigated. Abuse usually happens in private, and evidence is more than eyewitnesses: patterns of behaviour, others who come forward, messages, records. If a crime is involved, report it to the police; the church must not handle criminal abuse internally, and should help you report it. Speak to another elder or a trusted leader outside the situation. God defends the oppressed, and a church that protects an abuser to protect its reputation has abandoned this very passage.

What should I do if I hear an accusation against my pastor? Do not repeat it. Ask whoever brings it whether they have spoken to the person or to the other elders, and encourage them to, or to go to the authorities if it is criminal. If you have a concern yourself, take it to the elders, not to the congregation or social media. Then pray, and wait for a fair process. Being slow to believe an accusation is not refusing to believe it; it is letting the truth be established before you act, as you would want done for yourself.

parallels.desc: on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses

verseByVerse.quote: In the presence of God and of Christ Jesus and of the elect angels I charge you to keep these rules without prejudging, doing nothing from partiality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul solemnly charges Timothy, as before God, Christ Jesus and the angels, to apply these rules to everyone alike, deciding nothing in advance and favouring no one.

In the presence of God. One of the two most solemn sentences in the letter (the other is 6:13). I charge (diamartyromai) is solemnly testify, an oath-like formula (2 Timothy 4:1): Paul swears Timothy in, as a witness is sworn, and names three parties watching. The surprising one is the angels. The elect angels are those who did not fall with Satan, kept by God’s choice (contrast 2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6); Paul speaks of angels as observers of church life (1 Corinthians 4:9; 11:10; Ephesians 3:10), and they will come with Christ at the judgment (Matthew 25:31). It is a courtroom with an unseen gallery. They watch the little church in Ephesus, and the little church you belong to, because there the manifold wisdom of God is on display.

Without prejudging, doing nothing from partiality. Prejudging (prokrima) is having decided in advance; partiality (prosklisis) is literally leaning toward. Do not favour friends, the wealthy, the influential or those you like, for God shows no partiality (Deuteronomy 1:17; Romans 2:11; James 2:1–9). Why such weight? Timothy will like some elders and find others difficult, and when a charge comes in he will know before he hears it which way he wants it to go; that is what Paul puts him under oath about. Rules are easy to keep when the accused is a stranger; the test is the case where you already know whose side you are on, and Paul’s answer is not a better procedure but a reminder of who is watching.

Before Christ Jesus, the Judge without favourites. In his last letter Paul repeats the oath and names Christ Jesus as the one who is to judge the living and the dead (2 Timothy 4:1). Timothy must judge without partiality because the Lord watching him has none. Even his enemies, meaning to trap him, told him that he was true and was not swayed by appearances (Mark 12:14). It was flattery, and it was exactly right. He welcomed a despised tax collector and let a rich man walk away sorrowful, and in each case he looked at the heart. A church leader who refuses favouritism is copying his Lord.

In everyday life. Look today for where you have already decided before you have heard, about a colleague, a relative, someone in church you find difficult, and go and hear the other side.

What does it mean that angels are elect? God chose and kept some angels from falling when Satan and others rebelled: even in heaven, those who stand, stand by grace. But the elect angels never fell and needed no Saviour; elect sinners fell and were redeemed by Christ, who became man, not angel, to save us. That is why the angels look on the church with wonder (Ephesians 3:10; 1 Peter 1:12). They have always seen God’s power and holiness; in us they see his mercy.

How do I avoid partiality when someone I love is involved? Admit the bias first; you cannot correct what you will not name. Hear both sides fully before forming a view, ask what you would conclude if the names were reversed, and involve others without your attachment; in church matters a leader close to someone involved should often step back. Fairness is not coldness; it is loving everyone involved, including the person who is not your friend, enough to give them the same justice.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be hasty in the laying on of hands, nor take part in the sins of others; keep yourself pure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not appoint anyone to leadership in a hurry, for whoever sets a man apart shares responsibility for what he does; keep yourself clear of that.

Do not be hasty in the laying on of hands. In context, ordination: the public act by which the church sets a man apart, as the elders did for Timothy (4:14; see the uncertain wording below). It picks up 3:6 (not a recent convert) and 3:10 (first tested). Ephesus needed leaders, and some of its existing teachers were part of the problem, so the temptation to fill posts fast would have been considerable. Paul says no. That pressure is usually a matter of the heart: a church that wants to look successful, or a leader who wants to be rid of a burden, will see gifts and overlook character, because gifts can be put to work at once.

The sins of others. Take part (koinōneō) means be a partner: a man who ordains hastily is implicated in what the ordained man does, because he put him there (2 John 11). He cannot later plead ignorance; with proper testing (3:10) he often could have known, and haste is itself the fault.

Keep yourself pure. Pure (hagnos): free from complicity in others’ sins, and personally holy. Holiness is often kept or lost in decisions that look like mere procedure.

The Lord who chose after a night of prayer. Before he chose the twelve, Jesus spent the whole night in prayer to God (Luke 6:12–13). He knew all hearts and still did not hurry; the church, knowing far less, has more reason to wait, for haste presumes to know the choice of the ascended Christ, who gives shepherds to his church (Ephesians 4:11), before he has shown it. And this is our comfort: the Head of the church is never deceived, and he keeps his church even through our mistakes.

In everyday life. Before you recommend someone, for a church post, a job or a reference, take time to know them well: your endorsement is a responsibility.

What it does not mean. A church that acted with care is not guilty of the sin of a man who later fell. Nor must we keep away from sinners; Jesus ate with them (Luke 15:1–2).

How long should a church take before appointing someone? Scripture sets no period, but a principle: long enough for his character to be genuinely known (3:2–7, 10), usually years of observed faithfulness, not months of enthusiasm. A gifted speaker impresses quickly; self-control, a well-ordered home and gentleness are seen only over time. Talk to his wife and colleagues; watch how he handles disappointment and correction. The greater the responsibility, the longer the testing, and the same applies in proportion to youth leaders, small group leaders and anyone entrusted with the vulnerable.

Uncertain wording. The laying on of hands is not explained here. Most take it, as this commentary does, of appointing elders, since the setting is elders (vv. 17–20) and the phrase recalls Timothy’s own commissioning (4:14). Some read it of receiving back repentant sinners after discipline (v. 20), a practice found in the later church, but the context favours ordination.

verseByVerse.quote: No longer drink only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent ailments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy, who has been drinking only water, is to take a little wine for his health: purity does not require harming the body, and ordinary remedies are no failure of faith.

No longer drink only water. Medical advice, dropped into a passage about elders and discipline. The word (hydropotei) means be a water-drinker; Timothy apparently abstained from wine entirely, probably on principle. Paul has just told him to keep himself pure (v. 22), and the letter’s opponents were ascetics who forbade marriage and foods (4:3). A conscientious young minister, wanting to be above reproach and not a drunkard like the men excluded in 3:3, might well have given up wine to be safe, at some cost to a body already often unwell. Paul’s words show that purity does not require asceticism.

A little wine. Water was often contaminated, and wine was used medicinally (Luke 10:34). Paul does not argue theology; he prescribes. He is careful in both directions: “a little” gives no licence for heavy drinking, and he makes no rule that everyone must drink; those who abstain are not wrong (Romans 14:21).

Your frequent ailments. Timothy was often ill, and Paul answers with an ordinary remedy (compare Philippians 2:25–27).

A window into a friendship. In the middle of solemn instructions about elders, witnesses and the elect angels, Paul remembers that his friend is unwell and stops to say so, the same apostle who asked for his cloak and parchments (2 Timothy 4:13). Great theology and care for a body sit together without embarrassment. There is a lesson, too, for those whose conscience is stricter than God’s word. Timothy’s mistake was a good man’s mistake: trying to be blameless and overshooting into something that damaged him. Paul does not praise the strictness. He tells him to stop.

A high priest who knows weakness. The Son of God had a body that hungered (Matthew 4:2), slept exhausted in a boat (Mark 4:38) and thirsted on the cross (John 19:28). We have a high priest able to sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15), the word Paul uses for Timothy’s ailments. The Spirit who inspired the mystery of godliness also inspired a sentence about indigestion, so that we would never think our bodies, or the humble remedy (Psalm 104:15), beneath his notice. And the Lord who bore our griefs will raise these weak bodies in power, with no more frequent ailments, no more pain and no more death.

In everyday life. If you have been putting off a doctor’s appointment because it feels unspiritual to worry about yourself, make it. And if a rule you have taken on is quietly harming you, ask a wise friend whether it is godliness or needless strictness.

Why did Paul not simply heal Timothy? The apostle through whom God did extraordinary miracles (Acts 19:11–12) did not heal at will: he prescribes a remedy for his closest friend, and left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). God does not always heal miraculously, illness is not always a sign of sin or weak faith, and using medicine is no lack of trust. The apostles’ miracles were signs confirming the message in the founding era (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). Christians differ on whether gifts of healing like theirs continue; this commentary holds that those signs belonged to the founding era, while honouring brothers who expect them now. We pray for the sick, and God often answers, sometimes beyond what doctors expect (James 5:14–15); but we also take the medicine, and both are ways of looking to him.

I am often unwell, like Timothy. Does it mean God is displeased with me, or that I am less useful? No. Timothy was one of the most trusted men in the apostolic church, and he was frequently ill. Paul himself served with a thorn in the flesh that God would not remove, because his power is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:7–10). Illness can limit what you do, and that is a real grief, but it does not lower your standing before God or your worth to his church. Use the means: rest, see the doctor, take what helps. Bring the weakness to God honestly, and serve as your strength allows; prayer offered from a sickbed is not second-class ministry.

verseByVerse.quote: The sins of some people are conspicuous, going before them to judgment, but the sins of others appear later. So also good works are conspicuous, and even those that are not cannot remain hidden.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some people’s sins are plain at once and others come out later, and so with good works: nothing stays hidden for ever, so Timothy need not appoint in haste or overlook quiet faithfulness.

The sins of some people are conspicuous. These verses return to choosing elders (v. 22). Conspicuous (prodēlos) means obvious beforehand: some people’s sins walk ahead of them like heralds, reaching the court before the accused does.

The sins of others appear later. They follow behind and catch up eventually. Paul admits his careful procedure will not catch everything, but instead of tightening the rules he offers the assurance no procedure can give: nothing stays hidden, if not in this life then at the judgment. That is why haste is unnecessary as well as unwise.

Cannot remain hidden. Verse 25 turns it round. Some goodness is visible; much is not, and it cannot stay hidden either (Matthew 6:4). Timothy should not overlook a modest, faithful man because his virtues are not on display; like the widow’s unrecorded work (v. 10), it is not lost. Both records are being kept, and both will be read out.

Brought to light by Christ Jesus. God judges the secrets of men by Christ Jesus (Romans 2:16), and the Lord, when he comes, will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness (1 Corinthians 4:5). The eyes that will read both records are those of the risen Christ, which John saw like a flame of fire (Revelation 1:14; 2:23). That is sobering for the hypocrite, who has hidden his sins from every committee but not from him, and deep comfort for the faithful whom nobody noticed, because the Judge is the Lord who watched a widow put two small coins into the offering box and said she had put in more than all the rest (Mark 12:41–44).

In everyday life. Hold on to this if your faithfulness has gone unnoticed and someone else got the credit. And if there is something you hope will never come out, bring it to the God who has already covered it in Christ, and if it involves someone you have wronged, begin to put it right.

If all my sins will come to light, should I be afraid of the judgment? Not if you are in Christ. For the believer, those sins were judged at the cross, and there is now no condemnation (Romans 8:1); that day will show what grace forgave, not a debt still owing. So the best thing to do with hidden sin is to bring it into the light now: confess it to God, and where it is wise and fitting, to a trusted believer (James 5:16; 1 John 1:7–9). Hidden sin festers; confessed sin is cleansed. What should alarm us is not the light but the hope that we can keep anything from it.

Uncertain wording. Going before them to judgment could mean the church’s assessment of a candidate for office or God’s final judgment. The setting (v. 22) suggests the first and the wording the second, and Paul may have both in mind: what the church does not see now, God will expose.

5.text: <sup>1</sup>Do not rebuke an older man but encourage him as you would a father, younger men as brothers,<sup>2</sup>older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in all purity.<sup>3</sup>Honor widows who are truly widows.<sup>4</sup>But if a widow has children or grandchildren, let them first learn to show godliness to their own household and to make some return to their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God.<sup>5</sup>She who is truly a widow, left all alone, has set her hope on God and continues in supplications and prayers night and day,<sup>6</sup>but she who is self-indulgent is dead even while she lives.<sup>7</sup>Command these things as well, so that they may be without reproach.<sup>8</sup>But if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.<sup>9</sup>Let a widow be enrolled if she is not less than sixty years of age, having been the wife of one husband,<sup>10</sup>and having a reputation for good works: if she has brought up children, has shown hospitality, has washed the feet of the saints, has cared for the afflicted, and has devoted herself to every good work.<sup>11</sup>But refuse to enroll younger widows, for when their passions draw them away from Christ, they desire to marry<sup>12</sup>and so incur condemnation for having abandoned their former faith.<sup>13</sup>Besides that, they learn to be idlers, going about from house to house, and not only idlers, but also gossips and busybodies, saying what they should not.<sup>14</sup>So I would have younger widows marry, bear children, manage their households, and give the adversary no occasion for slander.<sup>15</sup>For some have already strayed after Satan.<sup>16</sup>If any believing woman has relatives who are widows, let her care for them. Let the church not be burdened, so that it may care for those who are truly widows.<sup>17</sup>Let the elders who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching.<sup>18</sup>For the Scripture says, "You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain," and, "The laborer deserves his wages."<sup>19</sup>Do not admit a charge against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses.<sup>20</sup>As for those who persist in sin, rebuke them in the presence of all, so that the rest may stand in fear.<sup>21</sup>In the presence of God and of Christ Jesus and of the elect angels I charge you to keep these rules without prejudging, doing nothing from partiality.<sup>22</sup>Do not be hasty in the laying on of hands, nor take part in the sins of others; keep yourself pure.<sup>23</sup>No longer drink only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent ailments.<sup>24</sup>The sins of some people are conspicuous, going before them to judgment, but the sins of others appear later.<sup>25</sup>So also good works are conspicuous, and even those that are not cannot remain hidden.

keyVerse.quote: Do not rebuke an older man but encourage him as you would a father, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in all purity.
keyVerse.note: These verses set the frame for the whole chapter: the church is a family, so every relationship in it, with the old and the young, with widows and with elders, is governed by the honour and care that fit a household. They also show how such a family corrects its members, gently and with complete purity. Behind them stands Jesus, who looked at those gathered round him and called them his mother and his brothers and sisters.

5.reflection:
Paul tells Timothy to treat the church as family: fathers, mothers, brothers and sisters (vv. 1–2). Which of these relationships is weakest in your church, and what would it look like to strengthen it this month?

Paul calls caring for parents and relatives godliness, and says that neglecting them denies the faith (vv. 4, 8). Why does he speak so strongly? What makes this hard in our culture, and how does the way Christ has provided for us change our motives?

The widow on Paul’s list is known for things nobody wrote down: hospitality, washing feet, caring for the afflicted (v. 10). Who are the quiet servants in your church, and how could you honour them? Where are you tempted to serve in order to be seen?

Verses 19–21 guard leaders against both rumour and cover-up, and demand judgment without favouritism. How should a church respond when a leader is accused, and where are you most tempted to decide before you have heard?

6.title: Godliness with Contentment Is Great Gain
6.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 6 closes the letter. It finishes the household instructions begun in 5:1 with a word to slaves, returns one last time to the false teachers of chapter 1, and ends with Timothy’s charge, the deposit he must guard, and grace.

The message. Godliness is not a way to get rich; godliness with contentment is itself the great gain. The false teachers had turned religion into a business. Against them Paul sets a man of God who runs from that love, fights for the faith and keeps his charge until Christ appears, and rich believers who hope in the God who richly provides and become rich in good works. Over it all stands the blessed and only Sovereign, who alone has immortality.

Why it was said. The error at Ephesus (see the introduction) had a hidden motive: its teachers were “imagining that godliness is a means of gain” (v. 5). Their quarrels had left a church full of envy and suspicion. The congregation held both wealthy members and slaves, some owned by believers, and each needed to know how the gospel touched their place in life. Timothy, young and under pressure, needed a last charge to hold on to.

How the chapter makes its case. Slaves are to honour their masters so that God’s name is not reviled (vv. 1–2). The false teacher is diagnosed by his conceit, his quarrels and his profit motive (vv. 3–5). Paul answers with the true gain of contentment (vv. 6–8) and warns that the desire to be rich drowns people (vv. 9–10). Timothy must flee, pursue and fight, keeping his charge as Christ kept his before Pilate (vv. 11–14), and the thought of Christ’s appearing lifts Paul into praise (vv. 15–16). The rich are told how to use their wealth (vv. 17–19), and Timothy to guard the deposit (vv. 20–21).

Where it leads. At the centre of a chapter about money stands a Person. Christ Jesus made the good confession before Pontius Pilate, the true King bound before a governor, and at the proper time God will display him as King of kings and Lord of lords. The God of unapproachable light has come near in him; and he who was rich became poor for our sake (2 Corinthians 8:9), so that in him we might take hold of “that which is truly life” (v. 19).

For us. Most readers of this chapter are among “the rich in this present age” (v. 17). It asks what we hope in, and whether we could lose what we have and still be content. Its cure is not a grim rule but a greater treasure: the God who gives us everything to enjoy, and his Son who gave himself.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The good name of the gospel can rest in the hands of a slave. Christians under a yoke are to honour their masters, so that outsiders do not slander God and the teaching because of them (v. 1). Those whose masters are believers must not presume on the brotherhood but serve all the better, because the one who benefits is a brother, believing and beloved (v. 2). So Paul finishes the household instructions begun in 5:1 with the concern that runs through them all: in every relationship, keep the gospel from reproach.
verseByVerse.theology:
What Paul Does and Does Not Say

Paul gives slaves a reason for their conduct: the honour of God’s name (see the note on vv. 1–2). Read it beside his condemnation of slave-trading (1:10) and his plea for Onesimus as a beloved brother (Philem 16), and see the box “Where Christians differ: does the New Testament approve of slavery?” at the end of the note on vv. 1–2.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Equality in Christ, Paul says, should make a slave serve a believing master better, not worse (v.2).

Now: On how long that change took, and where abolition came from, see the box “Where Christians differ” at the end of the note on vv. 1–2.

verseByVerse.quote: Let all who are under a yoke as bondservants regard their own masters as worthy of all honor, so that the name of God and the teaching may not be reviled. Those who have believing masters must not be disrespectful on the ground that they are brothers; rather they must serve all the better since those who benefit by their good service are believers and beloved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christian slaves are to honour their masters, so that God’s name and the gospel are not slandered because of them. Those whose masters are believers are to serve them all the better, not less, because the one who benefits is a brother.

Honour, to the end. These verses finish the household instructions of chapter 5, tied together by one word: widows honoured (5:3), elders worthy of double honour (5:17), masters worthy of all honour (6:1). In every relationship the question is what will keep the gospel from reproach.

Under a yoke. “Under a yoke” (hypo zygon) pictures servitude and burden, and “bondservants” (douloi) are slaves. Paul does not pretend the condition is light: he names it a yoke, the word for what God broke when he brought Israel out of Egypt and made them walk upright (Leviticus 26:13).

Worthy of all honor. “Masters” (despotai) are owners; our word despot comes from it. “All honor” (pasēs timēs) is full respect, owed even to unbelieving masters.

Not be reviled. “Reviled” (blasphēmeō) means slandered, blasphemed. If Christian slaves were rebellious or lazy, outsiders would say that Christianity destroys social order (Titus 2:9–10). The slave’s reason for honouring his master is not that the owner deserves it or that the arrangement is just. The reputation of God is, astonishingly, in the hands of a slave: the man with the least standing in Ephesus is entrusted with the honour of the highest name in the universe.

Not be disrespectful. “Disrespectful” (kataphroneō) means despise, look down on. Some had reasoned, understandably: he is my brother, so I need not work hard for him. Paul affirms the equality in the same breath, calling the master a brother, believing and beloved; but spiritual equality does not cancel earthly responsibilities.

Serve all the better. Serve them even more (mallon douleuetōsan). And there is a quiet revolution in the word beloved. The slave is told to see his owner as one whom God loves; the owner, hearing the same letter read aloud in the same room, is being told that his slave is his brother.

The setting. Slavery was everywhere in the Roman world; on some estimates a third of the population of a city like Ephesus were slaves, though the figures are uncertain. It was not based on race, and many slaves were educated and skilled, could own property and could hope for freedom; but legally they were property and could be cruelly treated. The church held slaves and masters as brothers in Christ (Galatians 3:28; Philemon 16), some slaves had Christian owners, and some may have thought, perhaps encouraged by the false teachers, that equality in Christ freed them from duty. A call for immediate abolition would very likely have been crushed as rebellion, as the slave revolt under Spartacus had been, and the gospel heard as a call to arms rather than as good news about Christ.

Serving the Lord Christ. In his letters to Colossae and Ephesus Paul gives slaves the deepest reason of all: work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward, for you are serving the Lord Christ (Colossians 3:23–24; Ephesians 6:5–8). To people who by law could inherit nothing, that was astonishing. Their owner was not their final master, so they could serve wholeheartedly without grovelling, offering every honest day’s work to a Lord who sees it and will reward it.

Sold for the price of a slave. The Lord of glory took the form of a doulos. He who owned the universe was sold for the price of a slave, thirty pieces of silver, and he washed feet. He is the Master in heaven who shows no partiality, and the Redeemer who buys slaves to set them free. In his house there are no slaves, only sons and daughters, and the slave who reveres his name in a Roman kitchen will sit at the marriage supper of the Lamb beside kings.

In everyday life. You already serve the Lord Christ, who bought you and sees what no manager sees; work today for him. Watch the moment when you are tempted to do less because no one will check, or because your manager is a Christian and will understand. Do the job well, speak well of the people above you, and let your work be the sermon your colleagues actually hear.

Does this mean I must put up with an abusive boss? No. An employee is not a slave: you are free to leave, to complain through proper channels and to seek justice, and you should when you are mistreated (1 Corinthians 7:21 shows Paul valued freedom where it was available). What carries over is the attitude: honest work and respect for those in authority, without sulking, cutting corners or badmouthing them. But respect is not complicity. Never do what is sinful because you are told to (Acts 5:29), and report harassment, abuse or illegal practice rather than enduring it in silence. Working well and standing up for what is right both keep God’s name from being reviled.

What about slavery and trafficking today? Christians must oppose it with all their strength. Modern slavery, forced labour, debt bondage and sex trafficking are exactly the kidnapping that God’s law punished with death (Exodus 21:16) and the slave-trading that Paul condemns in this very letter (1:10); nothing here gives them cover. Pray, support organisations that rescue and restore victims, ask where the goods you buy come from, and refuse to look away when something seems wrong in your community. The gospel that made Onesimus a beloved brother still sets captives free.

Where Christians differ: does the New Testament approve of slavery? Critics have accused the Bible of endorsing slavery, and slaveholders once used such texts to defend it. This commentary’s view: The New Testament regulates an institution it did not create and could not abolish by decree, while planting the principles that would undermine it. It condemns slave-trading (1:10), tells slaves to gain freedom if they can (1 Corinthians 7:21, on the most likely reading), commands masters to treat slaves justly and remember that they too have a Master (Ephesians 6:9; Colossians 4:1), and declares slave and free one in Christ (Galatians 3:28). Paul sends Onesimus back to Philemon “no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother” (Philemon 16). The race-based chattel slavery of later centuries, built on kidnapping, was condemned by Scripture’s own law (Exodus 21:16), and Christians who fought for abolition, like William Wilberforce, argued from these principles. That was the strategy: not a revolt that would have been drowned in blood, but a principle planted inside the institution that would eventually dissolve it. It took far too long, and for centuries Christians defended slavery by quoting verses like this one while ignoring 1:10 and Philemon, a grief and a shame to the church. But when abolition finally came, much of its moral force came from people arguing from this book.

Uncertain wording. The phrase translated “those who benefit by their good service” is compressed. The verb (antilambanomai) can mean receive a benefit but also devote oneself to something, and the noun (euergesia) usually means a kindness done by a benefactor; so some read the phrase as describing the masters as men devoted to doing their slaves good. Most translations, including the ESV, take it to mean the masters who benefit from their slaves’ good service, which fits the flow best. Either way, the master is a believer and beloved.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Religion turned into a business is a sickness, and its cure is contentment. Paul diagnoses the false teacher by his manner and his fruit: conceit, a craving for quarrels, a church left full of envy and suspicion, and beneath it all the belief that godliness pays (vv. 3–5). Then he takes their phrase and turns it round: godliness with contentment is great gain, for we leave the world as we entered it, and food and clothing are enough (vv. 6–8). The desire to be rich is a trap that drowns people, and the love of money has already drawn some away from the faith (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Root Beneath the Quarrels

The men behind the Ephesian error were making money from religion: they thought “godliness is a means of gain” (v.5). What their teaching produced was envy, quarrels and suspicion between people (v.4). The love of money is “a root of all kinds of evils” (see the note on vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul takes the false teachers’ word “gain” and says where it is really found: in godliness with contentment (v.6).

Now: Verse 9 warns those who desire to be rich, and a person can desire that on any income.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone teaches a different doctrine and does not agree with the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and the teaching that accords with godliness, he is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing. He has an unhealthy craving for controversy and for quarrels about words, which produce envy, dissension, slander, evil suspicions, and constant friction among people who are depraved in mind and deprived of the truth, imagining that godliness is a means of gain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A teacher who departs from Christ’s healthy words gives himself away by his conceit, his love of quarrels and the damage he leaves, and underneath he is using religion to make a profit. “Teaches a different doctrine” (heterodidaskalei) is the word of 1:3, so the letter ends where it began.

The sound words. “Agree with” (proserchomai) means adhere to, and “sound” (hygiainousi) is the medical word again: healthy. The “sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ” are either the teachings of Jesus himself or the apostolic gospel about him, which carries his authority. True doctrine produces spiritual health, and teaching is measured by the life it produces (“accords with godliness”), the letter’s yardstick since 1:5.

Puffed up with conceit. “Puffed up” (typhoō) is the inflation word again (3:6): swollen with air, or blinded by smoke. The pairing is deliberate: he thinks the most of himself and understands the least.

An unhealthy craving. Literally being sick (nosōn), the opposite of the sound teaching just named: an appetite that is itself a sickness. He does not merely tolerate argument; he needs it. “Controversy” (zētēseis) means speculative questions, as in 1:4, and “quarrels about words” (logomachias) are word-battles over technicalities, not substance (2 Timothy 2:14).

Envy, dissension, slander. Five words, and not one is a doctrinal error; all are damage done to relationships. “Envy” (phthonos) is jealousy. “Dissension” (eris) is strife, rivalry. “Slander” (blasphēmiai) is abusive speech. “Evil suspicions” (hyponoiai ponērai) are malicious suspicions, assuming the worst. “Constant friction” (diaparatribai) is mutual irritation, people rubbing against each other until the skin is raw. Paul judges the teaching by its wreckage: a congregation where people suspect each other and cannot stop arguing has a teaching problem, whatever is on its statement of faith.

Depraved in mind. “Depraved” (diephtharmenōn) means thoroughly corrupted; “deprived” (apestermenōn) means robbed. They once had access to the truth, but have been robbed of it, or have turned from it.

A means of gain. Then the root. “Means of gain” (porismos) is a source of profit, a money-making scheme. Beneath the genealogies and the quarrels was a business: these men had discovered that a reputation for spiritual insight brings money, standing and a following, and they taught for shameful gain (Titus 1:11). The danger reaches closer to home. Religion can be used for gain without any fee: for a reputation, for a sense of being better than others, or for a quiet bargain that if I am good, God owes me a good life. That too treats godliness as a means of gain, and the gospel ends it, because Christ is not a means to something else but the treasure himself (Philippians 3:8).

The words that make peace. The standard is not Paul’s own teaching but the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, carried by the men he sent, so that to hear them was to hear him (Luke 10:16). Set those words beside the five of verse 4. Jesus blessed the peacemakers (Matthew 5:9), washed his disciples’ feet, commanded them to love one another as he had loved them (John 13:34), and prayed that they would be one (John 17:21). A teaching that leaves envy, suspicion and friction behind it has wandered far from him. He never argued for the pleasure of winning, though he silenced every opponent; his truth bows the proud and lifts the humble, and it will be standing when every quarrel about words has fallen silent.

How can I tell the difference between defending the truth and loving controversy? Look at three things. The subject: is it something Scripture treats as central, such as the person of Christ, the gospel or the authority of the Bible, or a speculation Scripture does not settle? The manner: are you gentle, patient and willing to listen, or do you enjoy winning and look for the next fight (2 Timothy 2:24–25)? And the fruit: does the conversation leave people closer to Christ and to each other, or does it leave envy, suspicion and friction? A healthy defender of the faith would rather not argue, and does so for the sake of others; a lover of controversy would be lost without an opponent.

How do I recognise a teacher who is using religion for gain? Watch the money and the message together. Be wary when giving is tied to promised returns, when a teacher’s lifestyle is lavish and unaccountable, when pressure is applied to give more, or when the message flatters the wealthy and suits the teacher’s needs suspiciously well. Is there real accountability: elders, published finances, a church that can correct him? Gain need not be money; it can be fame, a platform or power over people. A faithful teacher can be paid (5:17–18), but he is not driven by it, and his teaching makes you want Christ, not him.

verseByVerse.quote: But godliness with contentment is great gain, for we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world. But if we have food and clothing, with these we will be content.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Godliness is itself great gain when it goes with contentment, for we leave the world as we entered it, and food and clothing are enough. Paul takes the false teachers’ phrase and turns it inside out.

Great gain. They imagined godliness was a means of financial gain; Paul says godliness is great gain, but only with contentment. “Contentment” (autarkeia) was a word the Stoic philosophers loved, and Paul gives it a new meaning. For the Stoic it meant self-sufficiency through inner strength, needing nothing outside yourself. For Paul it means having enough because of who supplies you: sufficiency in Christ (Philippians 4:11–13; 2 Corinthians 9:8).

We brought nothing. Paul gives two arguments, and the first is unanswerable (Job 1:21; Ecclesiastes 5:15). It is not a religious claim but an observation anybody can verify. We arrive naked and leave naked, and whatever a person accumulates is held for the middle stretch only. Why stake your life on what you cannot keep?

Food and clothing. The second argument names two items: not comfort or security, but food and covering (skepasmata, which can include shelter). With these we have enough to be content (Matthew 6:25–33). Paul is not saying it is wrong to have more; he will tell the rich that God gives us everything to enjoy (v. 17), which rules out asceticism. He is saying that everything above food and clothing is surplus, and a Christian should know it.
